Kutambua na kutumia msamiati wa lishe bora (mlo kamili, wanga, protini, vitamini, maji safi) na watoa huduma za afya (daktari, muuguzi, zahanati).
Kutambua na kutumia viambishi vya nyakati: wakati uliopo (-na-), wakati uliopita (-li-), na wakati ujao (-ta-) katika sentensi sahihi.
Kukanusha sentensi katika nyakati mbalimbali kwa kuzingatia viambishi sahihi vya kukanusha.
Kutambua na kutumia msamiati wa kibiashara (muuzaji, mnunuzi, soko, bei, faida, hasara, risiti, baki/chenji, mizani).
Kutambua noti na sarafu za Kenya na kueleza heshima na matumizi mazuri ya pesa bila ubadhirifu.
Kutunga na kubadilisha sentensi katika ngeli ya LI-YA kutoka umoja hadi wingi akizingatia viambishi vya 'li-' na 'ya-'.
Kutambua na kutumia msamiati wa wanyamapori (simba, tembo/ndovu, vifaru, chui, nyati, twiga, pundamilia, fisi) na hifadhi za kitaifa za Kenya.
Kutambua na kutumia vivumishi vya sifa (-kubwa, -dogo, -refu, -fupi, -kali, -zuri, -baya, -erevu) kwa upatanisho sahihi wa kisarufi.
Kueleza umuhimu wa wanyamapori, faida za utalii kwa uchumi wa Kenya, na kukemea ujangili na uharibifu wa makazi ya wanyama.
Kutambua na kutumia msamiati wa utunzaji wa mazingira (kitalu cha miti, miche, mbolea, mmomonyoko wa udongo, vyanzo vya maji, pipa la taka).
Kutambua na kubadilisha vitenzi kutoka kauli ya kutenda hadi kauli ya kutendwa (-wa-, -liwa-, -lewa-) kwa ufasaha.
Kueleza umuhimu wa kupanda na kutunza miti kwa kufuata mfano wa mashujaa wa mazingira kama vile Profesa Wangari Maathai.
Kutambua na kutumia msamiati wa vyombo vya usafiri (matatu, basi, treni ya SGR, kivukio/feri, baiskeli, tuktuk, ndege) na wahudumu wake (dereva, utingo/kondakta, nahodha, rubani).
Kueleza na kufuata kanuni za usalama barabarani (kivukio cha milia/zebra crossing, taa za trafiki, mkanda wa usalama, kutochungulia dirishani).
Kutambua na kutumia vihusishi vya mahali na mwelekeo (juu ya, chini ya, kando ya, mbele ya, nyuma ya, ndani ya, kati ya) kwa ufasaha katika sentensi.
Kutambua na kueleza msamiati wa haki za watoto (haki ya elimu, matibabu, ulinzi dhidi ya dhuluma, kutolazimishwa kufanya kazi ngumu) na wajibu wao.
Kutambua na kutumia viunganishi vya kisarufi (lakini, kwa sababu, ingawa, kwa hivyo, wala, au) kuunganisha sentensi mbili kwa mantiki sahihi.
Kueleza mpangilio wa barua ya kirafiki (anwani ya mwandishi, tarehe, maamkizi ya heshima, ujumbe/mwili, na hitimisho).
Distinguish between flowering plants (e.g. maize, beans, hibiscus) and non-flowering plants (e.g. ferns, mosses, conifers) in the local environment.
Identify common fungi such as edible mushrooms, toadstools, yeast, and bread mould, and understand their roles in nature.
Demonstrate safety precautions when handling plants and fungi, including wearing gloves and not eating wild, unidentified mushrooms.
Classify vertebrates into five main groups (mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, fish) based on observable characteristics and body coverings.
Identify common invertebrates in the local environment, with particular focus on insects (head, thorax, abdomen, six legs) and spiders.
Demonstrate safety measures when handling or observing animals, especially dangerous biting and stinging creatures such as bees, wasps, and scorpions.
Identify and describe the four types of human teeth: incisors (chisel-shaped for cutting), canines (pointed for tearing), premolars (ridged for grinding), and molars (broad for crushing).
Distinguish between temporary milk teeth (20 teeth) and permanent adult teeth (32 teeth), and understand the natural tooth shedding process in children.
Demonstrate proper tooth brushing techniques, identify causes of tooth decay (plaque and excess sugar), and care for oral health using both modern and traditional tools.
Identify and label the main organs of the human digestive system: mouth, gullet (oesophagus), stomach, small intestine, large intestine, rectum, and anus.
Explain the role of each digestive organ in mechanical breakdown, chemical digestion, and absorption of nutrients and water.
Demonstrate healthy habits that promote smooth digestion, including chewing food thoroughly, drinking sufficient water, and consuming dietary fibre (roughage).
Identify and describe four major types of environmental pollution: air, water, soil, and noise pollution, and cite common local sources.
Explain the harmful effects of environmental pollution on human health, crops, aquatic life, and animals.
Demonstrate practical methods of controlling pollution in the home and school, such as proper waste segregation, composting organic waste, and applying the 3Rs.
Identify natural and artificial sources of water in Kenya (rain, rivers, boreholes, dams, lakes) and explore domestic, agricultural, and industrial uses.
Demonstrate practical methods of water conservation, such as rainwater harvesting from roofs, repairing leaky taps, mulching, and using drip irrigation.
Construct and explain the operation of a simple layered water filter (gravel, coarse sand, fine sand, charcoal) and understand boiling and chemical treatment (WaterGuard).
Identify common digital devices found at home and school, such as laptops, tablets (DLP devices), desktop computers, smartphones, and digital cameras.
Classify computer hardware components into input devices (keyboard, mouse), processing unit (CPU/system unit), output devices (monitor, printer, speaker), and storage media (flash drive).
Demonstrate proper habits for handling and caring for digital equipment, including keeping liquids away, using dust covers, and safe shutdown.
Launch, interact with, and close basic digital applications such as text editors, drawing programs, digital cameras, and educational learning quests.

Demonstrate essential cyber safety practices, including keeping passwords secret, never sharing personal details (phone number, home location) with online strangers, and reporting suspicious online messages.
Practice digital ergonomics and balanced screen time, including sitting with an upright posture, keeping eyes at a comfortable distance, and taking regular breaks.
Identify and classify substances in the local environment into solids, liquids, and gases based on definite shape, volume, and ability to flow.
Investigate and explain the physical changes of state (melting, freezing/solidification, evaporation, and condensation) caused by adding or removing heat.
Demonstrate practical applications of changes of state in daily domestic and industrial activities, such as making ice blocks, drying laundry, boiling water, and observing morning dew.
Identify forces as pushes or pulls and demonstrate how force can move, stop, speed up, slow down, or alter the direction and shape of objects in daily life.
Investigate the effects of friction and gravity, identifying situations where friction is helpful or harmful, and demonstrating methods of reducing friction such as lubrication.
Identify and demonstrate the functioning of simple machines—including levers, inclined planes (ramps), and wheelbarrows—to make everyday work easier while observing tool safety.
Identify the importance of fertile topsoil in farming and describe common causes of soil erosion including running water, wind, and overgrazing.
Demonstrate practical soil conservation methods on agricultural land, including trash lines, mulching, cover crops, and contour grass strips.
Prepare and manage organic compost manure using crop residues, dry leaves, animal manure, and kitchen waste to enrich garden soil fertility.
Explain the importance of water for crop growth and identify reasons for conserving water during dry seasons in Kenya.
Construct and demonstrate innovative low-cost drip irrigation systems using perforated recycled plastic bottles and root mulching.
Apply efficient watering practices including early morning or evening irrigation routines, watering cans, and rooftop rainwater harvesting.
Prepare a fine-tilth nursery bed with fertile topsoil and organic compost, explaining why tiny seeds require a nursery bed rather than direct planting.
Demonstrate proper seed sowing techniques (shallow drilling, thin spreading, light soil covering, mulching) for vegetable crops such as kales, spinach, and tomatoes.
Care for emerging seedlings through routine watering, thinning, hand weeding, constructing shade canopies, and hardening off before field transplanting.
Demonstrate the proper procedure for transplanting hardened seedlings into prepared garden beds (late afternoon, root soil ball, watering before and after).
Carry out essential field management practices including spacing, mulching, watering, weeding, and earthing up around vegetable stems.
Identify common garden pests (cutworms, aphids, caterpillars) and demonstrate safe, eco-friendly pest control methods (hand-picking, wood ash, neem spray) and clean harvesting of leafy vegetables.
Explain the importance of container gardening for households with limited spaces, small homesteads, and urban environments.
Construct container gardens using recycled items such as buckets, crates, tyres, and plastic containers with proper drainage holes and soil mixes.
Construct and manage multi-storey vertical sack gardens using central gravel watering columns, staggered side slits, and routine watering.
Identify and classify common domestic animals reared in Kenyan communities (cattle, goats, sheep, poultry, rabbits, donkeys, camels).
Explain the domestic and economic benefits of farm animals including food production (milk, eggs, meat), manure for soil, wool, and draught power.
Demonstrate humane animal handling, proper carrying of small livestock (rabbits, poultry), and farm safety precautions around large animals.
Identify basic animal feed categories (fresh green forage, hay, commercial concentrates, mineral licks, clean water) and explain why animals need balanced diets.
Describe essential features of safe, hygienic shelters for domestic animals (clean ventilation, dry raised floors, predator protection for chicken coops and rabbit hutches).
Practice daily animal housing hygiene, waste clearance, parasite control (deticking, dusting against poultry mites), and recognizing symptoms of animal illness.
Identify and classify local Kenyan foods into the three major nutritional groups: energy-giving foods, body-building foods, and protective foods.
Plan and construct a balanced meal plate incorporating foods from all three groups, along with clean drinking water and dietary fibre.
Explain common nutritional deficiency disorders (kwashiorkor, marasmus, scurvy) and appreciate nutrient-dense indigenous Kenyan foods.
Demonstrate strict kitchen hygiene rules including washing hands with clean running water and soap, washing vegetables before slicing to conserve vitamins, and preventing cross-contamination.
Explain and practice simple, healthy cooking methods—including boiling, steaming, and roasting/baking—explaining why steaming preserves food nutrients best.
Observe essential kitchen safety rules when handling sharp tools (knives, peelers) and cooking fire appliances (jikos, gas stoves, hot sufurias).
Identify causes of food spoilage in homesteads (microorganisms, moisture, warmth, moulds, insect pests like maize weevils).
Demonstrate traditional and modern food preservation methods practiced in Kenyan communities—including sun-drying grains and vegetables, smoking fish, and hermetic PICS bags.
Practice proper granary hygiene, clean food storage on wooden pallets, meal planning to minimize leftover food wastage, and recycling food scraps into compost.
Identify the 4 cardinal compass directions (North, South, East, West) and 4 intermediate points (NE, SE, SW, NW) using sun position and magnetic compasses.
Identify the five key elements of a map (title, frame, key/legend, compass rose, scale) and explain their importance in reading geographical maps.
Draw simple sketch maps of the school compound or immediate neighbourhood showing key landmarks using map symbols and a key.
Identify relief features (mountains, hills, valleys, plains) and drainage features (rivers, lakes, swamps, oceans) in the local county and across Kenya.
Explain the importance of physical features to human life, farming, wildlife, and the county economy.
Demonstrate practical conservation measures to protect physical features like riverbanks, hillsides, and wetlands from degradation.
Identify elements of weather and explain the function and handling of meteorological instruments used in a school weather station.
Differentiate between day-to-day weather conditions and regional climate over an extended timeframe.
Describe how seasonal weather variations in Kenya (long rains March-May and short rains October-December) dictate agricultural calendars, clothing, and housing styles.
Group Kenyan communities into the three primary language groups: Bantus, Nilotes, and Cushites.
Describe the points of origin, migration routes, and county settlement locations of Kenyan communities.
Explain why our ancestors migrated (fertile soil, pasture, water, escaping diseases and drought) and promote peaceful inter-ethnic harmony.
Identify key components of culture including indigenous foods, traditional attire, folk music, dances, and vernacular architectural styles.
Categorize indigenous artifacts according to their utility in domestic life, agriculture, music, warfare, and cultural adornment.
Explain why and how Kenya's tangible and intangible cultural heritage is conserved for future generations.
Distinguish between subsistence crop farming and cash crop farming in Kenyan counties.
Identify key food crops (maize, beans, bananas) and commercial crops (tea, coffee, sugarcane, pyrethrum) and livestock types across Kenya.
Explain how agriculture generates employment, food security, and county revenue, and describe modern remedies for common farming hurdles.
Compare barter trade with modern monetary transactions using currency notes, coins, and mobile money.
Describe various trading facilities and market days operating across Kenyan sub-counties.
Demonstrate elementary financial management skills including budgeting pocket money, saving in piggy banks, and ethical trading.
Identify the four principal transport systems in Kenya and practice pedestrian road safety protocols.
Compare indigenous African methods of sending messages with contemporary electronic communication networks.
Explain how efficient transport corridors and digital networks support emergency services, commerce, and national integration.
Identify the structure and primary leaders of the County Government (Governor, Deputy Governor, Speaker, and MCAs).
Distinguish devolved county governance functions from National Government Administrative Officers (NGAO - County Commissioners, Chiefs).
Exemplify leadership values such as integrity, fairness, transparency, and accountability in school clubs and council elections.
Explain the concept of citizenship and how Kenyan citizenship is acquired by birth or registration.
Identify and honor Kenya's four National Symbols: the National Flag, National Anthem, Coat of Arms, and Public Seal.
Articulate the constitutional rights and corresponding responsibilities of children and demonstrate love and loyalty for Kenya.
Identify and apply fundamental elements of art (lines, geometric and organic shapes, texture, and form) in preliminary observational sketches.
Demonstrate four pencil shading techniques (cross-hatching, stippling, smudging/blending, and tonal gradation) to illustrate tonal contrast from light to dark.
Compose, sketch, and shade a balanced still life grouping of local Kenyan objects (traditional clay pot, calabash, and fresh fruits) incorporating light source and cast shadows.

lessons.title: Planting Rows with Amina
lessons.conceptIntro: Amina is helping her grandfather Mzee Juma plant sukuma wiki in their family shamba in Nakuru. Instead of counting seedlings one by one, she organizes them in tidy equal rows. When you have 5 rows and each row has 4 seedlings, multiplying 5 × 4 gives you the total of 20 seedlings in seconds!
lessons.kenyanContextNote: Sukuma wiki (collard greens) is grown in shamba plots across all 47 Kenyan counties.

keyVocabulary.meaning: The numbers you multiply together
The result of multiplication
A horizontal line of seedlings or items

lessons.didYouKnowKenyanFact: Nakuru County has some of the richest volcanic agricultural soils in the Great Rift Valley!

lessons.title: The Great Chapati Feast
lessons.conceptIntro: Imagine Mama Amina just cooked a hot, golden-brown chapati. Amina and her 3 cousins want an equal piece each. To be fair, Mama cuts the chapati straight across twice into 4 equal slices. Each slice is 1 out of 4 pieces, written as 1/4 (one quarter). If Juma eats 2 slices, he eats 2/4, which is the same as half (1/2) of the chapati!
lessons.kenyanContextNote: Sharing meals equally is an important Kenyan cultural value of Umoja and Undugu.

keyVocabulary.meaning: The top number showing how many pieces you have
The bottom number showing total equal parts
Fractions having the same value (like 2/4 and 1/2)

lessons.didYouKnowKenyanFact: Kenyan chapatis were influenced by maritime Indian Ocean trade and are celebrated during special gatherings!

lessons.title: Smart Shopper at Kongowea Market
lessons.conceptIntro: Baraka visits Kongowea Market in Mombasa to buy fresh fruits. A bunch of sweet bananas costs KES 80 and a fresh mango costs KES 40. Baraka calculates 80 + 40 = 120 shillings. He gives the trader a 200 shilling note. To find his change, he subtracts: 200 - 120 = 80 shillings!
lessons.kenyanContextNote: The Central Bank of Kenya issues coins featuring national wildlife and values.

keyVocabulary.meaning: The official currency of Kenya
Money returned to you after paying more than the cost
A plan of how you will spend your money wisely

lessons.didYouKnowKenyanFact: Kongowea Market in Nyali, Mombasa is one of the largest open-air food markets in East Africa!

lessons.title: The Miracle of the Maize Seed
lessons.conceptIntro: A dry maize seed looks sleeping, but inside is an embryo waiting to awaken. In our laboratory experiment, seeds kept without water never sprout. Seeds placed in a freezer without warmth stay dormant. But when seeds get clean water, fresh air, and warm sunlight, the radicle emerges downwards into the soil and the plumule reaches up towards the blue Kenyan sky!
lessons.kenyanContextNote: Maize is the staple food of Kenya, grown by millions of smallholder farmers.

keyVocabulary.meaning: The process of a seed beginning to grow into a plant
The first root that grows downwards
The seed leaf storing food for the baby sprout

lessons.didYouKnowKenyanFact: Kenya hosts the Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization (KALRO) developing climate-smart drought-resistant crops!

lessons.title: Market Day Subtraction with Juma at Kongowea
lessons.conceptIntro: Juma is helping his uncle count crates of sweet mangoes at Kongowea Market in Mombasa. In the morning, they received 486 crates. By mid-day, they had sold 234 crates to local fruit vendors. To find out how many crates are remaining, Juma subtracts place by place without regrouping: ones from ones (6 - 4 = 2), tens from tens (8 - 3 = 5), and hundreds from hundreds (4 - 2 = 2). They have 252 crates left!
lessons.kenyanContextNote: Kongowea Market in Mombasa is one of the largest open-air wholesale produce markets in East Africa.

keyVocabulary.meaning: The result when one number is subtracted from another
Taking away a number from another
The position of a digit showing its value (Hundreds, Tens, Ones)

lessons.didYouKnowKenyanFact: Kongowea market traders receive lorries of fresh mangoes from Kilifi, Kwale, and Kitui every morning!

lessons.title: Regrouping at the Kiosk with Amina
lessons.conceptIntro: Amina is working at her family's duka in Nakuru. She has 542 packets of maize flour on the shelves. A local school buys 268 packets for their lunch program. When Amina looks at the ones column (2 - 8), she cannot subtract 8 from 2! So she renames (regroups) 1 ten into 10 ones. Now 12 - 8 = 4 ones. In the tens column (3 - 6), she borrows 1 hundred to get 13 tens; 13 - 6 = 7 tens. Finally, 4 - 2 = 2 hundreds. Exactly 274 packets remain!
lessons.kenyanContextNote: Maize flour (unga wa mahindi) is a kitchen essential in homes and schools across Kenya for making ugali.

keyVocabulary.meaning: Exchanging 1 ten for 10 ones or 1 hundred for 10 tens when the top digit is smaller
The starting number from which another number is taken away
The number being taken away

lessons.didYouKnowKenyanFact: Nakuru is known for fertile farms that produce bumper maize harvests for the nation!

lessons.title: Planting Rows with Amina: Repeated Addition & Arrays
lessons.conceptIntro: Amina is helping her grandfather plant sukuma wiki in their shamba in Nakuru. She places 4 seedlings in each row. She has 3 rows. Instead of counting one by one (1, 2, 3...), she notices that 4 + 4 + 4 = 12. We can write this multiplication problem as 3 × 4 = 12! The first number (3) tells us how many rows or groups there are, and the second number (4) tells us how many items are in each row. The answer 12 is called the product!
lessons.kenyanContextNote: Sukuma wiki (collard greens) is grown in tidy nursery rows in homesteads and school gardens across Kenya.

keyVocabulary.meaning: An operation that combines equal groups
Adding the same number multiple times
Items arranged in neat rows and columns
keyVocabulary.swahiliTerm: Mfuatano wa safu na safu wima

lessons.didYouKnowKenyanFact: Kenyan farmers use spacing arrays to make sure each vegetable gets plenty of sunlight and water!

lessons.title: Multiplication Tables at the Duka with Mwangi
lessons.conceptIntro: Mwangi runs a busy fruit duka outside Gikomba market. He packs sweet ripe bananas in bunches of 5, and oranges in bags of 10. When a customer asks for 4 bunches of bananas, Mwangi calculates 4 × 5 = 20 bananas in a flash! Learning your 2, 3, 4, 5, and 10 times tables helps you calculate costs and inventory quickly without having to count each item.
lessons.kenyanContextNote: Fruit vendors at Gikomba and city markets often bundle fruits in groups of 3, 5, or 10 for easy pricing.

keyVocabulary.meaning: The answer to a multiplication problem
A number that is multiplied by another number
A set of multiplication facts for a particular number

lessons.didYouKnowKenyanFact: Counting in 5s and 10s is how shopkeepers count Kenyan coins and 50/100 shilling notes quickly!

lessons.title: Equal Sharing with Zawadi: What is Division?
lessons.conceptIntro: Zawadi has 12 sweet ripe mangoes from her grandmother's tree in Kitui. She wants to share them equally among her 3 cousins: Brian, Amina, and Juma. She gives 1 mango to each cousin at a time until all 12 are finished. Each cousin receives 4 mangoes! In mathematics, sharing 12 items equally among 3 people is written as 12 ÷ 3 = 4. The sign '÷' means divide or share equally. The number being shared (12) is the dividend, the number of groups (3) is the divisor, and each share (4) is called the quotient!
lessons.kenyanContextNote: Sharing fruits and meals fairly is a valued tradition in Kenyan families and communities.

keyVocabulary.meaning: Splitting a number into equal shares or groups
The total number being divided or shared
The answer or share in a division problem

lessons.didYouKnowKenyanFact: Division is the opposite (inverse) of multiplication! If 3 × 4 = 12, then 12 ÷ 3 = 4!

lessons.title: Repeated Subtraction & Dividing by 2, 3, 4, 5, and 10
lessons.conceptIntro: At a dairy cooperative in Nyandarua, Mwalimu Peter has 20 small packets of milk to pack into delivery bags of 5 packets each. How many bags does he need? He subtracts 5 again and again: 20 - 5 = 15 (bag 1), 15 - 5 = 10 (bag 2), 10 - 5 = 5 (bag 3), 5 - 5 = 0 (bag 4). He subtracted 5 four times, so 20 ÷ 5 = 4 bags! Division is repeated subtraction, just like multiplication is repeated addition!
lessons.kenyanContextNote: Dairy farmers in Nyandarua deliver fresh milk to community cooperative centers every morning.

keyVocabulary.meaning: Subtracting the same divisor until reaching zero to find the quotient
The number you divide by (the size or number of groups)
What is left over after dividing (in Grade 3 we focus on problems with zero remainder)

lessons.didYouKnowKenyanFact: Dividing by 2 is called halving, and dividing by 4 is called finding a quarter!

lessons.title: Sharing Chapatis with Halima: Parts of a Whole
lessons.conceptIntro: Halima's mother cooked warm, delicious chapatis in Mombasa. When Halima cuts 1 chapati into 2 equal pieces, each piece is called a half (written as 1/2). If she cuts each half again into 2 equal pieces, she gets 4 equal pieces! Each piece is a quarter (written as 1/4). If she cuts the 4 pieces once more into equal halves, she gets 8 equal slices! Each slice is one-eighth (written as 1/8). In a fraction, the bottom number (denominator) tells how many equal parts make the whole, and the top number (numerator) tells how many parts you have!
lessons.kenyanContextNote: Chapatis, mandazis, and watermelons are circular items commonly shared into halves and quarters in Kenyan kitchens.

keyVocabulary.meaning: An equal part of a whole or set
One of two equal parts
One of four equal parts
One of eight equal parts

lessons.didYouKnowKenyanFact: Two halves (1/2 + 1/2) make 1 whole chapati, and four quarters (1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4) make 1 whole chapati!

lessons.title: Fractions of a Group with Kiptoo at the Shamba
lessons.conceptIntro: Kiptoo is looking after a flock of 12 sheep in Eldoret. Half (1/2) of the sheep are white, and the other half are brown. To find 1/2 of 12 sheep, Kiptoo divides 12 by 2: 12 ÷ 2 = 6 white sheep! If he has 8 apples and gives a quarter (1/4) to his sister, he divides 8 by 4: 8 ÷ 4 = 2 apples. Finding a fraction of a set means dividing the total by the denominator!
lessons.kenyanContextNote: Counting and sorting livestock into equal pens is a real-life practice across pastoralist and farming counties in Kenya.

keyVocabulary.meaning: Finding equal shares of a group of items
The top number of a fraction showing chosen parts
The bottom number of a fraction showing total equal parts

lessons.didYouKnowKenyanFact: In Kenyan markets, vendors sell half a cabbage or a quarter of a watermelon when customers request smaller portions!

lessons.title: Measuring with Strides & Handspans with Achieng
lessons.conceptIntro: Achieng is measuring the length of the school playground in Kisumu. She counts 40 footsteps from the goalposts to the center line. Her friend Otieno walks the same distance and counts 36 footsteps! Why are their counts different? Because people have different foot and stride sizes! That is why footsteps, handspans, and paces are called non-standard units. They are useful for quick estimates, but people needed a standard unit that never changes.
lessons.kenyanContextNote: Traditional builders in Kenyan villages used arm spans (shubiri/fathoms) before adopting standard tape measures.

keyVocabulary.meaning: The distance from one end of an object to the other
Body measurements like handspans and strides that vary from person to person
A sensible guess close to the actual measurement

lessons.didYouKnowKenyanFact: Athletics tracks in Kenya (like Kasarani Stadium and Kipchoge Keino Stadium) are measured using exact standard meters!

lessons.title: The Standard Metre Rule with Fundi Omondi
lessons.conceptIntro: Fundi Omondi is a carpenter in Kisumu making wooden school desks. He uses a 1-metre wooden ruler (1 m). 1 metre is a standard unit of length accepted everywhere in Kenya and across the world. 1 metre is about the distance from the doorknob to the floor, or the width of a wide classroom window. We write 'm' for metre. Using standard metres ensures that desks, doors, and building timbers fit perfectly every time!
lessons.kenyanContextNote: Carpenters (mafundi) and tailors in Kenya carry wooden metre sticks and flexible measuring tapes for accurate craftwork.

keyVocabulary.meaning: The international standard unit for measuring length and distance
A straight measuring stick exactly one metre long
The measurement of how tall someone or something is

lessons.didYouKnowKenyanFact: A standard adult giraffe in Nairobi National Park can grow up to 5 metres tall!

lessons.title: Balancing Scales with Wanjiku: Heavier or Lighter?
lessons.conceptIntro: Wanjiku is helping at her mother's vegetable stall at Wakulima Market in Nairobi. She puts a big sweet pumpkin on one side of a simple beam balance, and 3 small red onions on the other side. The side with the pumpkin tilts downwards! That means the pumpkin is heavier than the onions, and the onions are lighter than the pumpkin. When both sides stay level in the middle, the two masses are equal (in balance)!
lessons.kenyanContextNote: Traditional beam balances and spring scales (mizani) are used in open-air markets across Kenya to weigh fresh produce.

keyVocabulary.meaning: The amount of matter or weight in an object
Having greater mass
Having less mass
A balancing tool with two pans used to compare mass

lessons.didYouKnowKenyanFact: Wakulima Market in Nairobi is the busiest early-morning fresh produce wholesale hub in Kenya!

lessons.title: The Standard Kilogram (kg) at the Duka with Juma
lessons.conceptIntro: Juma goes to the duka to buy 1 kilogram of sugar. The shopkeeper places a metal 1 kg block on one side of the scale, and scoops sugar into a brown paper bag until the scale balances perfectly. 1 kilogram (written as 'kg') is the standard unit of mass in Kenya. A 1 kg packet of unga, a 1 kg bag of rice, and a 1 kg block of metal all have the exact same mass: 1 kilogram!
lessons.kenyanContextNote: Packets of maize flour (unga wa mahindi) and rice sold in Kenyan supermarkets and kiosks typically weigh 1 kg or 2 kg.

keyVocabulary.meaning: The standard metric unit for measuring mass
An instrument for measuring mass
Having the exact same amount of kilograms

lessons.didYouKnowKenyanFact: A standard full burlap sack of dry maize in Kenya weighs 90 kilograms!

lessons.title: Water at the Well with Chebet: Holds More or Less?
lessons.conceptIntro: Chebet is fetching clean water with her yellow plastic jerrycan in Bomet. Her little brother has a small blue mug, while Chebet carries a 10-litre jerrycan. The jerrycan holds much more water than the mug! Capacity is the amount of liquid a container can hold when it is completely full. When Chebet fills 5 mugs with water, she notices they fill one cooking pot. The pot has a larger capacity than a single mug!
lessons.kenyanContextNote: Fetching water in yellow plastic jerrycans (mitungi) from rainwater tanks or community taps is a daily task in many Kenyan homesteads.

keyVocabulary.meaning: The amount of liquid a container can hold
Can hold a greater volume of liquid
Can hold a smaller volume of liquid
An object like a bottle, bucket, or pot used for holding liquids

lessons.didYouKnowKenyanFact: Water conservation is vital in Kenya! Turning off the tap while brushing teeth saves up to 5 litres of clean water!

lessons.title: The Standard Litre (l) at the Milk Kiosk with Amina
lessons.conceptIntro: Amina goes to the community milk ATM kiosk in Nakuru. She brings a clean 1-litre glass bottle. The machine dispenses fresh milk measured in standard litres. The standard unit for measuring capacity is the litre (written as 'l'). A standard packet of supermarket milk is half a litre (500 ml), so 2 small packets equal exactly 1 litre! Standard litres ensure that customers always get the exact amount of milk or cooking oil they pay for.
lessons.kenyanContextNote: Milk dispensing machines (Milk ATMs) are popular in Kenyan towns and suburbs for buying affordable fresh milk.

keyVocabulary.meaning: The standard metric unit for measuring liquid volume and capacity
A flowing substance like water, milk, or cooking oil
Filled to the very top without spilling

lessons.didYouKnowKenyanFact: A standard yellow water jerrycan (mtungi) in Kenya holds 20 litres of water!

lessons.title: Telling Time to the Hour & Half-Hour with Brian
lessons.conceptIntro: Brian looks at the round clock on the classroom wall in Nakuru. The clock face has two hands: a short hand that points to the hour, and a long hand that points to the minutes. When the long hand points straight up at 12, it is an exact hour (like 8:00 o'clock when the school bell rings!). When the long minute hand travels halfway around the circle and points straight down at 6, exactly 30 minutes have passed. We call this 'half past' the hour (for example, 8:30 or half past 8).
lessons.kenyanContextNote: School timetables across Kenya start at 8:00 AM, with morning tea break at 10:00 AM and lunch at 1:00 PM.

keyVocabulary.meaning: The short hand on a clock indicating the hour
The long hand on a clock showing minutes
30 minutes after an hour (long hand at 6)
An exact hour (long hand at 12)

lessons.didYouKnowKenyanFact: In Swahili time (saa za Kiswahili), counting starts at sunrise (7:00 AM is "saa moja asubuhi")!

lessons.title: Days of the Week & Months of the Year with Zawadi
lessons.conceptIntro: Zawadi checks the school calendar in her classroom. There are 7 days in a week: Monday (Jumatatu), Tuesday (Jumanne), Wednesday (Jumatano), Thursday (Alhamisi), Friday (Ijumaa), Saturday (Jumamosi), and Sunday (Jumapili). There are 12 months in a whole year! January is the first month when school terms begin, and December is the twelfth month when families celebrate end-of-year holidays. In Kenya, the long rains usually fall in April and May!
lessons.kenyanContextNote: The Kenyan primary school calendar has three terms, with holidays in April, August, and December.

keyVocabulary.meaning: A period of 7 days
A period of about 30 or 31 days (February has 28 or 29)
A chart showing days, weeks, and months of a year

lessons.didYouKnowKenyanFact: Mashujaa Day is celebrated on 20th October and Jamhuri Day is celebrated on 12th December across Kenya!

lessons.title: Kenyan Coins & Notes with Baraka
lessons.conceptIntro: Baraka is learning about Kenyan currency at school. Kenya's money is called the Kenyan Shilling (written as KES or Ksh). We use coins: 1 shilling, 5 shillings, 10 shillings, and 20 shillings. We also use colorful banknotes: green 50 shillings, yellow-orange 100 shillings, black/grey 200 shillings, grey/green 500 shillings, and maroon 1,000 shillings! Each note features unique national symbols such as Mount Kenya, agriculture, tourism, and the Kenyatta International Convention Centre (KICC).
lessons.kenyanContextNote: New-generation Kenyan currency notes feature Kenyan wildlife (lion, leopard, rhino, elephant, buffalo) and national heritage sites.

keyVocabulary.meaning: The official money used in a country
The value printed on a coin or note
The basic unit of money in Kenya

lessons.didYouKnowKenyanFact: The Central Bank of Kenya (CBK) in Nairobi is the only institution authorised to print Kenyan money!

lessons.title: Shopping & Calculating Change with Amina
lessons.conceptIntro: Amina goes to a duka with a 100-shilling note. She buys a packet of milk for KES 60. How much change should the shopkeeper hand back to her? Change is the money returned when you pay with more than the price. To find the change, Amina subtracts: 100 - 60 = 40 shillings! The shopkeeper hands her two 20-shilling coins (20 + 20 = 40). Checking your change carefully makes sure that shopping is always fair and accurate!
lessons.kenyanContextNote: Buying items and counting change at dukas, kiosks, and open markets is an essential practical life skill for Kenyan children.

keyVocabulary.meaning: Money returned when you pay more than the cost
The amount of money needed to buy an item
A plan for how much money you can spend

lessons.didYouKnowKenyanFact: Saving small coins in a piggy bank (kibuyu cha akiba) helps children buy school stationery and books!

lessons.title: Straight Lines with Baraka: Standing, Sleeping & Slanting
lessons.conceptIntro: Baraka is observing the lines in his classroom in Machakos. A straight line is the shortest path between two points. It never bends or wobbles! When a straight line stands straight up like a flagpole or the edge of a door, we call it a vertical line. When it lies flat like the horizon or a desk edge, it is a horizontal line. When it leans like a ladder against a wall, it is a slanting (diagonal) line! Using a ruler helps you draw clean, crisp straight lines every time.
lessons.kenyanContextNote: Straight lines form the painted white borders of football pitches and the chalk lines on classroom blackboards.

keyVocabulary.meaning: A line that extends in one direction without any curve or bend
A straight line standing upright from top to bottom
A straight line lying flat from side to side
A straight line leaning at an angle

lessons.didYouKnowKenyanFact: The railway tracks of the Kenya Standard Gauge Railway (SGR) run in parallel straight lines across the plains!

lessons.title: Curved Lines with Amina: Waves & Arches
lessons.conceptIntro: Amina watches the waves rolling gently onto the white sands of Diani Beach in Kwale. The waves form smooth, bending paths called curved lines! A curved line bends and turns smoothly without sharp corners. Rainbows in the sky, round wheels of a bicycle, banana contours, and the rim of a water cup are all examples of curved lines. In Kenyan beadwork and pottery, artists combine straight and curved lines to create stunning traditional patterns.
lessons.kenyanContextNote: Traditional Maasai bead necklaces and coastal earthenware pots showcase intricate combinations of curved and straight motifs.

keyVocabulary.meaning: A line that bends smoothly without sharp angles
A curved line that rolls up and down repeatedly
A closed curved line forming a round shape

lessons.didYouKnowKenyanFact: Traditional round thatched houses (manyattas) use flexible bent branches to form curved roof frames!

lessons.title: Exploring 2D Shapes with Otieno
lessons.conceptIntro: Otieno is looking for shapes around his home in Kisumu. The textbook cover has 4 straight sides and 4 square corners, with opposite sides equal—it is a rectangle! A samosa or road warning sign has 3 straight sides and 3 sharp corners—it is a triangle! A round coin and a chapati have 1 continuous curved boundary and zero corners—it is a circle! And a hen's egg viewed from the front is an oval (stretched circle). 2D shapes are flat figures with length and width.
lessons.kenyanContextNote: Road safety signs in Kenya use triangles for warnings, circles for orders, and rectangles for information.

keyVocabulary.meaning: A 4-sided flat shape where opposite sides are equal and parallel
A flat shape with 3 straight sides and 3 corners
A perfectly round flat shape with zero corners
An egg-like elongated curved shape

lessons.didYouKnowKenyanFact: The Kenyan national flag features a central Maasai shield that combines curved and straight geometric shapes!

lessons.title: Leso Patterns & Symmetry with Halima
lessons.conceptIntro: Halima's grandmother in Mombasa wears a vibrant leso (kanga). The border of the leso repeats a beautiful design: triangle, circle, triangle, circle! A pattern is a repeating arrangement of shapes, lines, or colors that follows a regular rule. When we know the rule, we can easily predict what comes next! Patterns are used in African textiles, basket weaving (ciondo), and beadwork across our country.
lessons.kenyanContextNote: Lesos and kiondo woven sisal baskets from Machakos and Kitui are famous worldwide for their intricate repeating patterns.

keyVocabulary.meaning: A repeating sequence of shapes, lines, or colors
The specific sequence that repeats
The point where two straight sides meet

lessons.didYouKnowKenyanFact: Kanga / leso cloths always feature an inspirational Swahili proverb (jina) printed along the bottom!

lessons.title: L-Blends in the School Yard with Wanjiku
lessons.conceptIntro: Wanjiku and her classmates in Nakuru are playing a sound game under the acacia tree. When two consonant sounds come together at the beginning of a word without a vowel between them, they form a blend! For example, when /b/ and /l/ hold hands, they make /bl/ as in black, blue, and blanket. When /c/ and /l/ meet, they say /cl/ as in clap, class, and clean. Both sounds are heard smoothly together. Let's practice saying: "The clean blue flag flies in the classroom!"
lessons.kenyanContextNote: Kenyan primary schools practice choral pronunciation and tongue-twisters to build oral fluency.

keyVocabulary.meaning: Two consonants sounded together where each individual sound is heard
The way in which a word or sound is spoken
The sound heard at the beginning of a word

lessons.didYouKnowKenyanFact: The Kenyan National Anthem is sung every Monday and Friday during school parades with clear pronunciation!

lessons.title: Polite Words at the Duka with Baraka
lessons.conceptIntro: Baraka is sent by his mother to buy salt at the neighbourhood duka. When the shopkeeper is talking to another customer, Baraka does not interrupt rudely. He waits and says politely, "Excuse me, Sir." When making his request, he says, "Please may I have a packet of salt?" When the shopkeeper hands him the packet, Baraka says, "Thank you very much!" Using polite words shows respect, builds friendship, and makes our communities peaceful.
lessons.kenyanContextNote: Respect for elders and courteous speech are core African cultural values emphasized across all CBC grades.

keyVocabulary.meaning: Polite and respectful behaviour and speech
A polite phrase used to get attention or apologize
A polite word used when making a request
An expression of gratitude

lessons.didYouKnowKenyanFact: Polite greetings in Kenya vary warmly across communities, always wishing health and peace to the family!

lessons.title: The Clever Hare and the Elephant with Mwalimu Peter
lessons.conceptIntro: Around an evening fire in Kitui, grandfather tells a story about the clever Hare (Sungura) and the mighty Elephant (Ndovu). The Elephant was boasting about his gigantic size, but little Hare challenged him to a tug-of-war across the river! Hare secretly tied the rope to a giant Hippopotamus on the other river bank. When Elephant pulled, Hippo pulled back! Hare won the contest by using his clever mind rather than physical strength. Good listeners pay attention to who the characters are, where the story takes place, and the moral lesson of the story!
lessons.kenyanContextNote: Oral storytelling (hadithi za sungura) has been passed down through generations across Kenyan communities to teach wisdom and virtues.

keyVocabulary.meaning: An account of connected events, real or imagined
A person or animal in a story
The time and place where a story happens
A good value or life lesson taught by a story

lessons.didYouKnowKenyanFact: In traditional African society, stories were often told under the moonlight (hadithi za mwezini) after dinner chores were done!

lessons.title: Story Retelling & Sequence with Amina
lessons.conceptIntro: Amina loves retelling stories to her classmates during English class. To tell a story clearly so that everyone understands, she uses sequence words: First (kwanza), Next (kisha), Then (baadaye), and Finally (hatimaye). First, Hare made a bet with Elephant. Next, Hare tied the rope to Hippo. Then, both giant animals pulled each other until they were exhausted! Finally, Hare laughed and showed that wisdom is more powerful than brute strength. Using time-order words makes your storytelling exciting and orderly!
lessons.kenyanContextNote: CBC emphasizes oral presentation skills and self-expression from early primary years.

keyVocabulary.meaning: The specific order in which events happen
To tell a story again in your own words
The three main sections of a story

lessons.didYouKnowKenyanFact: Kenya has over 40 indigenous languages, and each has its own unique animal trickster stories!

lessons.title: The Digraph Safari with Otieno (ch, sh, th, wh)
lessons.conceptIntro: Otieno is exploring letters on the word wall in Kisumu. Unlike a blend where you hear both letters, a consonant digraph happens when two letters join together to create ONE completely new sound! For example: c + h say /ch/ as in chair, chalk, and chapati. s + h say /sh/ as in sheep, ship, and shamba. t + h say /th/ as in thumb, three, and thank you. w + h say /wh/ as in wheel, white, and whistle. Digraphs are like best friends who whisper a single special secret sound together!
lessons.kenyanContextNote: Digraphs like "sh" and "ch" are frequent in both English and Kiswahili words spoken across Kenya.

keyVocabulary.meaning: Two letters that come together to produce a single new sound
A sound formed by the combination of two vowels in a single syllable
Common words that learners recognize instantly by sight without sounding out
keyVocabulary.swahiliTerm: Maneno ya kawaida yanayotambulika mara moja

lessons.didYouKnowKenyanFact: The Swahili word "shamba" and the English word "sheep" both start with the exact same /sh/ digraph sound!

lessons.title: Diphthongs & Sight Words with Halima (oi, oy)
lessons.conceptIntro: Halima is reading a storybook in Mombasa. She notices the special sound /oy/ in words like coin, point, soil, and boil (spelled "oi"), as well as boy, joy, and toy (spelled "oy")! Notice that "oi" is usually found inside the middle of a word, while "oy" is usually at the end. Halima also practices sight words like "because", "their", "always", and "through". Reading sight words quickly and smoothly helps you read whole sentences without stopping!
lessons.kenyanContextNote: Reading aloud in English and Swahili storybooks during school library hours builds confident reading fluency.

keyVocabulary.meaning: A gliding vowel sound such as /oi/ or /oy/
Reading smoothly, accurately, and with good expression
A single unbroken sound unit of a spoken word

lessons.didYouKnowKenyanFact: Kenyan copper and brass coins (sarafu) provide great practice for spelling the diphthong in "coin"!

lessons.title: Reading with Expression: The Tsavo Elephant Rescue
lessons.conceptIntro: Brian is reading an exciting true story about Tsavo National Park in Taita Taveta County. Rangers from the Kenya Wildlife Service (KWS) heard a baby elephant trumpeting in distress. The poor calf was stuck deep in the thick red mud near a dried waterhole! The rangers tied soft straps around the baby elephant and pulled together with all their might. With a great splash, the little elephant was freed and ran joyfully to join its herd. When reading aloud, Brian pauses at full stops and raises his voice with excitement at exclamation marks!
lessons.kenyanContextNote: Tsavo East and West National Parks form Kenya's largest wildlife sanctuary where elephants roam freely.

keyVocabulary.meaning: Understanding and making meaning of what you read
Reading with feeling and voice changes to match the story events
An officer who protects wildlife and national parks

lessons.didYouKnowKenyanFact: Kenya is home to the Sheldrick Wildlife Trust, which has rescued and raised over 260 orphaned baby elephants!

lessons.title: Finding Clues & Main Ideas: Harvest Day at the Shamba
lessons.conceptIntro: Chebet reads an informational passage about harvesting maize in Uasin Gishu County. The passage explains how farmers wait for the green maize stalks to turn golden brown and dry in the warm sun. Then family members work together to pick the cobs, remove the dry husks, and shell the sweet yellow kernels. Finding the "main idea" means asking: What is this whole passage mostly about? It is mostly about how Kenyan families harvest and store maize!
lessons.kenyanContextNote: Maize is Kenya's staple food crop, harvested in bulk in the North Rift region during October and November.

keyVocabulary.meaning: The most important thought or message in a paragraph or story
Figuring out something not directly said using clues in the text
The season or act of gathering mature crops from the field

lessons.didYouKnowKenyanFact: Uasin Gishu and Trans-Nzoia counties are called Kenya's "grain basket" because they produce millions of bags of maize each year!

lessons.title: Naming Words & Magical Irregular Plurals
lessons.conceptIntro: A noun is a naming word for a person, animal, place, or thing. Most nouns just add -s or -es to become more than one, like matatu -> matatus or box -> boxes. But watch out for trickster irregular nouns! They change their spelling completely or stay the exact same: one child becomes many children; one tooth becomes thirty-two teeth; one foot becomes two feet; one mouse becomes mice; and one sheep is still sheep! Memorizing these makes your English sparkle like morning dew on Mt. Kenya.

examples.text: One child was playing soccer -> Three children were playing soccer at the school pitch.
Mumbi brushed one sore tooth -> The dentist checked all her clean white teeth.
Uncle Juma has one woolly sheep -> Uncle Juma owns twenty healthy sheep.

lessons.summary: Regular plurals add -s or -es. Irregular plurals change their vowels or stay unchanged (child -> children, tooth -> teeth, foot -> feet, sheep -> sheep).

lessons.title: Pronoun Power: Replacing Nouns Smoothly
lessons.conceptIntro: Imagine saying: "Wanjiku woke up. Wanjiku washed Wanjiku's face. Wanjiku took Wanjiku's bag." That sounds repetitive! Pronouns come to the rescue by replacing nouns. We use "she" and "her" for a girl, "he" and "his" for a boy, "it" and "its" for an object or animal, "they" and "their" for more than one person, and "we" and "our" when we include ourselves. Pronouns make our sentences smooth and pleasant to listen to!

examples.text: Kiprono ran fast -> He ran fast to win the race.
Amina and Faith are sisters -> They are sisters and they share their books.
This is Baraka's toy -> This is his toy.

lessons.summary: Pronouns take the place of nouns so we do not repeat names over and over.

lessons.title: Action Time: Verbs and the -ing Continuous Wave
lessons.conceptIntro: A verb is an action word—it tells what someone or something is DOING! Run, skip, cook, write, sing, and read are all verbs. When something is happening RIGHT NOW at this very moment, we use the helping verb (am, is, are) plus an action verb ending in "-ing". For instance: "Mumbi is peeling potatoes," "The boys are herding cattle," or "I am reading my storybook." Remember: always pair "-ing" verbs with am, is, or are!

examples.text: Look! Juma is kicking the football towards the goal.
Mother and Auntie are making delicious mandazi in the kitchen.
I am drawing a picture of a crested crane.

lessons.summary: Verbs show action. Ongoing actions right now use: am/is/are + verb + -ing (e.g. is running, are playing).

lessons.title: Time Travel: Yesterday's Past Tense Adventures
lessons.conceptIntro: When we tell stories about things that already happened yesterday, last week, or this morning, we use the PAST TENSE. Many regular verbs just add "-ed": walk -> walked, kick -> kicked, plant -> planted. But just like nouns, some verbs are playful irregular acrobats! They don't use -ed: go becomes went, eat becomes ate, see becomes saw, buy becomes bought, and drink becomes drank! When you master these, you can tell thrilling tales around the fire!

examples.text: Yesterday, we walked to the market -> We bought ripe bananas and sweet pawpaw.
Faith saw a baby gazelle in Nairobi National Park.
The athlete drank fresh clean water after running the race.

lessons.summary: Past tense tells about finished actions. Regular verbs add -ed (walked). Irregular verbs change form (go -> went, eat -> ate, buy -> bought).

lessons.title: Describing Our Beautiful World with Adjectives
lessons.conceptIntro: Adjectives are magical describing words that tell us more about nouns! They tell us what kind, how many, what color, or what shape something is. Instead of just saying "a mango", an adjective helps us say "a sweet, ripe, yellow mango"! In our vibrant Kenyan communities, we see bright fabrics, tall giraffes, round calabashes, noisy markets, and warm sunny days. Using adjectives makes our stories jump off the page like playful monkeys in Kakamega forest!

examples.text: Akinyi wore a colorful kanga with intricate patterns.
The tall giraffe nibbled green leaves from the thorny acacia tree.
Mother sliced fresh, juicy watermelons for the hot afternoon.

lessons.summary: Adjectives describe nouns: color (red), size (huge), shape (round), taste (sweet), and feelings (happy).

lessons.title: Where Is It? Prepositions of Place and Direction
lessons.conceptIntro: Where did the puppy go? A preposition tells us the exact location or position of a person or object in relation to something else! Common prepositions of place include: in (inside the duka), on (on the wooden bench), under (under the shady neem tree), behind (behind the water tank), between (between two sweet orange trees), and next to (next to the gate). Prepositions help us give clear directions so nobody gets lost!

examples.text: The hen laid brown eggs inside the woven basket.
Baraka sat under the shady mango tree to read his book.
The school playground is between the dining hall and the library.

lessons.summary: Prepositions show position and location: in, on, under, behind, between, next to, and across.

lessons.title: Bridge Builders: Connecting Ideas with And, But, Because
lessons.conceptIntro: Conjunctions are bridge builders! They connect two short, choppy sentences into one smooth, elegant sentence. We use "AND" to add more information: "Kiprono has a red ball AND he has a new whistle." We use "BUT" to show contrast or an unexpected surprise: "Amina ran fast, BUT she missed the matatu." We use "BECAUSE" to give a reason or explanation: "Mumbi wore a warm sweater BECAUSE it was raining chilly drops." Using conjunctions makes your speech flow like the mighty Tana River!

examples.text: Father washed the car and Baraka polished the windows.
We wanted to play outside, but the rain began to pour.
Halima smiled happily because she passed her reading test.

lessons.summary: Conjunctions link sentences: "and" adds, "but" contrasts, and "because" explains why.

lessons.title: The Great Question Quest: Who, What, Where, When, Why, How
lessons.conceptIntro: Curious learners ask wonderful questions! Inquiry words help us discover truth and explore our world. We ask: "WHO" for a person (Who is knocking at the gate?), "WHAT" for an object or action (What did you eat for lunch?), "WHERE" for a location (Where is the health center?), "WHEN" for time (When will the school bus arrive?), "WHY" for a reason (Why do birds build nests?), and "HOW" for the manner or process (How do we plant sukuma wiki?). Remember: every question must end with a curvy QUESTION MARK (?)!

examples.text: Who won the 100m sprint race? Kiprono won the race!
Where did you buy those ripe mangoes? At Kongowea market!
Why do we boil drinking water? Because boiling kills harmful germs.

lessons.summary: Question words ask for specific information: Who (person), What (thing), Where (place), When (time), Why (reason), How (manner).

lessons.title: The Royal Rules of Capital Letters
lessons.conceptIntro: Capital letters (upper-case letters) are like kings and queens—they stand tall and proud! In English, we must ALWAYS capitalize: 1) The very first word of every sentence. 2) Special names of people, pets, and places (Wanjiku, Kiprono, Simba, Nairobi, Kenya, Lake Victoria). 3) Days of the week and months of the year (Monday, Friday, January, December). 4) The single pronoun "I" whenever you talk about yourself! When you follow these royal rules, your writing looks neat, proud, and easy to read.

examples.text: On Monday, Amani and I traveled to Mombasa by the SGR train.
Kenya is a beautiful country with rivers, mountains, and wildlife.
My best friend is Faith and we celebrate her birthday in August.

lessons.summary: Capitalize the start of sentences, proper nouns (names, places, Kenya), days, months, and the pronoun "I".

lessons.title: Punctuation Traffic Lights: Full Stops, Question Marks & Commas
lessons.conceptIntro: Imagine driving on a road with no traffic signs—everything would crash! Punctuation marks are the traffic signs of reading: 1) A FULL STOP (.) is a red light that brings a telling sentence to a complete halt. 2) A QUESTION MARK (?) signals an asking sentence and raises your voice at the end. 3) A COMMA (,) is a gentle yield sign that gives a tiny breath when listing things. For example: "Mother bought carrots, onions, tomatoes, and cabbage at the market." Notice how commas separate the items smoothly!

examples.text: Telling sentence: The sun rises early over the Aberdare Ranges.
Asking sentence: Did you bring your homework diary to school today?
List with commas: We saw zebras, giraffes, gazelles, and ostriches in the park.

lessons.summary: Full stop (.) ends statements; question mark (?) ends questions; commas (,) separate listed items.

lessons.title: Building a Super Paragraph (The Juicy Burger Model)
lessons.conceptIntro: Writing a paragraph is like building a delicious sandwich or chapati roll! 1) The Top Slice is your TOPIC SENTENCE—it introduces what the whole paragraph is about. 2) The Delicious Fillings are 2-3 SUPPORTING DETAIL SENTENCES—they give interesting facts, descriptions, and sensory details. 3) The Bottom Slice is the CONCLUDING SENTENCE—it wraps up your idea with a warm final thought. When all your sentences stick to one main topic, your paragraph is strong and sweet to read!

examples.text: Topic Sentence: Our school garden is a wonderful place to learn.
Supporting Details: We water the green sukuma wiki every morning. Beautiful yellow butterflies flutter over the bean flowers.
Concluding Sentence: I feel proud whenever we harvest healthy vegetables for our lunch.

lessons.summary: A strong paragraph has: 1 topic sentence, 2-3 supporting detail sentences, and 1 closing sentence.

lessons.title: Warm Words: Writing Friendly Thank-You Notes
lessons.conceptIntro: A friendly note is a special gift written from the heart! When someone helps you, gives you a gift, or visits you, a short thank-you note spreads sunshine and joy. A friendly note has three simple parts: 1) The Greeting (e.g., "Dear Grandmother," with a comma). 2) The Message (2-3 kind sentences saying what you are thankful for and how you felt). 3) The Sign-off and Your Name (e.g., "Your loving grandson, / Baraka"). Showing gratitude makes our communities happy and connected!

examples.text: Greeting: Dear Uncle Omari,
Message: Thank you so much for the colorful storybook you brought me from Nairobi. I enjoy reading it before bedtime every evening.
Sign-off: Your loving nephew, / Kiprono

lessons.summary: Friendly note layout: 1) Greeting (Dear...), 2) Grateful message, 3) Warm sign-off and your name.

lessons.title: Maamkizi ya Heshima Nyumbani na Shuleni
lessons.conceptIntro: Maamkizi ni daraja la upendo na heshima katika jamii zetu nchini Kenya. Mtoto anapokutana na mtu mzima, mzazi, au mwalimu, anamsalimu kwa kusema: "Shikamoo!" Naye mtu mzima huitikia kwa upendo: "Marahaba!" Unapokutana na rafiki yako wa rika moja, unamwambia: "Hujambo?" Naye anaitikia: "Sijambo!" Wakati wa asubuhi tunasema "Habari za asubuhi?" au "Sabalkheri?" (Aheri). Wakati wa jioni tunasema "Msalheri?" (Aheri). Kusalimia huleta baraka na furaha tele!

examples.text: Amani: "Shikamoo nyanya!" Nyanya: "Marahaba mjukuu wangu, umeshindaje?"
Baraka: "Hujambo Neema?" Neema: "Sijambo Baraka, u hali gani?"
Wanafunzi: "Habari za asubuhi mwalimu?" Mwalimu: "Nzuri sana watoto, karibuni darasani."

lessons.summary: Mtu mzima husalimiwa "Shikamoo" (huitikiwa "Marahaba"). Rika moja husalimiwa "Hujambo" (huitikiwa "Sijambo"). Asubuhi: Sabalkheri (Aheri).

lessons.title: Maneno ya Adabu na Nidhamu Jamani!
lessons.conceptIntro: Lugha ya Kiswahili ina maneno matamu ya adabu yanayoonyesha malezi mema na heshima ya hali ya juu. Unapohitaji msaada au kitu kutoka kwa mtu, daima anza na: "Tafadhali nisaidie..." Unapopewa kitu au kusaidiwa, sema mara moja: "Asante sana!" Na ukikosea mtu au ukimpiga kikumbo bila kukusudia, jishushe na useme kwa upole: "Samahani" au "Niwie radhi." Mtu anapokushukuru, unamkaribisha kwa kusema: "Karibu sana!" Maneno haya hupunguza ugomvi na kujenga urafiki imara.

examples.text: Tafadhali: "Tafadhali Juma, naomba uniazime kifutio chako."
Asante: "Asante sana mama kwa kunipikia chapati tamu."
Samahani: "Samahani rafiki yangu, sikukusudia kukanyaga kiatu chako."

lessons.summary: Maneno ya adabu: "Tafadhali" (kuomba), "Asante" (kushukuru), "Samahani" au "Niwie radhi" (kuomba msamaha).

lessons.title: Sauti Mseto za Kiswahili Sanifu
lessons.conceptIntro: Sauti mseto ni sauti inayotokana na muungano wa herufi mbili au zaidi zinazotoa sauti moja ya pekee inayovuma vizuri kooni au puani! Hebu tusikilize: /ch/ kama katika chakula, chapati, na chura; /dh/ kama katika dhahabu, dhoruba, na dhambi; /gh/ kama katika ghorofa, ghala, na ghali; /ng'/ (yenye mkato wa juu) kama katika ng'ombe, ng'ambo, na kung'aa; na /ny/ kama katika nyumba, nyota, na nyuki. Kutamka sauti hizi waziwazi kunafanya usomaji wako uwe na ladha tamu kama asali ya Kitui!

examples.text: /ch/: Chakula kitamu kilipikwa jikoni (chapati na maharagwe).
/ng'/: Ng'ombe wa babu anatoa maziwa mengi meupe.
/ny/: Nyuki wanajenga mzinga juu ya mti mrefu.

lessons.summary: Sauti mseto huunganisha herufi mbili kutoa sauti moja: ch (chapati), dh (dhahabu), gh (ghala), ng' (ng'ombe), ny (nyumba).

lessons.title: Tega Nitegue: Vitendawili na Mashairi ya Watoto
lessons.conceptIntro: Vitendawili ni michezo ya maneno inayochangamsha akili na kukuza fikira za watoto! Mtengaji husema kwa sauti: "Kitendawili!" Na wengine huitikia kwa hamu: "Tega!" Baada ya hapo, anatoa fumbo lake la werevu. Kwa mfano: "Kuku wangu hutagia miibani" — jibu lake ni NANASI! Au "Nyumba yangu haina mlango" — jibu lake ni YAI! Mashairi ya watoto nayo yana mahadhi na mahadhi yanayovutia tunapoimba na kupiga makofi kwa furaha.

examples.text: Mtengaji: "Kitendawili!" Wategozi: "Tega!" Fumbo: "Mwanangu analia porini?" Jibu: "Shoka likikata mti."
Fumbo: "Kila niendapo ananifuata nyuma?" Jibu: "Kivuli changu."
Fumbo: "Huku ng'o na kule ng'o?" Jibu: "Giza."

lessons.summary: Vitendawili: Mtengaji husema "Kitendawili", wasikilizaji huitikia "Tega", kisha fumbo huteguliwa kwa hekima na fikira.

lessons.title: Kusoma Maneno ya Silabi Tatu na Nne kwa Ufasaha
lessons.conceptIntro: Kusoma ni safari ya ajabu inayofungua milango ya hekima! Katika Gredi ya 3, tunajifunza kusoma maneno marefu yenye silabi tatu au nne kwa kuunganisha sauti kwa uhodari. Silabi ni kipande cha neno kinachotamkwa kwa mpigo mmoja wa hewa. Mfano: ki-ko-mbe (silabi 3), ma-ra-ha-ba (silabi 4), da-ra-sa-ni (silabi 4), mwa-na-fun-zi (silabi 4). Unaposoma, tamka kila silabi wazi kisha unganisha neno lote bila kukata tamaa. Kadiri unavyosoma kila siku, ndivyo ulimi wako unavyokuwa mwepesi kama maji mtoni!

examples.text: ki + ta + bu = kitabu (silabi 3)
mwa + li + mu = mwalimu (silabi 3)
te + le + vi + she + ni = televisheni (silabi 5)

lessons.summary: Unganisha silabi kutamka neno kamili: da-ra-sa-ni -> darasani. Soma kila siku ili uwe msomaji hodari.

lessons.title: Msamiati wa Mazingira Yetu (Shuleni, Nyumbani na Sokoni)
lessons.conceptIntro: Kila mahali tunapokwenda kuna maneno maalum ya kutaja vitu na shughuli. Shuleni tunatumia msamiati kama: ubao, chaki, kifutio, daftari, na gwaride. Nyumbani tunataja: sebule (chumba cha kupumzika na kupokea wageni), jiko, chumba cha kulala, na uani. Sokoni tunakutana na: muuzaji, mnunuzi, bidhaa, bei, shilingi, na mizani (chombo cha kupimia uzito). Kujua msamiati sahihi huifanya lugha yako iwe safi na ya kueleweka kwa kila mtu!

examples.text: Shuleni: Mwalimu aliandika nambari ubaoni kwa chaki nyeupe.
Nyumbani: Wageni waliketi kwenye viti vya kupendeza sebuleni.
Sokoni: Muuzaji alipima kilo mbili za maharagwe kwenye mizani.

lessons.summary: Msamiati ni maneno maalum ya mazingira: Shuleni (ubao, chaki), Nyumbani (sebule, jiko), Sokoni (mizani, mnunuzi, shilingi).

lessons.title: Hadithi: Safari ya Treni ya SGR Kuelekea Mombasa
lessons.conceptIntro: Soma hadithi hii kwa makini: "Asubuhi ya Jumamosi, Baraka na dada yake Amina waliamka mapema sana. Walifuatana na baba yao kuelekea kituo cha treni cha Syokimau jijini Nairobi. Walikuwa wanasafiri kwa treni ya kisasa ya Madaraka Express kuelekea Mombasa kuwatembelea babu na nyanya. Ndani ya treni, mabehewa yalikuwa safi na yenye kiyoyozi baridi. Treni ilipoanza mwendo kwa kasi ya ajabu, watoto walitazama madirishani kwa furaha. Walipofika eneo la Hifadhi ya Wanyama ya Tsavo, waliona tembo wakubwa wekundu wakinywa maji, twiga warefu, na pundamilia wenye milia mizuri. Saa chache baadaye, walifika salama kituo cha Miritini Mombasa na kupokelewa kwa tabasamu na shada za maua!"

examples.text: Swali: Baraka na Amina walisafiri kuelekea wapi? Jibu: Walisafiri kuelekea Mombasa.
Swali: Walitumia njia gani ya usafiri? Jibu: Walisafiri kwa treni ya kisasa ya Madaraka Express.
Swali: Waliona wanyama gani huko Tsavo? Jibu: Waliona tembo, twiga, na pundamilia.

lessons.summary: Kusoma ufahamu kunahitaji kuzingatia wahusika (Baraka, Amina, Baba), mahali (Nairobi, Tsavo, Mombasa), na matukio makuu.

lessons.title: Hadithi: Siku ya Mavuno Shambani mwa Babu Otieno
lessons.conceptIntro: Soma hadithi hii kwa makini: "Msimu wa mavuno ulipowadia, mvua za baraka zilikuwa zimesitisha matone yake kijijini Ugenya. Babu Otieno na Nyanya Akinyi waliwaita wajukuu zao kuwasaidia kuvuna mazao shambani. Asubuhi na mapema kabla ya umande kukauka, kila mtu alishika kikapu chake cha kiasili. Shamba lilikuwa na mahindi marefu yenye miaka mikubwa, mikunde ya maharagwe, na viazi vitamu chini ya ardhi. Wajukuu walivunja mahindi kwa furaha huku wakiimba nyimbo za kienyeji. Baada ya kazi ya bidii, Nyanya aliwapikia mahindi ya kuchoma na viazi vitamu vyenye mvuke na chai ya tangawizi. Babu aliwakumbusha: 'Umoja ni nguvu, na ardhi yetu ya Kenya ina utajiri mkubwa tukiilima kwa bidii!'"

examples.text: Swali: Mazao gani yalivunwa shambani? Jibu: Mahindi, maharagwe, na viazi vitamu.
Swali: Nyanya aliwapikia chakula gani baada ya kazi? Jibu: Mahindi ya kuchoma, viazi vitamu, na chai.
Swali: Methali gani iliyotajwa na Babu? Jibu: "Umoja ni nguvu."

lessons.summary: Kuelewa hadithi kunasaidia kubaini maadili ya jamii kama bidii ya kazi, umoja wa kifamilia, na kuthamini chakula cha kiasili.

lessons.title: Ngeli ya A-WA: Viumbe Hai na Watu
lessons.conceptIntro: Ngeli ni makundi ya maneno yenye tabia na upatanisho unaofanana katika sentensi. Ngeli ya kwanza na muhimu zaidi ni ngeli ya A-WA! Ngeli hii inajumuisha binadamu wote, wanyama, ndege, na wadudu. Katika UMOJA, kitenzi huanza na "A-": Mtoto a-nalala, mwalimu a-nafundisha, mbuzi a-nakula majani. Katika WINGI, kitenzi huanza na "WA-": Watoto wa-nalala, walimu wa-nafundisha, mbuzi wa-nakula majani. Tazama jinsi sauti za a- na wa- zinavyoimba kwa upatanisho mzuri!

examples.text: Umoja: Mvulana anacheza mpira -> Wingi: Wavulana wanacheza mpira.
Umoja: Daktari anamwona mgonjwa -> Wingi: Madaktari wanawaona wagonjwa.
Umoja: Simba amenguruma porini -> Wingi: Simba wamenguruma porini.

lessons.summary: Ngeli ya A-WA: Umoja kitenzi huchukua A- (mtoto anacheza); Wingi huchukua WA- (watoto wanacheza).

lessons.title: Ngeli ya KI-VI: Vitu na Vyombo
lessons.conceptIntro: Ngeli ya KI-VI inajumuisha vitu vingi visivyo na uhai vinavyoanza na ki- au ch- katika umoja. Katika UMOJA, nomino na kitenzi huanza na "KI-": Ki-tabu ki-meanguka, ki-kapu ki-mejaa, ch-akula ki-tamu ki-napikwa. Katika WINGI, nomino na kitenzi hubadilika kuwa "VI-": Vi-tabu vi-meanguka, vi-kapu vi-mejaa, vy-akula vi-tamu vi-napikwa. Kuweka ki- na vi- mahali pake sahihi hufanya Kiswahili chako kiwe sanifu na chenye mvuto!

examples.text: Umoja: Kiatu kimepasuka -> Wingi: Viatu vimepasuka.
Umoja: Kiti kimevunjika -> Wingi: Viti vimevunjika.
Umoja: Choo kimesafishwa -> Wingi: Vyoo vimesafishwa.

lessons.summary: Ngeli ya KI-VI: Umoja huchukua KI- (kitabu kimesomwa); Wingi huchukua VI- (vitabu vimesomwa).

lessons.title: Wakati Uliopo: Tendo la Sasa Hivi (-na-)
lessons.conceptIntro: Wakati uliopo hueleza matendo yanayotendeka hivi sasa tunapozungumza! Kiambishi cha wakati uliopo ni "-na-". Mfano: a-na-cheza, wa-na-soma, ni-na-andika, tu-na-imba. Mfano: "Sasa hivi Baraka anasoma hadithi darasani." Neno "sasa", "leo", au "hivi punde" mara nyingi huambatana na wakati uliopo. Wakati uliopo huifanya hadithi yako ionekane kama inatendeka mbele ya macho yako hivi sasa!

examples.text: Mama anapika chai tamu jikoni hivi sasa.
Wanafunzi wanakimbia uwanjani wakati wa mapumziko.
Ninachora picha ya twiga katika daftari langu.

lessons.summary: Wakati uliopo hutumia kiambishi -na- (anasoma, wanacheza) kueleza matendo ya sasa hivi.

lessons.title: Kusafiri Katika Nyakati: Uliopita (-li-) na Ujao (-ta-)
lessons.conceptIntro: Lugha yetu inatuwezesha kusafiri katika wakati kama mashine ya ajabu! Wakati uliopita hueleza matendo yaliyokwisha kutendeka jana, juzi, au zamani, na unatumia kiambishi "-li-": a-li-enda, tu-li-kula, wa-li-shinda. Wakati ujao nao hueleza mambo yatakayotendeka kesho, baadaye, au mwakani, na unatumia kiambishi "-ta-": a-ta-enda, tu-ta-kula, wa-ta-shinda. Kutawala nyakati hizi tatu hukufanya uwe mwandishi na msimuliaji hodari wa Kiswahili!

examples.text: Uliopita: Jana tulitembelea mbuga ya wanyama ya Nakuru.
Ujao: Kesho tutaandika mtihani wa kusoma darasani.
Mabadiliko: Baraka alisoma (jana) -> anasoma (sasa) -> atasoma (kesho).

lessons.summary: Wakati uliopita hutumia -li- (alisoma jana). Wakati ujao hutumia -ta- (atasoma kesho).

lessons.title: Vivumishi vya Sifa: Kupamba Majina Yetu
lessons.conceptIntro: Vivumishi ni maneno maalum yanayotoa sifa au maelezo zaidi kuhusu nomino. Badala ya kusema "embe", tunasema "embe tamu na zuri"! Shina la kivumishi hupokea kiambishi kulingana na ngeli ya jina linalosifiwa: Katika ngeli ya A-WA: mtoto m-zuri, watoto wa-zuri; mbuzi m-kubwa, mbuzi wa-kubwa. Katika ngeli ya KI-VI: kitabu ki-zuri, vitabu vi-zuri; chakula ki-tamu, vyakula vi-tamu. Vivumishi huleta mvuto na kuifanya lugha ya Kiswahili ing'ae kama almasi safi!

examples.text: A-WA: Mwalimu mpole anafundisha wanafunzi watiifu.
KI-VI: Kikapu kidogo kimejaa ndizi mbivu na tamu.
Sifa: Simba mkali alifukuzwa na tembo mkubwa.

lessons.summary: Vivumishi vya sifa hupatana na ngeli: A-WA huchukua m-/wa- (mtoto mzuri/watoto wazuri); KI-VI huchukua ki-/vi- (kiti kizuri/viti vizuri).

lessons.title: Viashiria: Kuonyesha Vitu Karibu na Mbali
lessons.conceptIntro: Viashiria ni maneno yanayotumiwa kuonyesha au kunyooshea kidole kitu au mtu kulingana na umbali wake kutoka kwa mzungumzaji. 1) Vitu vilivyo KARIBU: A-WA tunasema "huyu" (mtoto huyu) na wingi "hawa" (watoto hawa). KI-VI tunasema "hiki" (kitabu hiki) na wingi "hivi" (vitabu hivi). 2) Vitu vilivyo MBALI: A-WA tunasema "yule" (mtoto yule kule) na wingi "wale" (watoto wale kule). KI-VI tunasema "kile" (kiti kile kule) na wingi "vile" (viti vile kule). Viashiria hutusaidia kuonyesha vitu bila kusita!

examples.text: Karibu: Mtoto huyu anasoma kitabu hiki.
Mbali: Ndege yule anaruka juu ya mti ule kule mbali.
Wingi wa karibu: Vikapu hivi vimejaa vyakula hivi vitamu.

lessons.summary: Viashiria vya karibu: huyu/hawa, hiki/hivi. Viashiria vya mbali: yule/wale, kile/vile.

lessons.title: Vinyume vya Maneno: Pande Mbili za Sarafu
lessons.conceptIntro: Kinyume cha neno ni neno lenye maana iliyo tofauti kabisa au kinyume na neno lingine, kama vile usiku ulivyo kinyume cha mchana! Katika maisha yetu, kila tendo lina kinyume chake: simama kinyume chake ni keti (au kaa); lia kinyume chake ni cheka; panda mlima kinyume chake ni shuka; fungua mlango kinyume chake ni funga; nene kinyume chake ni konda; na mrefu kinyume chake ni mfupi. Kujua vinyume huongeza utajiri wa maneno kichwani mwako!

examples.text: Asubuhi jua linapanda, jioni linashuka chini ya upeo.
Musa alicheka kwa furaha, lakini mtoto mdogo alilia kwa njaa.
Baraka alifungua mlango, kisha dada akafunga mlango usiku.

lessons.summary: Kinyume ni maana iliyo kinyume au tofauti: simama/keti, cheka/lia, panda/shuka, nene/konda, fungua/funga.

lessons.title: Vihusishi vya Mahali: Wapi Kitu Kilipo?
lessons.conceptIntro: Vihusishi vya mahali ni maneno madogo yenye kazi kubwa ya kutuambia mahali mtu, mnyama, au kitu kilipo kuhusiana na kingine! 1) NDANI YA: kalamu ipo ndani ya mkoba. 2) JUU YA: kitabu kimewekwa juu ya meza. 3) CHINI YA: paka amelala chini ya uvungu wa kitanda. 4) KANDO YA: watoto wanatembea kando ya barabara. 5) MBELE YA: mwalimu amesimama mbele ya darasa. 6) NYUMA YA: mbwa anajificha nyuma ya mlango. Vihusishi hutusaidia kupata vitu vilivyopotea haraka!

examples.text: Wanafunzi wameketi ndani ya darasa safi.
Chupa ya maji imewekwa juu ya dawati la mwalimu.
Kuku amekimbia na kujificha chini ya gari.

lessons.summary: Vihusishi vya mahali hueleza eneo: ndani ya, juu ya, chini ya, kando ya, mbele ya, nyuma ya.

lessons.title: Kanuni za Dhahabu za Herufi Kubwa
lessons.conceptIntro: Herufi kubwa ni kama wakuu wenye taji—huanza mambo makubwa na majina maalum! Katika lugha ya Kiswahili, daima tunaandika herufi kubwa: 1) Mwanzoni mwa kila sentensi. 2) Majina ya watu (Amani, Baraka, Wanjiku, Kiprono). 3) Majina ya nchi na miji (Kenya, Nairobi, Mombasa, Kisumu). 4) Siku za juma (Jumatatu, Ijumaa) na miezi ya mwaka (Januari, Desemba). 5) Majina ya mito, maziwa, na milima (Mto Tana, Ziwa Victoria, Mlima Kenya). Mwandiko wenye herufi kubwa mahali pake unaonyesha mwanafunzi makini!

examples.text: Siku ya Ijumaa, Amina alisafiri kuelekea Mombasa kwa treni.
Kenya ni taifa letu lenye amani, upendo, na mshikamano.
Sikukuu ya Jamhuri huadhimishwa mwezi wa Desemba kila mwaka.

lessons.summary: Tumia herufi kubwa: mwanzo wa sentensi, majina ya watu na maeneo (Kenya, Nairobi), siku za juma, na miezi.

lessons.title: Alama za Uakifishaji: Taa za Trafiki ya Kusoma
lessons.conceptIntro: Alama za uakifishaji humwongoza msomaji kama taa za barabarani! 1) KITONE (.): Ni taa nyekundu inayoleta sentensi ya kawaida tamati kamili. 2) ALAMA YA KUULIZA (?): Huwekwa mwishoni mwa swali lolote (k.m. "Je, umekula chakula cha mchana?"). Sauti yako hupanda juu kidogo unaposoma swali! 3) MKATO (,): Ni pumzi ndogo inayotenganisha vitu vinavyoorodheshwa: "Mama alinunua mahindi, maharagwe, ndizi, na sukari sokoni." Alama hizi huweka mpangilio safi usio na mkanganyiko!

examples.text: Kitone (.): Shule yetu inaitwa Jifuno Academy.
Alama ya kuuliza (?): Je, unajua kuhesabu sarafu za Kenya?
Mkato (,): Tuliona twiga, tembo, simba, na pundamilia mbugani.

lessons.summary: Kitone (.) humaliza sentensi; alama ya kuuliza (?) humaliza swali; mkato (,) hutenganisha orodha ya vitu.

lessons.title: Kutunga Kifungu cha Sentensi 3 hadi 5 (Muundo wa Chapati Roll)
lessons.conceptIntro: Kutunga insha au kifungu ni kama kusuka kikapu kizuri—kila sentensi inashikamana na nyingine kwa uzuri! Kifungu kizuri cha Gredi ya 3 kina sehemu tatu: 1) SENTENSI KUU YA MADA: Hii ni sentensi ya kwanza inayomweleza msomaji kile unachoandikia (k.m. "Shule yetu ya Jifuno ni mahali pazuri pa kujifunzia."). 2) SENTENSI ZA MAELEZO (sentensi 2-3): Hutoa sifa, rangi, na mifano halisi (k.m. "Kuna madarasa safi na uwanja mkubwa wa kuchezea mpira. Walimu wetu ni wapole na wanatufundisha kwa upendo."). 3) SENTENSI YA HITIMISHO: Hufunga kifungu kwa furaha na fahari ("Ninajivunia sana kusoma katika shule yetu."). Sentensi zote zikiwa na mshikamano, kifungu chako kinapata alama bora!

examples.text: Sentensi kuu: Shamba la babu yangu lina rutuba na mimea mingi ya kuvutia.
Maelezo: Analima mahindi marefu, ndizi mbivu, na viazi vitamu. Kila asubuhi tunamwagilia mboga kwa maji safi ya mtoni.
Hitimisho: Ninapenda sana kutembelea shamba hili wakati wa likizo.

lessons.summary: Muundo wa kifungu: 1) Sentensi kuu ya mada, 2) Sentensi za maelezo, 3) Sentensi ya hitimisho inayofunga kifungu.

lessons.title: Barua ya Kirafiki na Ujumbe wa Shukrani
lessons.conceptIntro: Kuandika barua ya kirafiki au kadi ya shukrani ni njia tamu ya kuonyesha upendo na kuwashukuru wazazi, walimu, na marafiki! Barua ya kirafiki ina sehemu nne rahisi: 1) TAREHE (k.m. "14 Oktoba 2026"). 2) MAAMKIZI YA KIRAFIKI (k.m. "Kwa rafiki yangu mpendwa Amani," ikifuatiwa na mkato). 3) UJUMBE WA MOYONI (sentensi 2-3 za kueleza sababu ya shukrani au kumjulia hali). 4) HITIMISHO NA JINA (k.m. "Wako akupendaye, / Baraka"). Ujumbe wa shukrani huleta tabasamu na kuimarisha urafiki!

examples.text: Tarehe: 20 Novemba 2026
Maamkizi: Kwa Nyanya mpendwa,
Ujumbe: Asante sana kwa kuniletea asali tamu na ndizi mbivu kutoka kijijini. Nilikula na nikafurahi sana.
Kumalizia: Mjukuu wako mpendwa, / Kiprono

lessons.summary: Sehemu za barua ya kirafiki: 1) Tarehe, 2) Maamkizi (Kwa...), 3) Ujumbe, 4) Hitimisho na jina la mwandishi.

lessons.title: Sky Watchers: Reading Weather Symbols
lessons.conceptIntro: Look up at the sky! What does it look like today? Weather is the condition of the atmosphere at a particular time and place. In Kenya, we experience five major weather conditions: 1) SUNNY: A bright golden sun shines warmly; we use a picture of a round yellow sun. 2) RAINY: Dark grey clouds drop refreshing raindrops; we use a cloud with falling blue drops. 3) CLOUDY: Puffy white or grey clouds cover the blue sky; we draw two soft clouds. 4) WINDY: Strong rushing air bends tall eucalyptus trees and blows dust; we draw blowing swirls or a tree swaying. 5) CALM: The air is still, and smoke from a kitchen chimney rises straight up into the air without blowing sideways. Recording weather helps farmers plan planting and harvesting!

examples.text: Sunny: Bright sun shines over Mombasa beach; air feels warm and bright.
Rainy: Drops fall over Kericho tea plantations; puddles form on paths.
Windy: Tree branches sway and kite strings tug upwards in the sky.

lessons.summary: Weather conditions: sunny (sun), rainy (cloud with rain drops), cloudy (clouds), windy (swaying tree/wind lines), and calm (straight rising smoke).

lessons.title: Dressing and Living with Kenyan Weather
lessons.conceptIntro: The weather tells us how to dress and what activities to do! On a cold, chilly morning in Limuru or Nyandarua, we put on warm woolen sweaters, scarves, and socks to protect our chests from coughing. On a hot, sunny day in Garissa or Mombasa, we wear light, breathable cotton clothes, drink plenty of cool drinking water, and wear wide sunhats. On a muddy rainy day, we carry sturdy umbrellas and step out in rubber gumboots so our feet stay dry. When it is sunny, parents dry freshly washed clothes on the clothesline and farmers dry their harvested maize grain in the courtyard!

examples.text: Cold weather: Heavy jackets, woolen caps, and warm socks prevent chills.
Sunny weather: Light clothes, drinking clean water, and playing under shady trees.
Rainy weather: Gumboots, raincoats, and harvesting clean rainwater from iron roofs.

lessons.summary: Dress for the weather: warm jackets for cold days, light cotton for sunny days, and gumboots/umbrellas for rainy days.

lessons.title: Where Water Comes From: Rivers, Lakes and Taps
lessons.conceptIntro: Water is life! Without clean water, people, animals, and crops cannot survive. Water comes from two main types of sources: 1) NATURAL SOURCES created by nature: Rain falling from clouds, flowing rivers (like River Tana and River Athi), natural freshwater lakes (like Lake Victoria and Lake Naivasha), natural springs bubbling from underground rocks, and oceans. 2) MAN-MADE OR ARTIFICIAL SOURCES built by human beings: Boreholes drilled deep into the ground, water wells, earth dams storing runoff, and treated tap water piped to homes and schools.
