Identifying our water sources helps us protect them from dirt and pollution!

examples.text: Natural sources: Rain, River Athi, Lake Victoria, natural freshwater springs.
Artificial sources: School water taps, county boreholes, community earth dams.
Uses of water: Drinking, cooking ugali, bathing, watering crops, and washing utensils.

lessons.summary: Water sources: Natural (rain, rivers, lakes, springs) and Artificial (taps, boreholes, wells, dams).

lessons.title: Making Water Safe to Drink & Saving Every Drop
lessons.conceptIntro: Clear water is not always safe water! Even water that looks sparkling can hide tiny invisible disease germs that cause stomach aches, cholera, and typhoid. To make drinking water 100% safe: 1) BOILING: Heat water until it bubbles vigorously for several minutes to kill all harmful bacteria. 2) FILTERING: Pour water through a clean filter cloth or ceramic filter to trap dirt particles. After boiling, store water in a clean, covered container with a tap or clean ladle! We must also SAVE water because water is precious: Always turn off taps tightly after washing hands, fix leaking pipes, and harvest rainwater from roof gutters into clean storage tanks!

examples.text: Safe water: Boiling water until it bubbles kills microscopic germs.
Storage: Keep boiled water in a clean covered pot or jerrican.
Conservation: Turn off taps tightly; reuse rinse water to mop verandas or water trees.

lessons.summary: Purify drinking water by boiling and filtering. Conserve water by turning off taps, harvesting rainwater, and reusing clean rinse water.

lessons.title: Soil Detective: Clay, Sand, and Loam
lessons.conceptIntro: Soil is the loose top layer of the Earth where plants take root! There are three main types of soil in Kenya: 1) SAND SOIL: Has large, coarse, gritty particles that feel rough between your fingers. It lets water drain through very quickly like a sieve, so it dries fast. 2) CLAY SOIL: Has tiny, microscopic particles. When wet, it feels sticky, smooth, and plastic-like; when dry, it hardens and forms cracks. It holds water tightly for a long time. 3) LOAM SOIL: The champion soil! It is a balanced mix of sand, clay, and dark decayed plant matter called humus. It is dark brown or black, soft, crumbly, and holds just the right amount of air and moisture for healthy plant roots!

examples.text: Sand: Found along coastal beaches and dry riverbeds; gritty texture.
Clay: Found in river valleys; sticky when wet, used for making bricks.
Loam: Found in fertile shambas; rich, dark humus ideal for growing maize.

lessons.summary: Three soils: Sand (rough, drains fast), Clay (smooth, sticky, holds water), and Loam (dark, fertile, best for crops).

lessons.title: Soil in Action: Farming, Modeling, and Building
lessons.conceptIntro: Soil gives us food, shelter, and art! 1) FARMING CROPS: Loam soil is the best soil for growing vegetables like sukuma wiki, sweet potatoes, and maize because it is rich in natural nutrients (humus). 2) MODELING & POTTERY: Sticky clay soil can be kneaded with water like chapati dough and molded into beautiful clay cooking pots, flower vases, beads, and toy animals, then fired in a kiln to become stone-hard. 3) BUILDING & CONSTRUCTION: Sand is mixed with cement and water to make strong mortar and concrete for building houses, classrooms, and bridges! Without soil, our world would have no food or sturdy homes.

examples.text: Farming: Loam soil in Kiambu and Kisii produces abundant bananas and greens.
Pottery: Women potters in Western Kenya mold clay cooking pots (nyungu).
Construction: River sand mixed with cement builds brick walls in towns.

lessons.summary: Soil uses: Loam for farming vegetables, Clay for modeling pots and bricks, Sand mixed with cement for building.

lessons.title: The Wonderful Anatomy of a Plant
lessons.conceptIntro: Plants are living organisms that provide us with food, oxygen, shade, and medicine! A flowering plant has five key parts, each with an essential job: 1) ROOTS: Grow underground, anchor the plant firmly in the soil, and absorb water and mineral salts. 2) STEM: The plant's sturdy backbone; it holds leaves up to the sun and transports water from roots to leaves. 3) LEAVES: The plant's green food factory! Leaves use sunlight, green chlorophyll, and water to make food (photosynthesis). 4) FLOWERS: The colorful reproductive parts that attract bees and butterflies to make seeds. 5) FRUITS: Protect the seeds inside and provide delicious nutrition for humans and animals!

examples.text: Roots: Carrot and cassava store food underground in their roots.
Stem: Sugarcane stores sweet juice in its thick tall stem.
Leaves: Sukuma wiki and spinach are delicious edible leaves.

lessons.summary: Plant parts: Roots (absorb water), Stem (supports & transports), Leaves (make food), Flowers (make seeds), Fruit (protects seeds).

lessons.title: Plant Guardians: Caring for Crops and Safety
lessons.conceptIntro: Plants need love and care to thrive! In our school 4K Club and home gardens, we care for plants by: 1) WATERING: Giving plants clean water at the base in early morning or late evening. 2) WEEDING: Uprooting unwanted wild weeds (like blackjack and sodom apple) that steal water and nutrients from crops. 3) MULCHING: Covering bare soil around plants with dry grass or leaves to conserve moisture and stop weeds from sprouting. 4) TREE PLANTING: Planting indigenous trees to protect the climate. SAFETY RULE: Never eat unknown wild berries or touch milky sap from plants like euphorbia, which can irritate eyes and skin!

examples.text: Watering: Water vegetables early in the morning so the sun doesn't evaporate moisture.
Mulching: Dry banana leaves around tomato plants keep the soil damp and cool.
Safety: Wash hands with soap after weeding, and never taste unknown wild fruit.

lessons.summary: Care for plants: water early, weed unwanted plants, mulch with dry leaves, and stay safe by avoiding poisonous wild plants.

lessons.title: Domestic Animals: Homes, Needs, and Care
lessons.conceptIntro: Domestic animals are animals kept by humans at home or on the shamba for companionship, work, or food. Common Kenyan domestic animals include cattle (cows, bulls), goats, sheep, chickens, donkeys, cats, and dogs. They need four basic things to thrive: clean water, good food, fresh air, and secure shelter! Cows live in a cattle shed or boma; chickens live in a coop or hutch; pigs live in a sty; bees live in a beehive. Domestic animals reward us with milk, eggs, meat, wool, honey, security, and transport. We must show kindness to animals by feeding them regularly, giving them clean drinking water, keeping their shelters clean, and treating sick animals.

examples.text: Dairy Cow: Lives in a zero-grazing shed or boma; eats Napier grass; provides nutritious milk and manure for crops.
Chicken (Kuku): Lives in a chicken coop; pecks grains and seeds; gives eggs and meat.
Donkey: Helps carry heavy water jerricans and farm produce from the shamba to the village market.

lessons.summary: Domestic animals depend on humans for food, water, and clean shelters (boma, coop, hutch). They give us food, wool, and help with transport.

lessons.title: Wild Animals and Staying Safe in Nature
lessons.conceptIntro: Wild animals live freely in nature, such as in forests, savannas, rivers, and national parks like Nairobi National Park or Maasai Mara. Kenyan wild animals include lions, elephants, zebras, giraffes, monkeys, gazelles, snakes, and birds. While they are a national treasure and attract tourists from all over the world, wild animals can be dangerous if approached! Never tease, provoke, or throw stones at monkeys, baboons, or stray dogs. If you see a snake or scorpion, stay still, do not touch it, and slowly move backward while alerting an adult or teacher immediately. Protect yourself from bees and wasps by avoiding throwing stones at their hives.

examples.text: Kenya Wildlife: Elephants and lions live safely in game parks protected by Kenya Wildlife Service (KWS) rangers.
Safety rule: If you spot a snake in the compound, freeze, do not run frantically or try to hit it; call an adult calmly.
Beehive safety: Never disturb bee hives or hornets nests on trees; bee stings can be painful and dangerous.

lessons.summary: Wild animals live freely in nature. Admire them safely from a distance, never tease them, and alert adults immediately if you spot venomous or dangerous animals.

lessons.title: Illuminating Energy: Light and Heat in Daily Life
lessons.conceptIntro: Energy makes things happen! Light allows our eyes to see colors and shapes. The biggest natural source of light is the SUN! Artificial sources include solar lanterns, electric bulbs, candles, torches, and gas lamps. When light is blocked by an opaque object, a SHADOW forms behind it! HEAT is energy that makes things warm or hot. The Sun gives us heat to dry our washed clothes and harvested maize cobs. Other sources of heat include cooking fires (firewood, charcoal jiko), gas burners, and electric kettles. SAFETY RULES: Never look directly into the blazing sun—it can damage your eyesight! Always be careful around open flames, hot jikos, and boiling water to prevent severe scalds and burns.

examples.text: Sun: Natural champion giving both light to see and heat to dry beans and clothes.
Solar lamp: Charges during the day using sunlight, provides clean bright light for doing homework at night.
Safety: Always use protective oven mitts or cloth when moving a hot metal sufuria from a jiko.

lessons.summary: The Sun provides natural light and heat. Artificial sources include lamps and jikos. Never stare at the sun, and stay safe around open fires.

lessons.title: Sound Waves and Ear Protection
lessons.conceptIntro: Sound is energy produced when objects vibrate (move back and forth rapidly)! When you pluck an acoustic guitar string, beat a traditional drum (ngoma), or blow into a horn, vibrations travel through the air into your ears. Sounds can be soft (whispering, wind rustling leaves), loud (thunder, airplane engine, matatu horn), pleasant (melodious singing, gentle birds chirping), or unpleasant noise (screeching brakes, blasting sirens, loud construction drills). NOISE POLLUTION occurs when excessive loud sounds disturb peace, sleep, and learning. PROTECT YOUR EARS: Never push sharp objects (matchsticks, toothpicks, wires) into your ears! Avoid listening to blaring loudspeakers or very loud headphones, which can permanently damage your delicate eardrums.

examples.text: Musical sound: Beating an authentic African drum (ngoma) creates rhythmic, pleasant vibrations.
Animal alerts: A rooster crowing at sunrise warns the village that morning has arrived.
Ear safety rule: If ears itch, wipe only the outer ear with a damp soft towel—never insert sharp pencils or sticks inside!

lessons.summary: Sound comes from vibrations. Pleasant sounds bring joy; loud noise damages hearing. Protect your ears by keeping sharp objects out and avoiding loud volumes.

lessons.title: Landmarks and Landscapes: Hills, Valleys, and Rivers
lessons.conceptIntro: Physical features are natural shapes and landforms on the surface of the Earth. In Kenya, our counties have diverse features: 1) MOUNTAINS AND HILLS: High elevated lands with steep slopes. Mount Kenya is the highest snow-capped mountain in our country! Hills provide cool climates and scenic views. 2) VALLEYS: Low-lying land between hills or mountains, often with a river flowing through it (like the magnificent Great Rift Valley). 3) PLAINS: Broad, flat expanses of grassland where pastoralists herd cattle and wild herbivores graze. 4) RIVERS AND LAKES: Fresh bodies of flowing water (River Tana, River Athi) and large lakes (Lake Victoria, Lake Naivasha) that provide drinking water, fish, and irrigation for farming.

examples.text: Mountain: Mount Kenya (Kirinyaga) provides water towers feeding rivers across the country.
Valley: The Great Rift Valley stretches across Kenya, creating fertile farmlands and scenic escarpments.
River: River Tana is Kenya’s longest river, powering hydroelectric dams like Masinga.

lessons.summary: Physical features include mountains, hills, valleys, plains, rivers, and lakes. They supply fresh water, fertile soil for food, and natural habitats.

lessons.title: Finding Your Way: Compass Directions and Road Safety
lessons.conceptIntro: To find your way around school, your village, or town, we use the four CARDINAL POINTS of the compass: North (N), South (S), East (E), and West (W). An easy memory trick: "Never Eat Soggy Watermelons" (N-E-S-W clockwise)! How to tell directions with the Sun: The Sun always rises in the EAST in the morning and sets in the WEST in the evening. If you stand facing the morning sunrise (East) with your arms outstretched, your back faces WEST, your left hand points NORTH, and your right hand points SOUTH! ROAD SAFETY: When walking to school, always walk on the right-hand pavement facing oncoming vehicular traffic so you can see vehicles approaching. Cross wide roads at the ZEBRA CROSSING or footbridge, look Right-Left-Right before stepping onto the tarmac, and obey traffic lights (Red means Stop, Yellow/Amber means Prepare, Green means Go)!

examples.text: Sunrise check: Stand facing the rising sun in the morning: you are facing East, your left arm points North!
Zebra crossing: White stripes painted across tarmac roads where pedestrians have the right-of-way to cross safely.
Traffic light: Red light warns drivers to stop completely so school children can cross safely.

lessons.summary: The four cardinal points are North, East, South, and West. Sun rises in the East and sets in the West. Always cross at zebra crossings and walk facing oncoming traffic.

lessons.title: Kenya’s Cultural Tapestry: Heritage and Traditions
lessons.conceptIntro: Culture is the special way of life of a group of people! Kenya is blessed with over 40 distinct ethnic communities, each contributing rich traditions that make our nation colorful and vibrant. Our heritage includes: 1) INDIGENOUS FOODS: Nutritious traditional dishes like mukimo (potatoes, pumpkin leaves, maize), mursik (fermented milk in a seasoned gourd), ingokho (traditional chicken), aluru (quail), and matoke (cooked green bananas). 2) TRADITIONAL ATTIRE & BEADWORK: Maasai and Samburu shúkàs with intricate bead necklaces, Kikuyu and Kamba woven kiondos, and coastal coastal lesos and kitenges. 3) ARTIFACTS AND MUSIC: Traditional calabashes, wooden stools, musical kayambas, and ceremonial spears. Our diverse traditions teach us mutual respect, peaceful coexistence, and pride in our African roots!

examples.text: Traditional food: Mursik preserved in traditional soot-treated gourds among the Kalenjin.
Craft: Handwoven sisal kiondo baskets crafted skillfully by Kamba and Kikuyu women.
Attire: Colorful red shuka and ornate glass bead necklaces worn proudly in Maasailand.

lessons.summary: Culture includes traditional foods, clothing, music, and crafts. Kenya’s diverse cultural communities unite under one flag with love and mutual respect.

lessons.title: Symbols of Pride: Flag, Anthem, and National Holidays
lessons.conceptIntro: National symbols unite all Kenyan citizens regardless of tribe, religion, or county! 1) THE KENYAN FLAG: Has four symbolic colors: BLACK (the people of Kenya), RED (the blood shed during the struggle for freedom), GREEN (our fertile land and natural wealth), and WHITE stripes (peace and unity). In the center sits the Maasai shield and two crossed spears (readiness to defend our freedom). 2) THE NATIONAL ANTHEM: A prayer to God asking for peace, justice, and prosperity ("Ee Mungu Nguvu Yetu"). When singing or listening to the anthem, stand straight at attention with arms at your sides as a mark of supreme respect! 3) NATIONAL CELEBRATIONS: Madaraka Day (June 1st - commemorating internal self-rule), Mashujaa Day (October 20th - honoring national heroes who fought for freedom and made Kenya proud), and Jamhuri Day (December 12th - celebrating full independence and republic status).

examples.text: Flag colors: Black (people), Red (blood shed for freedom), Green (land), White (peace and unity).
Anthem etiquette: Stand still at attention, do not walk around or talk while the national anthem plays.
Holidays: Mashujaa Day on October 20th celebrates heroes like Mekatilili wa Menza, Koitalel arap Samoei, and Wangari Maathai.

lessons.summary: Our national symbols are the Flag, Anthem, and Coat of Arms. Stand at attention for the anthem. We celebrate Madaraka, Mashujaa, and Jamhuri Days.

lessons.title: Enterprise in the Community: Farms, Dukas, and Markets
lessons.conceptIntro: Economic activities are jobs and work that people do to earn income (money) and produce goods or services! In Kenyan communities, people work hard in many different sectors: 1) FARMING: Growing cash crops (tea, coffee, sugarcane) and food crops (maize, beans, bananas, sukuma wiki) or rearing cows, goats, and poultry. 2) TRADING: Selling groceries, clothes, and household items in open-air markets like Kongowea in Mombasa, Gikomba in Nairobi, or at local village dukas. 3) TRANSPORT: Matatu drivers, conductors, and boda boda riders who transport commuters and farm goods safely. 4) CRAFTS & TRADES: Carpenters making desks, tailors stitching school uniforms, and masons building houses. All honest work provides honest food and builds a thriving community!

examples.text: Mama Mboga: Sells fresh kales, spinach, and tomatoes at the market stall, earning money to feed her children.
Boda Boda Rider: Ferries passengers from rural markets to town centers safely.
Carpenter (Fundi): Uses timber to construct strong wooden study desks and chairs for school classrooms.

lessons.summary: Economic activities include farming, trading, transport, and artisan craftsmanship. Every honest job contributes to the family and builds the nation.

lessons.title: Prudent Money Habits: Needs, Wants, and Saving
lessons.conceptIntro: Money earned through honest work must be managed wisely! We use Kenyan currency (KES coins: 1, 5, 10, 20 shillings; notes: 50, 100, 200, 500, 1000 shillings) to purchase things. It is very important to understand the difference between NEEDS and WANTS: 1) NEEDS: Things we must have to survive and stay healthy, such as nutritious food, clean water, warm clothing, a shelter/home, and school stationery. 2) WANTS: Things that are fun or nice to have but we can live comfortably without, such as sweets, soda, expensive plastic toys, and video games. SAVING MONEY: When parents or relatives give you pocket money, do not spend it all at once! Save some in a piggy bank (kibuyu cha akiba) or a student bank account. Saving helps you buy important school items later or handle unexpected emergencies.

examples.text: Need: A school uniform and exercise books are essential needs for attending classes.
Want: A bag of colorful lollipops is a want that can be skipped to save coins.
Saving: Putting aside Ksh 10 every week into a piggy bank to buy a storybook at the end of the term.

lessons.summary: Needs are essentials for life; wants are desires we can live without. Save part of your money in a home bank (kibuyu cha akiba) for future needs.

lessons.title: Clean Environment: Waste Sorting and the 3Rs
lessons.conceptIntro: A clean compound keeps diseases away and makes our environment beautiful! Solid waste comes in two major types: 1) ORGANIC (BIODEGRADABLE) WASTE: Fruit peelings, maize husks, dry leaves, and leftover food. These rot naturally and should be thrown into a COMPOST PIT to decompose into rich organic manure for crops! 2) INORGANIC (NON-BIODEGRADABLE) WASTE: Plastic bottles, polythene, glass, and metal cans. These do not rot and can pollute soil and choke animals for decades! To beat pollution, practice the 3Rs: REDUCE (use less disposable packaging), REUSE (turn empty plastic jerricans into flower pots or water scoops), and RECYCLE (collect plastics and scrap metal for factories to manufacture new items). Cleanliness is everyone’s civic duty!

examples.text: Compost pit: Banana peels and dry leaves rot into fertile compost for school sukuma wiki beds.
Reuse: Cleaning an empty margarine tub to store paper clips or seedlings in the classroom.
Reduce: Bringing your own reusable cloth bag to the market instead of buying single-use plastic bags.

lessons.summary: Sort waste into organic (for compost pits) and inorganic (plastics, glass). Practice the 3Rs: Reduce, Reuse, and Recycle to protect nature.

lessons.title: Safety First: Hygiene, Basic First Aid, and Personal Protection
lessons.conceptIntro: Good hygiene and safety awareness protect our health and bodies! HAND HYGIENE: Wash hands thoroughly with clean running water and soap at critical times: after visiting the toilet/latrine, before eating meals, and after touching soil or domestic animals. Use a simple water-saving "tippy-tap" (leaky tin) if running taps are unavailable. BASIC FIRST AID: If you get a small scrape or cut, wash it gently with clean water, dry it with clean gauze, and apply a sterile plaster or bandage. For a mild burn, pour cool clean running water over it for ten minutes—never smear flour, grease, or toothpaste on burns! PERSONAL SAFETY: Never take sweets, money, or lifts in cars from unknown strangers. If someone makes you feel uncomfortable or unsafe, scream "NO!", run to a safe public area, and tell a trusted teacher, parent, or police officer immediately!

examples.text: Tippy-tap: A foot-operated water bottle or jerrycan allowing hygienic handwashing with zero tap contamination.
First Aid for cuts: Wash clean with safe water, pat dry, and cover with a sterile adhesive plaster.
Stranger safety: Always walk to school in groups with friends, never walk alone along deserted bushes.

lessons.summary: Wash hands with soap and running water. Cool mild burns with clean water. Never accept gifts from strangers, and report discomfort to trusted adults immediately.

lessons.title: Dancing Lines and Playful Patterns
lessons.conceptIntro: Every great drawing starts with a simple line! A line is a moving dot. In art, we use different types of lines to express feelings and show textures: 1) Straight lines (vertical like a flagpole, horizontal like the horizon, diagonal like falling rain). 2) Curved lines (smooth like a river or a rainbow). 3) Zigzag lines (sharp like lightning bolts or crocodile teeth). 4) Wavy and spiral lines (like ocean waves at Mombasa or smoke rising from a kitchen chimney). When we repeat lines closely together, we create PATTERNS and TEXTURES, like cross-hatching to show rough tree bark or smooth shading on a ripe avocado!

examples.text: Zigzag lines: Draw sharp teeth of a crocodile swimming in the Mara River.
Wavy lines: Draw gentle ripples of water in Lake Victoria.
Spiral line: Draw a coiled snail shell or chameleon tail in the shamba.

lessons.summary: Lines can be straight, curved, zigzag, wavy, or spiral. Repeating lines creates rhythm, texture, and beautiful patterns.

lessons.title: Still Life: Drawing Fruits and Traditional Pots
lessons.conceptIntro: Still-life drawing means drawing objects that stay completely still, like a bowl of delicious tropical fruits (mangoes, bananas, pawpaws) or a traditional clay cooking pot (nyungu). TIPS FOR ARTISTS: 1) Look closely at the shapes: a mango is an oval with a gentle curve, an orange is a round sphere, a calabash has a narrow neck and round base. 2) Sketch lightly with your pencil first so mistakes can be rubbed off easily. 3) Color neatly inside the outlines using crayons or colored pencils without scribbling outside the borders. 4) Use light and dark pressure to make your drawing look real and three-dimensional!

examples.text: Mango drawing: Sketch an oval shape, add a small stem at the top, and color warm yellow and orange with a splash of red.
Clay pot: Draw a wide oval mouth, curved belly, and shade the side to show shadow.
Neatness: Hold the crayon comfortably and shade in one steady direction.

lessons.summary: Still-life is drawing stationary objects. Sketch lightly first, observe shapes carefully, and color smoothly within outlines.

lessons.title: Color Magic: Primary and Secondary Colors
lessons.conceptIntro: Color brings the world to life! 1) PRIMARY COLORS: The three root colors that cannot be made by mixing any other colors together are RED, YELLOW, and BLUE! 2) SECONDARY COLORS: When you mix two primary colors together in equal parts, magic happens: Red + Yellow = ORANGE (like a juicy citrus fruit or sunset)! Yellow + Blue = GREEN (like fresh leaves on a maize plant)! Blue + Red = PURPLE / VIOLET (like a ripe plum or passion fruit)! PAINTING TIPS: Always wash your paintbrush in a water container before dipping into a new color so your paints stay bright and clean.

examples.text: Red + Yellow = Orange: Mix yellow and red on your palette to paint a glowing African sunrise.
Yellow + Blue = Green: Mix blue and yellow to paint lush tea bushes in Kericho.
Brush hygiene: Swirl your paintbrush in clean water and wipe gently on a damp cloth between colors.

lessons.summary: Primary colors are Red, Yellow, and Blue. Mixing them creates secondary colors: Orange, Green, and Purple.

lessons.title: Textured Art: Mosaic and Collage Creations
lessons.conceptIntro: You do not always need paint to make stunning pictures—you can use scraps from nature and home! 1) MOSAIC: Creating a picture by gluing tiny square tesserae or small pieces of colored paper or natural seeds (yellow maize grains, brown beans, black sorghum) side by side with small gaps. 2) COLLAGE: Creating art by pasting together different materials with varied textures—such as fabric pieces (kitenge, leso), dry banana leaves, eggshells, and magazine clippings. Collage allows you to recycle waste materials into creative masterpieces while keeping our school environment clean!

examples.text: Seed mosaic: Pasting yellow maize kernels and red beans to fill in the feathers of a crested crane.
Fabric collage: Gluing scraps of floral kitenge cloth to make a colorful dress on a drawn figure.
Banana leaf collage: Pasting brown dried banana bark to create the textured walls of a traditional hut.

lessons.summary: Mosaic uses small pieces or seeds placed side by side. Collage combines varied materials (fabric, dry leaves, paper) into a textured picture.

lessons.title: The Rhythm of Weaving: Over and Under
lessons.conceptIntro: Weaving is one of the oldest and most useful indigenous crafts in Africa! To weave, we need two sets of strands: 1) WARP: The vertical strands held straight and tight in place. 2) WEFT: The horizontal strand that moves across the warp. THE GOLDEN RULE OF WEAVING: Go OVER the first strand, UNDER the next, OVER the third, UNDER the fourth! On the next row, reverse it: go UNDER where you went over, and OVER where you went under! In Kenya, artisans weave stunning items: sleeping mats (mikeka) from palm fronds at the coast, table mats from dried banana fiber, and world-famous kiondo bags from natural sisal twine.

examples.text: Paper weaving: Cut slits in a base paper for the warp, and weave colored paper weft strips over and under.
Mkeka: Traditional coastal woven palm mat used for sitting and prayers.
Sisal: Strong natural fiber from the spiky sisal plant used for ropes and kiondo baskets.

lessons.summary: Weaving uses warp (vertical) and weft (horizontal) strands in an over-and-under pattern to make mats, baskets, and cloth.

lessons.title: Plaiting and Paper Folding Magic
lessons.conceptIntro: Crafts let our nimble fingers work wonders! 1) PLAITING: Taking three strands of natural fiber (like sisal or banana bark) and crossing the outer strands over the middle strand one by one (left over center, right over center). Plaited ropes are super strong and are used to make kiondo handles, skipping ropes, and traditional headbands! 2) PAPER FOLDING (ORIGAMI): Using clean folds without scissors or glue to turn flat paper into 3D objects: a folding fan for hot afternoons, a paper boat that floats in a basin of water, or a folded drinking cup. Origami teaches accuracy, neat creases, and patience!

examples.text: 3-strand plaiting: Weave sisal strings to create a sturdy handle for a shopping kiondo.
Origami boat: Fold rectangular paper into triangles and unfold to sail a paper dhow in water.
Pleated fan: Fold paper forward and backward like an accordion to make a cooling hand fan.

lessons.summary: Plaiting uses three strands crossed over the center. Paper folding (origami) creates 3D shapes through precise creases without glue.

lessons.title: Clay Craft: Pinch Pots and Coils
lessons.conceptIntro: Clay is natural earth that becomes soft and plastic when mixed with water! Before modeling, we must KNEAD and WEDGE the clay with our palms to squeeze out trapped air bubbles. If air bubbles stay inside, the pot might crack or explode when drying or firing! 1) PINCH POT METHOD: Roll a smooth ball of clay, press your thumb into the center to create a deep well, and gently pinch the walls outward and upward between your thumb and fingers until the sides are even. 2) COIL METHOD: Roll long snakes of clay (coils) on a flat board and layer them on top of each other, smoothing the joints together to build tall vases and storage pots!

examples.text: Pinch pot: Press thumb into a clay sphere and pinch evenly to make a small cup or bowl.
Coil pot: Roll clay ropes and spiral them upward to form a traditional cooking pot (nyungu).
Smoothing: Use a damp thumb or wet sponge to smooth cracks on the outer clay walls.

lessons.summary: Knead clay to remove air bubbles. Use thumb pinching or rolled coils to shape hollow clay pots. Smooth cracks with damp fingers.

lessons.title: Sculpting Animals and Traditional Pots
lessons.conceptIntro: Sculpting brings three-dimensional characters to life! When modeling animals like a hump-backed Zebu bull, a perky chicken, or a horned goat: 1) Pull legs, head, and ears gently from the main body lump (pulling method) or attach separate pieces securely by scratching cross-hatching marks on both parts and applying wet clay glue called SLIP (scratch-and-slip method). 2) SURFACE TEXTURES: Use twigs, feathers, or bottle caps to press decorative patterns, fish scales, or cow spots into the damp clay (incising). 3) DRYING: Dry your clay models slowly in the SHADE. Never dry fresh clay directly under hot blazing sun, or it will crack and shatter!

examples.text: Bull sculpture: Model a sturdy body, shape the muscular hump, and pull out strong curved horns.
Slip adhesive: Mix clay and water into a creamy paste (slip) to glue ears and legs firmly to the body.
Shade drying: Keep clay pots in a breezy, shaded classroom corner for 3 to 5 days to dry safely.

lessons.summary: Attach clay parts securely using the scratch-and-slip method. Use twigs to carve decorative patterns. Always dry clay creations in the shade.

lessons.title: Melody & Voice: Patriotic Songs and Lullabies
lessons.conceptIntro: Singing is musical storytelling powered by the human voice! 1) SINGER’S POSTURE: Stand tall with your feet shoulder-width apart, shoulders relaxed, and breathe deeply into your belly (diaphragm). Never slouch or strain your neck! 2) VOCAL WARM-UPS: Hum gently like a honeybee (Mmm...) or glide up and down like a siren (Ooo...) to warm up your vocal cords before singing. 3) TYPES OF SONGS: Patriotic songs praise our nation Kenya, celebrate unity, and inspire hard work ("Kenya Yetu", "Tushangilie Kenya"). Lullabies are gentle, soft, rocking songs sung soothingly by mothers and caregivers to lull babies to peaceful sleep.

examples.text: Posture: Stand straight like a proud acacia tree, relaxed and breathing smoothly.
Lullaby: Sing with a soft, gentle, rocking whisper that comforts a resting baby.
Patriotic song: Sing with bright energy, clear pronunciation (diction), and a proud smile.

lessons.summary: Good singing requires upright posture, deep belly breathing, and warm-ups. Sing patriotic songs with pride and lullabies with gentle tenderness.

lessons.title: Kenyan Singing Games and Playful Dances
lessons.conceptIntro: Singing games are musical activities where singing is combined with fun rules, movement, and dramatization! Kenyan children love traditional singing games played in school playgrounds and village fields: 1) CIRCLE GAMES: Children hold hands in a circle, skip clockwise, and take turns performing playful actions in the center (such as "Koti Koti", "Barua Ndefu", or "Oware"). 2) RHYTHMIC ACTIONS: Clapping rhythms, stomping feet in time with the song’s beat, and mimicking characters (hopping like a frog, swooping like an eagle). Singing games build strong friendships, train your sense of musical rhythm, and bring boundless joy to learning!

examples.text: Clapping game: Clap your own hands, then clap your partner’s palms in sync with the song syllables.
Action song: Sing and touch head, shoulders, knees, and toes in lightning-fast rhythm.
Circle dramatization: A child acts out picking ripe mangoes in the middle of a dancing circle.

lessons.summary: Singing games combine music, movement, and play. They teach rhythm, cooperation, and traditional games passed down through childhood.

lessons.title: Pulse and Beat: Rhythm, Tempo, and Dynamics
lessons.conceptIntro: Music is built on rhythm and heartbeat! 1) STEADY BEAT (PULSE): The regular, continuous heartbeat of music that never stops (tick-tock of a clock or the steady thump of your heart). 2) RHYTHM: The pattern of long and short sounds and silences arranged over the beat (like the rhythm of the words in your name). 3) TEMPO: How fast or slow the music moves! A lullaby has a slow, gentle tempo; a running song has a fast, energetic tempo. 4) DYNAMICS: The volume of music! Soft like a whisper (piano) or loud and powerful like thunder (forte). Mastering beat and tempo allows you to play in perfect synchronization with an orchestra!

examples.text: Steady beat: Tap your foot steadily on the floor like a heartbeat: 1, 2, 3, 4!
Tempo change: A locomotive train starting slow (chug... chug...) and speeding up to fast (chug-chug-chug-chug)!
Dynamics: Singing a quiet whisper (soft) followed by a celebratory shout (loud).

lessons.summary: The beat is the steady pulse; rhythm is the pattern of notes. Tempo is speed (fast or slow); dynamics is volume (loud or soft).

lessons.title: Orchestra of Kenya: Ngoma, Kayamba, and Horns
lessons.conceptIntro: Kenya possesses a treasure chest of indigenous traditional musical instruments! 1) PERCUSSION INSTRUMENTS (MEMBRANOPHONES & IDIOPHONES): Sound made by striking or shaking. NGOMA (traditional drum with stretched animal skin, beaten with hands or sticks). KAYAMBA (woven reed tray filled with hard seeds, shaken rhythmically across the coast). CHIVOTI / FLUTES (AEROPHONES - wind instruments blown with air to produce sweet piping melodies). ABU / CORO (horns carved from hollow animal horns, blown to produce deep resonant ceremonial calls). NYATITI / ORUTU (CHORDOPHONES - stringed lyres plucked to accompany storytelling). Playing our traditional instruments keeps our heritage alive and vibrant!

examples.text: Ngoma: Stretched cowhide drum beaten with palms to provide the heartbeat of traditional dances.
Kayamba: Shaken back and forth with thumbs and wrists to produce a crisp sh-sh-sh sound.
Abu: Traditional long gourd and animal horn blown to announce important community ceremonies.

lessons.summary: Kenyan instruments include drums (ngoma), shaken rattles (kayamba), wind flutes (chivoti), horns (abu), and plucked lyres (nyatiti).

lessons.title: Motion Masters: Locomotor & Non-Locomotor Skills
lessons.conceptIntro: Our bodies are designed to move with grace, power, and speed! 1) LOCOMOTOR MOVEMENTS: Skills that travel your body from one spot to another across space. These include RUNNING (lightly on the balls of your feet with pumped arms), SKIPPING (a step-and-hop rhythm), GALLOPING (one foot leads while the back foot chases), HOPPING (bouncing on one foot), and DODGING (quick zigzag direction changes to evade an opponent). 2) NON-LOCOMOTOR MOVEMENTS: Movements performed while staying anchored in one place without traveling! Examples include BENDING at the waist, TWISTING the torso, STRETCHING arms high to the sky, SWAYING, and BALANCING steadily on one foot. SPATIAL AWARENESS: Always look ahead into open space to move smoothly without bumping into classmates!

examples.text: Skipping: Step on right foot, hop on right foot; step on left foot, hop on left foot.
Dodging: Feint to the left, then explode quickly to the right to evade a tagger on the field.
Flamingo balance: Stand stationary on one leg with arms outstretched like wings for 10 seconds.

lessons.summary: Locomotor moves travel through space (running, skipping, dodging). Non-locomotor moves stay in one spot (stretching, twisting, balancing).

lessons.title: Gymnastics Jungle: Animal Walks and Balances
lessons.conceptIntro: Gymnastics builds incredible core strength, flexibility, and balance! In Grade 3, we mimic the agile movements of Kenyan animals: 1) FROG JUMP: Crouch low into a deep squat with knees wide, place hands on the ground, and explode forward into a leaping hop! 2) CRAB WALK: Sit on the ground, place hands behind your back with palms flat, lift your hips high off the floor into a bridge, and scuttle backward or sideways like a coastal sea crab! 3) BEAR CRAWL: Walk forward on all fours with hands and feet flat on the ground and knees kept slightly bent. 4) STORK BALANCE: Stand tall on one leg with the sole of the opposite foot pressed against your inner calf and arms held wide like wings. Focus your eyes on a still point to remain perfectly steady!

examples.text: Frog jump: Squat deep, touch grass with palms, and leap forward powerfully like a tree frog.
Crab walk: Lift stomach high, walk on hands and heels across the gym mat.
Focus point: Stare at a fixed leaf or spot on the wall to hold a one-legged balance without wobbling.

lessons.summary: Animal walks (frog jump, crab walk, bear crawl) strengthen muscles. Focusing your eyes on a still point helps you balance like a stork.

lessons.title: Ball Play Fundamentals: Throw, Catch, and Kick
lessons.conceptIntro: Ball games are thrilling and teach teamwork! 1) CATCHING: Always keep your eyes glued to the incoming ball. Extend both hands forward with fingers spread soft like a basket ("soft hands") and pull the ball gently into your chest as you catch to absorb the impact! 2) PASSING: Chest pass (push the ball outward from your chest with both thumbs pointing down) and bounce pass (bounce the ball two-thirds of the way toward your teammate). 3) KICKING: Use the INSTEP (the flat inside of your foot) for accurate, controlled passing along the ground, rather than toe-poking which hurts your toes and sends the ball wild! 4) IMPROVISED BALLS: You can make an amazing soccer ball by wrapping plastic shopping bags or old socks tightly with banana twine or sisal rope!

examples.text: Soft hands catch: Reach forward, let ball meet fingertips, cushion inward to the chest.
Instep pass: Turn foot sideways, strike center of ball with the inside arch to pass accurately.
Improvised ball: Stuff old socks and polythene, bind tightly with sisal twine into a durable soccer ball.

lessons.summary: Catch with soft hands pulling to the chest. Pass with chest or bounce pass. Kick using the instep. Improvise balls using socks and twine.

lessons.title: Kenyan Playground Classics: Kati, Kibe, and Fair Play
lessons.conceptIntro: Kenyan playgrounds are full of laughter with traditional games! 1) KATI (DODGEBALL): Two throwers stand at opposite ends, while players dodge in the middle trying not to get hit below the waist. Catching the ball earns a "life" to save an eliminated friend! 2) KIBE (HIDE AND SEEK TAG): The seeker counts with eyes closed against a home tree or wall while others hide. Once found, players race back to the home base ("kibe base") before the seeker tags them! 3) BANO (MARBLES): Players flick glass marbles into a small ground hole or strike opponents’ marbles. 4) FAIR PLAY & SPORTSMANSHIP: True champions respect the referee, never cheat, encourage struggling teammates, and shake hands with opponents with a warm smile after every match!

examples.text: Kati: Jump, duck, and dodge as the soft ball flies across the middle court.
Kibe: Sprint to touch the home tree shouting "Kibe!" before the seeker catches you.
Sportsmanship: High-fiving your opponent after the final whistle and saying "Great game!"

lessons.summary: Traditional games like Kati and Kibe promote agility and strategic play. Play with honesty, follow game rules, and celebrate fair play.

lessons.title: Fit and Fuelled: Warm-Ups, Water, and Rest
lessons.conceptIntro: A healthy body is your greatest treasure! 1) WARM-UPS: Always start physical activities with 5 minutes of gentle dynamic movements (jogging on the spot, arm circles, high knees). Warm-ups increase heart rate, warm cold muscles, and prevent painful muscle strains! 2) COOL-DOWNS: After intense play, slow down gradually with gentle walking and slow static stretches (calf stretch, hamstring reach) to help heart rate return to normal. 3) HYDRATION: When you run and sweat, your body loses precious water! Drink clean, safe drinking water before, during, and after exercise—never wait until you are severely parched. 4) REST & SLEEP: Children need 8 to 10 hours of peaceful sleep each night so growing muscles and brains can repair and recharge for a bright new day!

examples.text: Dynamic warm-up: High knees and gentle arm swings for 3 minutes before a race.
Hydration: Sip clean water from your school water bottle during halftime.
Cool-down: Gentle walking around the track and slow toe-touch stretches.

lessons.summary: Warm up before sports to prevent injury; cool down after play. Drink clean water to stay hydrated, and get 8-10 hours of sleep for healthy growth.

lessons.title: Aquatic Guardians: Water Safety and River Rules
lessons.conceptIntro: Water is wonderful for swimming and cooling down, but it requires deep respect and strict safety rules! 1) GOLDEN RULE: NEVER swim alone or enter water without a responsible adult or lifeguard watching! 2) RIVER & FLOOD SAFETY: During the rainy seasons in Kenya, rivers and seasonal dry riverbeds (lagas) can swell rapidly into deadly flash floods! Never attempt to cross flooded rivers or play near muddy, slippery riverbanks. 3) POOL RULES: Walk—never run—on wet slippery pool decks to prevent bad falls. Do not push friends into the water. Only enter the shallow end if you are learning to swim! 4) RESCUE RULE: If a friend struggles in deep water, NEVER jump in yourself! Reach with a long stick or branch, throw a floating plastic jerrycan or tyre tube, and shout loudly for adult help immediately!

examples.text: Reach and throw: Extend a long bamboo stick or throw an empty sealed jerrycan to someone struggling in water.
Never swim alone: Always have a teacher, parent, or certified lifeguard present at the water.
Rainy season rule: Stay far away from raging swollen rivers like River Nzoia or Tana during downpours.

lessons.summary: Never swim alone. Stay away from swollen flooded rivers. In an emergency, reach with a stick or throw a floating object and call an adult immediately.

lessons.title: Wonderfully Made: God’s Gift of Life and Senses
lessons.conceptIntro: The Bible teaches us in Psalm 139:14: "I praise you because I am fearfully and wonderfully made!" God created every child unique with a special name, purpose, and loving heart. God also blessed our bodies with FIVE SENSES: 1) Eyes to see the beautiful sunrise over Mount Kenya and read Bible stories. 2) Ears to hear church hymns and listen to parents and teachers. 3) Nose to smell fragrant acacia flowers and fresh rain on the soil. 4) Tongue to taste sweet ripe mangoes and speak kind words. 5) Skin to feel warm sunshine and gentle hugs. We honor God by keeping our bodies clean, eating nutritious food, and using our senses to do good deeds!

examples.text: Unique creation: Even identical twins have different fingerprints created by God!
Sense of speech: Using our tongues to speak truth and encourage sad friends.
Body care: Bathing daily, brushing teeth, and avoiding dangerous substances.

lessons.summary: God created each of us uniquely in His image. Our five senses are gifts from God that we must care for and use to do good.

lessons.title: Caring for God’s World: Shambas, Plants, and Animals
lessons.conceptIntro: In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth, the lush green plants, and every animal that walks, flies, or swims (Genesis 1). God placed human beings in the Garden of Eden to care for and protect His creation! As Kenyan children, we are God’s junior caretakers: 1) We plant and water seedlings in the school shamba so they grow into fruit-bearing trees. 2) We feed our domestic livestock (cows, goats, chickens) and never mistreat animals. 3) We do not litter plastic waste or pollute streams. When we protect nature, we show reverence and love to God our Creator!

examples.text: Tree planting: Planting an indigenous tree seedling at school to provide shade and clean air.
Humane care: Giving clean drinking water to thirsty working donkeys and chickens.
Clean streams: Refusing to throw polythene trash into community water sources.

lessons.summary: God made the earth, plants, and animals, and appointed us as caretakers. We honor God by planting trees, watering crops, and being kind to animals.

lessons.title: The Holy Book: Old and New Testaments
lessons.conceptIntro: The Bible is no ordinary book—it is the Holy Word of God! God inspired holy prophets and apostles over hundreds of years to write His promises and guidance for us. The Bible is divided into TWO MAIN PARTS: 1) OLD TESTAMENT: Contains 39 books, starting with Genesis and ending with Malachi. It tells the story of creation, Abraham, Moses, and the journey of the people of Israel before Jesus was born. 2) NEW TESTAMENT: Contains 27 books, starting with Matthew and ending with Revelation. It tells the life, teachings, miracles, death, and resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ, and how the early church grew! Together, there are 66 books in the Bible. HANDLING THE BIBLE: Keep your Bible in a clean, dry place, turn pages gently with clean hands, and read a verse every day to light your path (Psalm 119:105)!

examples.text: Old Testament: 39 books sharing stories of Noah, Abraham, Moses, and David.
New Testament: 27 books containing the four Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke, John).
Total books: 39 + 27 = 66 books making up the Holy Bible!

lessons.summary: The Bible has 66 books: 39 in the Old Testament and 27 in the New Testament. It is God’s Word that guides our daily lives.

lessons.title: Heroes of Faith: Young Samuel and Brave David
lessons.conceptIntro: The Bible is filled with young boys and girls who trusted God! 1) YOUNG SAMUEL: When Samuel was a young boy serving Priest Eli in the temple at Shiloh, God called him at night: "Samuel! Samuel!" Samuel ran to Eli thinking Eli was calling him. Eli realized God was calling the boy and told him to reply: "Speak, Lord, for your servant is listening." Samuel listened obediently and became a great prophet of God! 2) BRAVE DAVID: David was a young shepherd boy who watched over his father’s sheep in the fields. When the giant Philistine warrior Goliath terrified King Saul’s entire army, David was not afraid. Armed only with his shepherd’s staff, five smooth river stones, a sling, and deep FAITH IN GOD, David defeated Goliath! David declared: "You come against me with sword and spear, but I come against you in the name of the Lord Almighty!"

examples.text: Samuel’s obedience: Saying "Speak, Lord, for your servant is listening" whenever we pray or hear God’s Word.
David’s faith: Facing big challenges with courage because God is always greater than any giant problem!
Five smooth stones: Trusting God’s power rather than heavy armor and weapons.

lessons.summary: Young Samuel listened to God’s voice with obedience. Shepherd boy David defeated giant Goliath through steadfast faith in God.

lessons.title: The Savior is Born: Bethlehem, Shepherds, and Wise Men
lessons.conceptIntro: Christmas is the joyful celebration of the birth of Jesus Christ, the Son of God! Jesus was not born in a grand golden palace, but in a humble animal stable in the small town of Bethlehem because there was no room in the inn (Luke 2). His mother Mary wrapped Him in swaddling clothes and laid Him in a feeding trough (manger). Angels lit up the night sky singing "Glory to God in the highest!" to humble shepherds tending their sheep in the fields. Guided by a bright shining star, Wise Men (Magi) traveled from the East to worship Baby Jesus and presented three royal gifts: GOLD (for a King), FRANKINCENSE (incense for God), and MYRRH (sweet-smelling ointment). Jesus’ humble birth shows that God loves everyone, especially the humble and poor!

examples.text: Manger: A wooden or stone feeding box for cattle where Baby Jesus lay asleep.
Wise Men’s gifts: Gold, Frankincense, and Myrrh presented to King Jesus.
Christmas spirit: Sharing food and gifts with poor neighbors during Christmas in Kenya.

lessons.summary: Jesus was born in a humble manger in Bethlehem. Shepherds and Wise Men praised Him with gifts. Christmas celebrates God’s love and giving.

lessons.title: River Jordan and the Call to Follow: Baptism and Disciples
lessons.conceptIntro: When Jesus grew into a man, He walked to River Jordan where His cousin, John the Baptist, was preaching repentance. Even though Jesus was sinless, He asked John to baptize Him to fulfill all righteousness! As Jesus came up out of the water, heaven opened, the Holy Spirit descended like a gentle DOVE, and God’s voice boomed from heaven: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased!" (Matthew 3:17). Soon after, while walking along the shores of the Sea of Galilee, Jesus saw two fishermen brothers, Simon Peter and Andrew, casting nets. Jesus called them: "Come, follow me, and I will make you fishers of men!" They immediately left their fishing nets to follow Jesus. They were later joined by James, John, and others, forming the twelve disciples!

examples.text: Holy Spirit symbol: Descended like a gentle white dove onto Jesus at baptism.
God’s confirmation: The Father’s voice from heaven declaring Jesus as His beloved Son.
Fishers of men: Disciples were called to spread the gospel and win people’s hearts to God.

lessons.summary: John baptized Jesus in River Jordan as the Holy Spirit descended like a dove. Jesus called fishermen Peter and Andrew to become fishers of men.

lessons.title: The Wonder-Working Savior: Storms and Bread
lessons.conceptIntro: Jesus performed miracles because of His deep love and divine authority! 1) CALMING THE STORM: One evening, a fierce storm struck the boat carrying Jesus and His disciples on the Sea of Galilee. Giant waves threatened to sink the boat, but Jesus was asleep on a cushion! Terrified, the disciples woke Him: "Teacher, don’t you care if we drown?" Jesus stood up, rebuked the wind, and commanded the raging waves: "Quiet! Be still!" Immediately, the storm ceased and there was perfect calm! 2) FEEDING THE FIVE THOUSAND: A huge crowd of hungry people had followed Jesus all day. A young boy generously offered his small lunch: FIVE BARLEY LOAVES AND TWO SMALL FISH. Jesus gave thanks to God, broke the bread, and miraculously fed over 5,000 people, with twelve baskets of leftovers gathered! When we give what little we have to Jesus, He multiplies it to bless everyone!

examples.text: Peace in storms: Praying to Jesus when feeling frightened by dark thunderstorms or sickness.
A boy’s lunch: Giving a little shared snack to feed many hungry friends in need.
Leftovers: Twelve full baskets gathered, showing God’s bountiful abundance.

lessons.summary: Jesus calmed the fierce storm with a word and fed 5,000 with a boy’s five loaves and two fish. Jesus has power over nature and provides for our needs.

lessons.title: Who is My Neighbor? The Good Samaritan
lessons.conceptIntro: When an expert in the law asked Jesus, "Who is my neighbor?", Jesus told this unforgettable parable (Luke 10): A Jewish traveler was walking down from Jerusalem to Jericho when robbers attacked him, beat him, stole his clothes, and left him half dead by the roadside. Soon, a PRIEST walked by, saw the injured man, and passed by on the other side. A LEVITE came next, looked at him, and also crossed to the opposite side without helping. Then, a SAMARITAN (whom Jews disliked) arrived. Filled with deep pity, the Samaritan bound the man’s wounds with oil and wine, set him on his own donkey, took him to an inn, and paid for all his medical care! Jesus asked: "Which of these three was a true neighbor?" The expert replied: "The one who showed mercy." Jesus commanded: "Go and do likewise!"

examples.text: Mercy over prejudice: Helping anyone who is hurt regardless of their tribe, county, or religion.
First aid compassion: Bandaging wounds and taking care of the sick.
True neighbor: Showing love in practical action, not just words.

lessons.summary: The Good Samaritan showed mercy to a wounded stranger when religious leaders ignored him. Jesus commands us to love and help anyone in need.

lessons.title: Transformed Heart: The Story of Zacchaeus
lessons.conceptIntro: God’s love has the power to change any heart! In the town of Jericho, there lived a chief tax collector named ZACCHAEUS. He was very wealthy because he often cheated taxpayers and took more money than required, so people despised him. Because Zacchaeus was short in stature and could not see over the large crowd, he ran ahead and climbed a SYCAMORE-FIG TREE so he could catch a glimpse of Jesus passing by! When Jesus reached the spot, He looked up and called with warmth: "Zacchaeus, hurry down! Today I must stay at your house!" Filled with overwhelming joy that Jesus showed him love, Zacchaeus repented: "Look, Lord! Here and now I give half of my possessions to the poor, and if I have cheated anybody out of anything, I will pay back FOUR TIMES the amount!" Jesus declared: "Today salvation has come to this house!"

examples.text: Sycamore tree: Climbing up to seek Jesus despite being short in stature.
Restitution: Paying back four times what he cheated to make things right.
Grace: Jesus offers forgiveness and a fresh clean start to anyone who repents.

lessons.summary: Short Zacchaeus climbed a sycamore tree to see Jesus. Welcomed by Christ’s love, he repented of cheating, paid back fourfold, and gave half his wealth to the poor.

lessons.title: Fruit of the Spirit: Obedience, Sharing, and Peace
lessons.conceptIntro: As followers of Jesus, our everyday lives should shine with God’s love! 1) OBEDIENCE TO PARENTS: Ephesians 6:1-3 tells us: "Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right. Honor your father and mother—which is the first commandment with a promise—that it may go well with you and that you may enjoy long life on the earth!" 2) FORGIVENESS: When someone wrongs us or takes our pencil without asking, we choose to forgive them just as God forgives our mistakes (Ephesians 4:32). We never hold grudges or plan revenge. 3) SHARING AND CHARITY: James 1:27 teaches that pure religion before God is visiting orphans and widows in their distress. When we share our harvest, old clothes, or storybooks with disadvantaged children, we share the light of Christ in Kenya!

examples.text: Obedience: Doing home chores promptly and cheerfully without grumbling.
Forgiveness: Saying "I forgive you" with a sincere heart when a friend apologizes.
Charity: Donating food to a local children’s home during school thanksgiving.

lessons.summary: Honor and obey parents for a blessed life. Forgive those who hurt you, and share blessings with orphans and the needy.

lessons.title: Surah Al-Fatihah and Surah Al-Ikhlas
lessons.conceptIntro: The Holy Qur'an is the divine, unchangeable Word of Allah (SWT) revealed to our beloved Prophet Muhammad (SAW) through Angel Jibril (AS)! 1) SURAH AL-FATIHAH ("The Opening"): The greatest Surah in the Qur'an and the foundation of every prayer (Salah). It teaches us to praise Allah, the Lord of all the worlds, Most Gracious, Most Merciful, and ask Him alone for guidance along the straight path (Sirat al-Mustaqim). 2) SURAH AL-IKHLAS ("The Sincerity"): Proclaims Tawhid—the absolute Oneness of Allah! "Say: He is Allah, the One! Allah, the Eternal Refuge! He neither begets nor is born, nor is there to Him any equivalent!" Reciting Surah Al-Ikhlas rewards the reader with the blessing equivalent to one-third of the entire Qur'an!

examples.text: Al-Fatihah in Salah: Recited in every single unit (Rak’ah) of the five daily prayers.
Tawhid in Al-Ikhlas: Allah is Unique, has no partners, no parents, and no children.
Reverence: Saying "A’udhu billahi minash-shaytanir-rajim" and "Bismillahir-Rahmanir-Rahim" before recitation.

lessons.summary: Surah Al-Fatihah opens the Qur'an and is recited in every Salah. Surah Al-Ikhlas affirms that Allah is One, Eternal, and has no partners.

lessons.title: The Mu’awwidhatayn and Respecting the Holy Qur'an
lessons.conceptIntro: Allah provides divine protection through His sacred words! 1) SURAH AL-FALAQ ("The Daybreak") and SURAH AN-NAS ("Mankind"): Together they are called the MU’AWWIDHATAYN (the two Surahs of protection). In Al-Falaq, we seek refuge with the Lord of daybreak from the evil of created things and from envy. In An-Nas, we seek refuge with the Lord and King of mankind from whispers of the devil (Waswas). Prophet Muhammad (SAW) taught us to recite them before sleeping for protection. 2) ETIQUETTE OF THE QUR'AN: Always be in a state of cleanliness (Wudhu) before touching the physical Arabic text (Mushaf). Place the Qur'an on a clean, elevated table or stand (Rihal), never place other items on top of it, and listen quietly with respect when it is recited!

examples.text: Nightly protection: Cupping hands, reciting Al-Ikhlas, Al-Falaq, and An-Nas, and wiping over the body before sleep.
Mushaf care: Keeping the Holy Book wrapped in clean cloth on a high, dignified shelf.
Attentive listening: Remaining silent and listening when the Qur'an is recited in the mosque or home.

lessons.summary: Surah Al-Falaq and An-Nas grant divine protection against evil whispers. Treat the Holy Qur'an with deep respect, handle it with Wudhu, and place it high.

lessons.title: Blessed Beginnings: Birth and Childhood in the Desert
lessons.conceptIntro: Prophet Muhammad (SAW) was born in the holy city of Makkah in the Year of the Elephant (570 CE) on the 12th of Rabi’ al-Awwal. His father, Abdullah, passed away before he was born. In accordance with Arab tradition, baby Muhammad was entrusted to a loving foster mother named HALIMAH AS-SA’DIYYAH from the desert tribe of Banu Sa’d. While raising Muhammad, miraculous blessings filled Halimah’s home: their sheep produced abundant milk and their shamba flourished! Young Muhammad grew up strong, speaking the purest Arabic, and learning patience. When he was six years old, his mother Aminah passed away on their journey back from Madinah. His loving grandfather ABDUL MUTTALIB cared for him until he too passed away, after which his kind uncle ABU TALIB raised him with great affection!

examples.text: Birthplace: Born in the holy city of Makkah into the noble Hashim clan of Quraysh.
Halimah’s blessings: Her animals and household were showered with divine Barakah.
Orphan’s care: Experiencing loss early taught Muhammad (SAW) deep empathy for orphans and the poor.

lessons.summary: Prophet Muhammad (SAW) was born in Makkah, spent his early childhood in the desert with Halimah, and was cared for by grandfather Abdul Muttalib and uncle Abu Talib.

lessons.title: The Trustworthy One: The Title Al-Amin
lessons.conceptIntro: As young Muhammad (SAW) grew into a young man, he worked as a shepherd herding sheep, and later accompanied his uncle Abu Talib on trading caravans to Syria. Everyone in Makkah admired him because he NEVER told a lie, never cheated in weighing or measuring goods, never broke a promise, and never worshiped idols! The people of Makkah—even those who later opposed Islam—trusted him with their most precious jewelry and money for safekeeping. Because of his exceptional truthfulness and reliability, all of Makkah gave him the title AL-AMIN (The Trustworthy) and AS-SADIQ (The Truthful)! A Muslim child should strive to be like Prophet Muhammad (SAW): always tell the truth, return borrowed items in perfect condition, and keep promises!

examples.text: Al-Amin in trade: Accurately calculating change and never exaggerating product quality.
Safe custodian: Citizens trusted Muhammad (SAW) to guard their wealth when traveling.
Childhood reflection: Returning a borrowed pencil or ruler to a classmate promptly and undamaged.

lessons.summary: Prophet Muhammad (SAW) was known as Al-Amin (The Trustworthy) because of his flawless honesty, justice in trade, and reliability.

lessons.title: Peaceful Greetings and Dining Manners
lessons.conceptIntro: Islam is a complete way of life that teaches beautiful manners from morning to night! 1) THE GREETING OF PEACE: When meeting a fellow Muslim, greet with warmth: "AS-SALAMU ALAYKUM WA RAHMATULLAHI WA BARAKATUH" (May the peace, mercy, and blessings of Allah be upon you!). The response is even better: "WA ALAYKUMUS-SALAM WA RAHMATULLAHI WA BARAKATUH!" Spreading Salam spreads love, removes hatred, and earns multiple rewards. 2) SUNNAH DINING MANNERS: Always wash hands before eating. Say "BISMILLAH" (In the name of Allah) before taking the first bite. Eat with your RIGHT HAND, eat from what is directly in front of you on the plate, chew food quietly, and do not waste a single grain. When finished, express gratitude to Allah by saying: "ALHAMDULILLAH" (All praise is due to Allah)!

examples.text: Salam: Greet classmates, family members, and teachers with a smiling "As-salamu alaykum".
Eating right: Use your right hand to eat ugali, rice, or chapatis, following the Prophet’s Sunnah.
Saying Bismillah: Saying Bismillah invites Allah’s Barakah into your food.

lessons.summary: Spread the greeting of Salam to build love. When eating, say Bismillah, use your right hand, eat moderately, and say Alhamdulillah when finished.

lessons.title: Honoring Parents and Loving Neighbors
lessons.conceptIntro: Good character (Akhlaq) is the heaviest deed on the scales on the Day of Judgment! 1) BIRR AL-WALIDAYN (HONORING PARENTS): Allah commands us in the Qur'an right after worshiping Him to be kind and obedient to parents (Surah Al-Isra 17:23). Never say even "Uff!" (a sign of disrespect or irritation) to your mother or father! A man asked the Prophet (SAW): "Who deserves my best companionship?" The Prophet replied: "Your mother, then your mother, then your mother, then your father!" 2) HUSN AL-JIWAR (KINDNESS TO NEIGHBORS): Angel Jibril emphasized kindness to neighbors so often that the Prophet thought neighbors would inherit property! We must never disturb our neighbors with loud noise, and we should share food and assist them during sickness.

examples.text: Helping parents: Sweeping the compound, fetching water, and answering parents promptly with "Na'am".
Mother’s status: Paradise lies beneath the feet of mothers, taught our Prophet (SAW).
Neighbor’s soup: The Prophet advised adding extra water to stew so you can share a bowl with your neighbor!

lessons.summary: Honor parents with love and obedience; a mother holds highest status. Be kind to neighbors by sharing food and maintaining peace.

lessons.title: The Five Pillars of Islam and Steps of Wudhu
lessons.conceptIntro: Islam is built upon FIVE STRONG PILLARS: 1) SHAHADAH: Declaring "Ash-hadu an la ilaha illallah, wa ash-hadu anna Muhammadan Rasulullah" (There is no god but Allah, and Muhammad is His Messenger). 2) SALAH: The five daily prayers connecting us directly to Allah. 3) ZAKAT: Giving charity to the poor and needy. 4) SAWM: Fasting during the holy month of Ramadhan. 5) HAJJ: Pilgrimage to the Holy Ka’bah in Makkah once in a lifetime for those who are able. THE KEY TO SALAH IS WUDHU (Ablution): Without clean Wudhu, prayer is not accepted! Wudhu steps in order: Intention (Niyyah) and Bismillah -> Wash hands to wrists 3x -> Rinse mouth 3x -> Sniff water into nose and blow out 3x -> Wash face completely 3x -> Wash arms from fingertips to elbows (right then left) 3x -> Wipe wet hands over hair from front to back 1x -> Wipe inside and outside of ears 1x -> Wash feet up to the ankles (right then left) 3x! Always conserve water and never waste drops!

examples.text: Shahadah: The fundamental testimony of faith entering Islam.
Water conservation: The Prophet (SAW) performed complete Wudhu using only one Mudd (a small cup of water).
Sequence: Performing each step of Wudhu in its correct order without skipping.

lessons.summary: The 5 Pillars are Shahadah, Salah, Zakat, Sawm, and Hajj. Wudhu is ritual purification required for prayer; wash in sequence and conserve water.

lessons.title: The Five Daily Prayers: Timings and Rak'ahs
lessons.conceptIntro: Salah is the daily spiritual heartbeat of a Muslim! Allah gifted us FIVE OBLIGATORY PRAYERS (Fardh) each day: 1) FAJR: The dawn prayer before sunrise (2 Rak'ahs). It wakes your soul to praise Allah! 2) DHUHR: The midday prayer just after noon (4 Rak'ahs). 3) ASR: The afternoon prayer before the sun begins to set (4 Rak'ahs). 4) MAGHRIB: The sunset prayer immediately after the sun dips below the horizon (3 Rak'ahs). 5) ISHA: The night prayer when darkness sets in (4 Rak'ahs). Total daily obligatory units: 2 + 4 + 4 + 3 + 4 = 17 RAK'AHS! Salah teaches us punctuality, cleanses our sins like bathing five times a day in a pure river, and brings peace to our hearts!

examples.text: Fajr (2 Rak'ahs): Dawn prayer starting the day in Allah’s light.
Dhuhr & Asr (4 Rak'ahs each): Midday and afternoon prayers renewing our focus.
Maghrib (3 Rak'ahs) & Isha (4 Rak'ahs): Evening prayers concluding the day in gratitude.

lessons.summary: The five daily prayers are Fajr (2), Dhuhr (4), Asr (4), Maghrib (3), and Isha (4), totaling 17 Rak'ahs. Salah cleanses sins and brings inner peace.

lessons.title: Paramatma and the Trimurti
lessons.content: Paramatma is the one Supreme Reality who fills the entire universe with life and beauty. In Hindu tradition, Paramatma's three cosmic cosmic duties are represented by the Trimurti: Lord Brahma brings forth creation, Lord Vishnu preserves and cares for life, and Lord Shiva brings about healthy renewal and transformation. When we look at nature—trees blossoming, rivers flowing, and seasons changing—we witness this wonderful cosmic harmony.
lessons.workedExample: Aarav in Mombasa watches the ocean tide. He remembers that Paramatma sustains the sea and all living creatures through divine order.
lessons.kenyanExample: Children visiting Nairobi National Park thank Paramatma for the majestic zebras and tall acacia trees created in nature.

lessons.title: Avatars of Righteousness: Rama and Krishna
lessons.content: An Avatar is a divine manifestation that descends whenever the world needs protection, peace, and righteous guidance (Dharma). Shri Rama showed everyone how to be an obedient child, a loyal brother, and a fair ruler who always speaks the truth. Shri Krishna taught love, joy, friendship, and duty, advising us to always protect good people and do our best without selfishness.
lessons.workedExample: Meera shares her storybook with classmates in Kisumu. She says, 'Shri Krishna taught us that true friendship is based on kindness and generosity.'
lessons.kenyanExample: In Parklands, Grade 3 pupils stage a short play depicting how Prince Rama respected his parents and kept his promises.

lessons.title: Sacred Scriptures: Vedas and Gita
lessons.content: Sacred scriptures are books of divine wisdom that guide our thoughts and actions. The Vedas are the earliest and most sacred scriptures, containing hymns of praise to the divine. The Ramayana tells the inspiring life story of Shri Rama and Sita Devi. The Bhagavad Gita is the sacred conversation where Shri Krishna teaches the warrior Arjuna about courage, duty, devotion, and peace.
lessons.workedExample: Siddharth handles the Bhagavad Gita gently with clean hands, placing it on a clean cloth stand with reverence.
lessons.kenyanExample: Pupils in Parklands Hindu Temple library read illustrated stories from the Ramayana to learn about courage and truth.

lessons.title: Sacred Symbols: Aum and the Diya
lessons.content: Hindu tradition uses sacred symbols to remind us of divine truths. Aum (Om) is the primordial sacred sound representing Paramatma and the entire universe; chanting Aum brings calm to our minds. The Swastika is an ancient sacred symbol representing good fortune, peace, and auspiciousness. The Diya is a small clay oil lamp whose gentle flame reminds us that knowledge dispels darkness and ignorance.
lessons.workedExample: Ananya chants 'Aum Shanti Shanti Shanti' before studying. She feels peaceful, focused, and ready to learn.
lessons.kenyanExample: During Diwali celebrations in Nairobi, families place lighted Diyas at their front doors to welcome peace and brightness into their homes.

lessons.title: Sadachar: Satya, Ahimsa, and Sewa
lessons.content: Sadachar means good and noble conduct. Three foundational virtues guide every Hindu learner: Satya (speaking the truth gently and honestly), Ahimsa (non-violence, never harming any creature through words, thoughts, or deeds), and Sewa (selfless service to help others without seeking praise). When we help clean our classroom, feed hungry animals, or assist elderly neighbors, we practice true Dharma in daily life.
lessons.workedExample: Kunal finds a lost pencil case in class. Remembering Satya, he promptly hands it to the teacher so it can be returned to its owner.
lessons.kenyanExample: Pupils at Visa Oshwal Primary in Nairobi participate in a food donation drive, preparing grain packets for needy families as an act of Sewa.

lessons.title: Festivals of Joy: Diwali and Holi
lessons.content: Hindu festivals bring communities together in gratitude, prayer, and joy. Diwali (Festival of Lights) celebrates the victory of light over darkness and good over evil; families wear festive clothes, light Diyas, and share sweets. Holi (Festival of Colors) celebrates the arrival of spring, friendship, and forgiveness, where people gently sprinkle bright organic colors. Janmashtami celebrates the joyful birth of Shri Krishna with bhajans, dancing, and devotion.
lessons.workedExample: Diya prepares delicious barfi sweets with her mother and packs boxes to share with their Kenyan neighbors of all faiths during Diwali.
lessons.kenyanExample: In Mombasa, Hindu families open their homes during Diwali to share sweets and good wishes with their neighbors, promoting national unity and friendship.

lessons.title: Place Value and Total Value up to 10,000
lessons.content: In Grade 4, numbers expand into thousands! In a 4-digit number like 4,825, each digit holds a specific place: Thousands (Th), Hundreds (H), Tens (T), and Ones (O). The place value is the position of the digit, while the total value is what that digit is actually worth. For example, in 4,825, the digit 4 is in the Thousands place, so its total value is 4 × 1,000 = 4,000.
lessons.workedExample: Find the total value of 7 in 6,732. The digit 7 sits in the Hundreds place, so its total value is 7 × 100 = 700.
lessons.kenyanExample: A farmers' cooperative in Nyeri harvested 5,340 bags of coffee beans. In 5,340, the digit 5 has a total value of 5,000 bags!

lessons.title: Number Words, Rounding Off, and Even/Odd Numbers
lessons.content: We write numbers in words by stating thousands, hundreds, tens, and ones clearly. To round off to the nearest 10, examine the ones digit: if it is 5, 6, 7, 8, or 9, round up to the next ten; if it is 0, 1, 2, 3, or 4, keep the ten and change ones to 0. Even numbers end in 0, 2, 4, 6, or 8, while odd numbers end in 1, 3, 5, 7, or 9.
lessons.workedExample: Round 347 to the nearest 10. The ones digit is 7, which is 5 or more. So 347 rounds up to 350.
lessons.kenyanExample: At Machakos bus terminus, a conductor counts 48 passengers boarding a bus to Kitui. Rounded to the nearest 10, there are 50 passengers.

lessons.title: Adding 4-Digit Numbers without Regrouping
lessons.content: When adding large numbers vertically, write each digit directly under its correct place value: Ones under Ones, Tens under Tens, Hundreds under Hundreds, and Thousands under Thousands. Always begin adding from the Ones column on the right and work your way steadily to the left.
lessons.workedExample: Add 3,214 + 1,462. Ones: 4 + 2 = 6. Tens: 1 + 6 = 7. Hundreds: 2 + 4 = 6. Thousands: 3 + 1 = 4. The total sum is 4,676.
lessons.kenyanExample: A community dairy cooperative in Meru collected 2,340 litres of milk on Friday and 1,525 litres on Saturday. In total, they received 2,340 + 1,525 = 3,865 litres of milk.

lessons.title: Adding with Regrouping (Carrying Over)
lessons.content: When the sum in any place value column is 10 or greater, we regroup. We write the ones digit in that column and carry the tens over to the next column to the left. Remember to add the carried-over digit to that column!
lessons.workedExample: Add 4,586 + 2,745. Ones: 6 + 5 = 11 (write 1, carry 1). Tens: 8 + 4 + 1 = 13 (write 3, carry 1). Hundreds: 5 + 7 + 1 = 13 (write 3, carry 1). Thousands: 4 + 2 + 1 = 7. The sum is 7,331.
lessons.kenyanExample: Pupils in Machakos planted 1,685 tree seedlings in Term 1 and 2,478 seedlings in Term 2. Total trees planted = 1,685 + 2,478 = 4,163.

lessons.title: Subtracting 4-Digit Numbers without Regrouping
lessons.content: When subtracting large numbers vertically, write each digit directly under its corresponding place value. Always begin subtracting the bottom digit from the top digit starting at the Ones column on the right, moving leftward through Tens, Hundreds, and Thousands.
lessons.workedExample: Subtract 5,876 - 2,431. Ones: 6 - 1 = 5. Tens: 7 - 3 = 4. Hundreds: 8 - 4 = 4. Thousands: 5 - 2 = 3. The difference is 3,445.
lessons.kenyanExample: A wholesale duka in Gikomba market started with 4,980 kg of dry beans. By noon, 2,650 kg were sold. The remaining stock is 4,980 - 2,650 = 2,330 kg.

lessons.title: Subtracting with Regrouping (Borrowing)
lessons.content: When a top digit is smaller than the bottom digit in the same column, we borrow (regroup) from the next column to the left. 1 ten becomes 10 ones, 1 hundred becomes 10 tens, and 1 thousand becomes 10 hundreds. Subtract each column carefully after regrouping.
lessons.workedExample: Subtract 6,325 - 2,784. Ones: 5 - 4 = 1. Tens: 2 is smaller than 8; borrow 1 hundred (leaves 2 hundreds) to make 12 tens; 12 - 8 = 4. Hundreds: 2 is smaller than 7; borrow 1 thousand (leaves 5 thousands) to make 12 hundreds; 12 - 7 = 5. Thousands: 5 - 2 = 3. Result = 3,541.
lessons.kenyanExample: A school rainwater tank in Kitui holds 8,500 litres. The school used 3,745 litres for cooking and the tree nursery. Remaining water = 8,500 - 3,745 = 4,755 litres.

lessons.title: Multiplying 2-Digit Numbers by 1-Digit Numbers
lessons.content: When multiplying a 2-digit number by a 1-digit number, multiply the ones digit first, then multiply the tens digit. If the product of the ones digit is 10 or more, write the ones digit and carry over the tens to add after multiplying the tens.
lessons.workedExample: Multiply 36 × 4. Ones: 6 × 4 = 24 (write 4, carry 2). Tens: 3 × 4 = 12. Add carried 2: 12 + 2 = 14. The product is 144.
lessons.kenyanExample: A poultry farmer in Kiambu packs eggs in trays. If she has 8 trays with 30 eggs each, she has 30 × 8 = 240 eggs altogether.

lessons.title: Multiplying by Multiples of 10 and 2-Digit Numbers
lessons.content: When multiplying any number by 10, shift each digit one place to the left and append a 0. For example, 45 × 10 = 450. When multiplying by a 2-digit number, calculate partial products: multiply by the ones digit first, then by the tens digit (inserting a 0 in the ones place), and add the results.
lessons.workedExample: Multiply 23 × 14. Partial product 1: 23 × 4 = 92. Partial product 2: 23 × 10 = 230. Add: 92 + 230 = 322.
lessons.kenyanExample: A fruit trader in Kongowea market sells boxes of mangoes. Each box holds 25 mangoes. For 15 boxes, there are 25 × 15 = 375 mangoes.

lessons.title: Division without Remainder and Inverse of Multiplication
lessons.content: Division means sharing an amount equally or grouping items into sets. Division is the inverse (opposite) of multiplication. For example, because 4 × 8 = 32, we know that 32 ÷ 4 = 8. In division, the number being divided is the dividend, the number dividing it is the divisor, and the answer is the quotient.
lessons.workedExample: Divide 72 ÷ 6. Divide tens: 7 ÷ 6 = 1 ten (with 1 ten left over). Regroup 1 ten with 2 ones to make 12 ones. 12 ÷ 6 = 2 ones. The quotient is 12.
lessons.kenyanExample: A farmer in Kisii harvested 84 avocados and packed them equally into 4 baskets. Each basket holds 84 ÷ 4 = 21 avocados.

lessons.title: Division with Remainder
lessons.content: When an amount cannot be divided into equal groups exactly, the leftover amount is called the remainder. The remainder must always be smaller than the divisor. For example, in 23 ÷ 4, we get 5 full groups of 4 (which makes 20) with 3 left over: 5 remainder 3.
lessons.workedExample: Divide 47 ÷ 5. 5 × 9 = 45. 47 - 45 = 2. So 47 ÷ 5 = 9 with a remainder of 2.
lessons.kenyanExample: A teacher in Garissa has 50 exercise books to share equally among 8 pupils. Each pupil receives 6 books, and 2 books remain.

lessons.title: Understanding Fractions: Numerator, Denominator and Types
lessons.content: A fraction represents equal parts of a whole. The top number is the numerator (parts counted), and the bottom number is the denominator (total equal parts in the whole). In a proper fraction, the numerator is strictly smaller than the denominator (like 3/4). In an improper fraction, the numerator is equal to or larger than the denominator (like 5/4).
lessons.workedExample: In 3/5, 3 is the numerator and 5 is the denominator. It represents 3 parts out of 5 equal parts.
lessons.kenyanExample: At lunch in Nakuru, Amina cuts a hot round chapati into 4 equal slices and eats 3. She ate 3/4 of the chapati, leaving 1/4.

lessons.title: Equivalent Fractions and Comparing Fractions
lessons.content: Equivalent fractions name the exact same amount even though they use different numbers. You can make an equivalent fraction by multiplying both the numerator and the denominator by the same number. To compare fractions with the same denominator, look at the numerators: the one with the larger numerator is greater.
lessons.workedExample: Find an equivalent fraction for 2/3. Multiply both numerator and denominator by 2: (2 × 2) / (3 × 2) = 4/6. So 2/3 = 4/6.
lessons.kenyanExample: Juma has 2/4 of a tank of water and Wanjiku has 1/2 of a tank. They have the exact same amount because 2/4 is equivalent to 1/2!

lessons.title: Understanding Tenths and the Decimal Point
lessons.content: A decimal is another way to write fractions with a denominator of 10. The decimal point separates the whole number part on the left from the fractional part on the right. One-tenth (1/10) is written as 0.1. A number with 3 wholes and 4 tenths is written as 3.4. The digit right after the point is in the tenths place.
lessons.workedExample: Write 7/10 as a decimal. 7/10 = 0.7. In 0.7, 0 represents zero whole units and 7 represents 7 tenths.
