questions.prompt: Grandmaster Challenge: Baraka and his 3 friends (4 children altogether) helped weed a kitchen garden in Embu on Saturday morning. The owner paid them KES 80 in total. If they share the money equally, how much does each child receive?
questions.storyScenario: Youth community gardening and fair reward distribution.
questions.explanation: KES 80 ÷ 4 children = KES 20 each. (Because 4 × 20 = 80).
questions.socraticHint: Divide 80 by 4. (Think: 8 tens divided by 4 = 2 tens).
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Earning pocket money for honest community chores teaches self-reliance and teamwork.

questions.prompt: When a circular chapati is cut into 2 equal parts, what is each part called?
questions.storyScenario: Sharing breakfast with a sibling in Mombasa.
questions.explanation: One of two equal parts of a whole is called a half (1/2).
questions.socraticHint: The bottom number is 2 because there are 2 equal parts. What is 1 out of 2 called?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Halving chapatis or mandazis is common during Kenyan tea time.

questions.prompt: How many equal quarters (1/4) make one whole circular chapati?
questions.storyScenario: Assembling fractions back into a whole.
questions.explanation: Four quarters make one whole: 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 = 4/4 = 1.
questions.socraticHint: Look at the denominator (bottom number) of 1/4. It tells you how many parts make the whole!
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Primary school geometry and fractions lessons use paper folding to model quarters.

questions.prompt: True or False: In any fraction, all the parts must be exactly equal in size.
questions.storyScenario: Defining what makes a fair fraction.
questions.explanation: True! A fraction is only correct if the whole is divided into equal-sized parts.
questions.socraticHint: If one brother gets a giant piece and another gets a tiny crumb, is that a fair half?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Fairness and integrity are core values embedded in CBC mathematics.

questions.prompt: A birthday cake in Nakuru is cut into 8 equal slices. One slice is written as [BLANK] as a fraction.
questions.explanation: One part out of 8 equal parts is written as 1/8 (one-eighth).
questions.socraticHint: Write 1 as the top number and 8 as the bottom number with a slash in between.
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Sharing celebratory cakes into 8 equal portions at school birthdays.

questions.prompt: Which fraction is the largest?
questions.explanation: 1/2 is the largest. When you divide a whole into fewer pieces (2 pieces instead of 8), each piece is much bigger!
questions.socraticHint: Would you get a bigger slice of watermelon if it is shared between 2 people or between 8 people?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Understanding that larger denominators make smaller slices is a key fraction insight.

questions.prompt: Match each fraction symbol with its correct name:
questions.storyScenario: Matching fraction cards on the display board.
questions.explanation: 1/2 is one half; 1/4 is one quarter; 1/8 is one eighth.
questions.socraticHint: Look at the bottom number: 2 is half, 4 is quarter, 8 is eighth.
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Matching symbols with written names supports mathematical vocabulary.

questions.prompt: True or False: 2 quarters (1/4 + 1/4) is equal to 1 half (1/2).
questions.explanation: True! If you put two quarters together, they cover exactly the same space as one half.
questions.socraticHint: If you cut a half chapati down the middle, how many quarters do you get? Exactly 2!
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Hands-on folding of paper circles helps learners discover equivalence naturally.

questions.prompt: Arrange these fractions in order from smallest piece to largest piece:
questions.explanation: 1/8 is the smallest, followed by 1/4, then 1/2, and 1 whole is the largest.
questions.socraticHint: The more pieces a chapati is cut into, the smaller each slice becomes! 8 pieces gives tiny slices.
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Logical ordering of fractions builds foundational rational number sense.

questions.prompt: Amina folds a square piece of paper in half, and then folds it in half again. When she opens it, the paper is divided into 4 equal rectangles. She colors 1 rectangle red. What fraction of the paper is colored red?
questions.storyScenario: Origami and paper folding in Grade 3 creative arts and mathematics.
questions.explanation: 1 part colored out of 4 equal parts is 1/4 (one quarter).
questions.socraticHint: How many total rectangles are there? That is the bottom number. How many are colored? That is the top number.
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Cross-curricular linkage between Art & Craft and Mathematics under CBC.

questions.prompt: How many eighths (1/8) make one half (1/2)? There are [BLANK] eighths in one half.
questions.blankTemplate: There are [BLANK] eighths in one half.
questions.explanation: 4 eighths make one half: 4/8 = 1/2. Since 8 eighths make a whole, half of that is 4 eighths.
questions.socraticHint: A whole has 8 eighths. How many eighths are in half of that whole? (Half of 8 is ?)
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Partitioning models sharpen mental fraction agility.

questions.prompt: In the fraction 1/4, what does the number 4 represent?
questions.storyScenario: Understanding the role of the denominator.

options.text: The total number of equal parts the whole is divided into
The number of parts taken away

questions.explanation: The denominator (bottom number) shows the total number of equal parts that make the complete whole.
questions.socraticHint: Does the bottom number tell you how many total slices were cut, or just the slice you ate?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Formal mathematical terminology (denominator / asili) is introduced in Grade 3.

questions.prompt: Juma buys a long loaf of bread at a duka in Machakos. He cuts it into 8 equal slices. He eats 1 slice for breakfast and gives 1 slice to his sister. What fraction of the bread did Juma eat?
questions.explanation: Juma ate 1 slice out of the 8 equal slices, so he ate 1/8 of the loaf.
questions.socraticHint: The question asks specifically for what Juma ate, not both children together.
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Sharing daily bread reflects familial care and cooperation.

questions.prompt: What is 1/2 of 12 sheep?
questions.storyScenario: Sorting livestock into pens in Eldoret.
questions.explanation: To find 1/2 of 12, divide by 2: 12 ÷ 2 = 6 sheep.
questions.socraticHint: Divide 12 by 2. What is half of 12?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Livestock management in the Rift Valley requires quick group division.

questions.prompt: What is 1/4 of 16 mangoes?
questions.storyScenario: Finding a quarter of a fruit basket.
questions.explanation: To find 1/4 of 16, divide by 4: 16 ÷ 4 = 4 mangoes.
questions.socraticHint: Divide 16 by 4. (What number multiplied by 4 gives 16?)
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Selling quarter-baskets of fruits is common in village markets.

questions.prompt: True or False: 1/2 of 20 shillings is 10 shillings.
questions.storyScenario: Calculating half of a pocket money amount.
questions.explanation: True! 20 ÷ 2 = 10 shillings.
questions.socraticHint: If you have a 20-shilling coin and share it equally with a friend, each gets 10 shillings.
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: The 20-shilling brass coin is a familiar everyday denomination for Kenyan children.

questions.prompt: A farmer in Nyeri has 24 chickens. An eighth (1/8) of the chickens are brown roosters. How many brown roosters does he have? [BLANK]
questions.storyScenario: Farming inventory on a poultry plot.
questions.explanation: 1/8 of 24 = 24 ÷ 8 = 3 brown roosters.
questions.socraticHint: Divide 24 by 8. (Think: 8 × ? = 24).
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Indigenous chickens (kienyeji) are widely reared in rural homesteads.

questions.prompt: What is 1/4 of 20 exercise books?
questions.storyScenario: Distributing books to a reading corner.
questions.explanation: 1/4 of 20 = 20 ÷ 4 = 5 exercise books.
questions.socraticHint: Divide 20 by 4. (Think: what number times 4 equals 20?)
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Standard exercise books are distributed at the start of each school term.

questions.prompt: Match each fraction problem with its correct amount:
questions.storyScenario: Card pairing challenge with fractions of sets.
questions.socraticHint: Divide each number by the fraction's denominator: 14÷2, 28÷4, 16÷8.
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Encouraging mental division through fraction manipulation.

questions.prompt: True or False: 1/4 of 12 is greater than 1/2 of 12.
questions.storyScenario: Comparing fractions of the same group.
questions.explanation: False! 1/4 of 12 = 3, while 1/2 of 12 = 6. 6 is greater than 3, so a half is greater than a quarter.
questions.socraticHint: Calculate both: 1/4 of 12 is 3. 1/2 of 12 is 6. Which one is bigger?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Reasoning about fraction sizes reinforces relational thinking.

questions.prompt: Arrange these fractions of 16 in order from smallest result to largest result:
questions.storyScenario: Sorting fraction quantities in ascending order.
questions.socraticHint: Calculate each value: 16÷8=2, 16÷4=4, 16÷2=8. Now order them from least to greatest.
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Comparing parts of sets builds proportional reasoning.

questions.prompt: Mwangi harvested 32 sweet watermelons in Garissa. He sold 1/4 of them to a local hotel on Friday morning. How many watermelons did the hotel buy?
questions.storyScenario: Watermelon sales from an irrigated farm along the Tana River.
questions.explanation: 1/4 of 32 = 32 ÷ 4 = 8 watermelons.
questions.socraticHint: Divide 32 by 4. (Think: 4 × ? = 32).
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Watermelon farming along the Tana River basin provides fresh produce across eastern Kenya.

questions.prompt: There are 40 pupils in a Grade 3 class in Kisumu. Exactly 1/2 of the pupils are girls. How many girls are in the class? [BLANK]
questions.blankTemplate: There are [BLANK] girls in the class.
questions.socraticHint: What is half of 40? (Divide 40 by 2).
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Gender parity in school enrollment is championed across all 47 counties.

questions.prompt: What is 1/8 of 32 bottle tops?
questions.socraticHint: Divide 32 by 8. (Think: what number times 8 gives 32?)
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Token counting engages pupils with practical hands-on arithmetic.

questions.prompt: Grandmaster Challenge: Mzee Omondi has 24 cows. Half (1/2) of them are dairy cows, and one-quarter (1/4) of them are young calves. How many dairy cows and calves does he have altogether?
questions.explanation: Dairy cows: 1/2 of 24 = 12. Calves: 1/4 of 24 = 6. Total together: 12 + 6 = 18!
questions.socraticHint: Step 1: Find 1/2 of 24 (12). Step 2: Find 1/4 of 24 (6). Step 3: Add them together (12 + 6).
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Managing dairy herds and calves is a real-life practice for farmers in western Kenya.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is an example of a non-standard unit of length?
questions.storyScenario: Classroom discussion on early ways of measuring.
questions.explanation: A handspan is a body-based non-standard unit because different people have different hand sizes.
questions.socraticHint: Which unit changes depending on whose body is being used to measure?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Handspans (shubiri) have been traditionally used in Kenya to measure ropes and fabrics.

questions.prompt: Why do two pupils measuring the same classroom with their footsteps get slightly different answers?

options.text: One of the pupils cannot count
Their foot sizes and step lengths are different
The classroom changes length when they walk

questions.explanation: People have different shoe and stride sizes, so footstep counts naturally vary.
questions.socraticHint: Does an older teacher take the exact same size stride as a Grade 3 child?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Understanding why standard units were invented is an inquiry objective in CBC.

questions.prompt: True or False: Using a short stick of the same length to measure a flowerbed gives a consistent measurement.
questions.storyScenario: Using a fixed object as a temporary measuring tool.
questions.explanation: True! If the same stick is used from end to end, the count remains consistent.
questions.socraticHint: Does the stick change its length while you are measuring with it?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Pupils in Kenya often cut a stick to a set length to space seedlings in agriculture projects.

questions.prompt: Achieng measures her desk and finds it is 5 pencils long. If each pencil is about 15 cm, the pencil is being used as a [BLANK] unit of length.
questions.blankTemplate: The pencil is being used as a [BLANK] unit of length.
questions.explanation: Pencils vary in length (especially after sharpening), so a pencil is a non-standard unit.
questions.socraticHint: Is a pencil an official internationally accepted unit like a metre, or a non-standard object?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Pupils use stationery items as informal measurement tools.

questions.prompt: Which tool is best for finding the distance between two trees in a wide school orchard?

options.text: Long strides or a measuring tape

questions.explanation: Long distances require larger units like strides or a long measuring tape rather than tiny pencils or coins.
questions.socraticHint: Would you want to lay down a matchbox 500 times to measure across a whole garden?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Selecting appropriate measurement tools is a key competency in CBC.

questions.prompt: Match each non-standard body measurement with its description:

matchingPairs.rightText: Distance from tip of thumb to tip of little finger stretched
Distance covered in one full walking step
Distance from fingertip to fingertip with arms outstretched

questions.explanation: Handspan is thumb to little finger; stride is one walking step; arm span is outstretched arms fingertip to fingertip.
questions.socraticHint: Think about how you stretch your hand vs how you step with your feet.
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: These traditional Swahili measurement concepts connect cultural heritage to mathematics.

questions.prompt: True or False: If Fundi Omondi uses his arm span to cut roofing timber and sells it in Nairobi, it will match what another builder in Mombasa measured with his arm span.
questions.storyScenario: Why non-standard units fail in trade.
questions.explanation: False! Different adults have different arm spans. Without a standard metre, the timbers will not match!
questions.socraticHint: Are all carpenters in Kenya the exact same height with the exact same arm length?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Trade and construction in Kenya require standardized units across counties.

questions.prompt: Arrange these objects in order of length from shortest to longest:
questions.explanation: A matchstick is shortest, followed by a pencil, a desk, and a matatu is the longest.
questions.socraticHint: Visualize each object: which one fits in your pocket, and which one takes up a whole parking bay?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Real-world visual estimation is essential for everyday safety and spatial sense.

questions.prompt: Baraka paces out the width of the school gate and counts 6 paces. His friend Brian paces the same gate and counts 7 paces. If both walked carefully, what is the best estimate of the width of the gate in paces?
questions.explanation: Since the measurements were 6 and 7 paces, a sensible estimate is about 6 to 7 paces.
questions.socraticHint: Both pupils got numbers very close together (6 and 7). What does that tell you about the approximate width?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Working in pairs to compare estimates builds collaborative inquiry in CBC.

questions.prompt: When you make a sensible guess about how long an object is before measuring it, you are making an [BLANK].
questions.explanation: An estimate (kadirio) is a reasonable guess based on observation before actual measurement.
questions.socraticHint: Starts with the letter "e". In Swahili it is called "kadirio".
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Estimation before measuring develops number sense and critical thinking.

questions.prompt: Which of these is the most accurate statement about non-standard units?

options.text: They are measured in kilograms and litres
They are convenient for quick estimates but not reliable for fair trade
They are used by doctors and engineers to build bridges
They give the exact same measurement for every person in the world

questions.explanation: Non-standard units are quick and accessible, but because they vary, they cannot be used for official trade.
questions.socraticHint: Would a shopkeeper sell cloth by his own handspan if a customer with larger hands wanted more cloth?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Fairness in trade is governed by Kenya Bureau of Standards (KEBS) metrology laws.

questions.prompt: Pupils in Grade 3 use identical 30-cm rulers to measure the blackboard. Otieno places the ruler end-to-end 8 times. What is the total length of the blackboard in centimetres?
questions.explanation: 8 ruler lengths × 30 cm = 240 cm. (8 × 30 = 240).
questions.socraticHint: Multiply 8 by 30. (8 × 3 tens = 24 tens = 240).
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Classroom blackboards in Kenya are standard green or black timber/cement boards.

questions.prompt: What is the standard unit of length used across Kenya and internationally?
questions.explanation: The standard international unit of length is the metre, abbreviated as 'm'.
questions.socraticHint: Which unit is used on tape measures and metre rulers?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Standard metric units have been Kenya's official measurement system since independence.

questions.prompt: Which short symbol is used to write the word "metre"?
questions.explanation: The symbol for metre is the lowercase letter 'm'.
questions.socraticHint: It is the first letter of the word "metre".
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Accurate notation is required in CBC exercise books.

questions.prompt: True or False: The height of a classroom door in Kenya is usually about 2 metres.
questions.explanation: True! Standard building doors in Kenyan schools and homes are approximately 2 metres tall.
questions.socraticHint: A tall adult is nearly 2 metres tall and can walk through the door without bending.
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Standard door frames in Kenya follow architectural guidelines (approx 2.1 m).

questions.prompt: Fundi Omondi uses a wooden stick that is exactly 100 centimetres long. This stick is called a 1-[BLANK] rule.
questions.blankTemplate: This stick is called a 1-[BLANK] rule.
questions.explanation: A 100-cm ruler is called a 1-metre rule.
questions.socraticHint: What standard unit equals 100 centimetres?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Yellow wooden metre rules are staple equipment in Kenyan school science and math kits.

questions.prompt: A tailor at Gikomba market needs 3 metres of kitenge fabric to make a dress, and 2 metres for a shirt. How many metres of fabric does she need in total?
questions.explanation: 3 m + 2 m = 5 metres of fabric.
questions.socraticHint: Add 3 and 2 together: 3 + 2 = ?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Kitenge and wax prints are tailored for traditional ceremonies across Kenya.

questions.prompt: Match each everyday item with its most sensible estimated length in metres:

matchingPairs.leftText: Length of a school soccer pitch
Length of a pupil's exercise book

questions.explanation: A soccer pitch is around 90 m; a classroom wall is around 3 m; an exercise book is less than 1 m.
questions.socraticHint: Which is huge (stadium size), which is room height, and which is smaller than your desk?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: School soccer pitches follow Ministry of Education standard sports dimensions.

questions.prompt: True or False: A standard pencil is about 2 metres long.
questions.storyScenario: Checking realistic vs unrealistic metric lengths.
questions.explanation: False! 2 metres is the height of a doorway! A pencil is only about 15 to 18 centimetres long, much less than 1 metre.
questions.socraticHint: A classroom door is 2 metres tall. Could a pencil ever be as tall as a classroom door?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Developing sensible physical benchmarks for metric units.

questions.prompt: Arrange the steps for measuring the length of a veranda with a 1-metre stick in correct order:
questions.storyScenario: Proper protocol for measuring with a single metre rule.

options.text: Place one end of the metre rule at the starting corner of the veranda
Mark where the 1-metre stick ends with a piece of chalk
Move the metre stick forward so its start touches the chalk mark
Repeat and count the total number of metres to the far end

questions.explanation: Start at the edge, mark the end, shift the stick forward to the mark, and count total lengths.
questions.socraticHint: Why do you need to mark with chalk before picking up the stick to move it forward?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Accurate marking prevents overlap or gaps during school measurements.

questions.prompt: Mzee Juma is fencing a sheep pen in Naivasha. One side is 8 metres long, and the opposite side is also 8 metres long. How many metres of wire does he need for just these two sides?
questions.explanation: 8 m + 8 m = 16 metres of fencing wire.
questions.socraticHint: Double 8 metres: 8 + 8 = ?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Fencing pastures and enclosures protects livestock from predators in rural areas.

questions.prompt: A water pipe was 15 metres long. A plumber cut off 6 metres to connect a kitchen sink in Nakuru. How many metres of pipe are left? [BLANK]
questions.blankTemplate: There are [BLANK] metres of pipe left.
questions.explanation: 15 m - 6 m = 9 metres left.
questions.socraticHint: Subtract 6 from 15: 15 - 6 = ?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: PVC water piping is commonly installed in home plumbing projects.

questions.prompt: During sports day in Eldoret, Baraka jumped 2 metres in the long jump. Brian jumped 3 metres. How much farther did Brian jump than Baraka?
questions.explanation: 3 m - 2 m = 1 metre farther.
questions.socraticHint: Find the difference between 3 metres and 2 metres.
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Athletics competitions (track and field) are held annually across Kenyan schools.

questions.prompt: Grandmaster Challenge: The school agriculture club in Kiambu wants to plant sweet potatoes along a rectangular plot. The plot is 10 metres long and 5 metres wide. What is the total distance all the way around the plot (perimeter)?
questions.storyScenario: Multi-step perimeter problem for Grade 3 garden plot.
questions.explanation: A rectangle has two lengths and two widths: 10 m + 5 m + 10 m + 5 m = 30 metres all the way around!
questions.socraticHint: Walk all four sides: 10 metres + 5 metres + 10 metres + 5 metres = ?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: School kitchen gardens (shamba ya shule) produce fresh vegetables for school feeding schemes.

questions.prompt: When an object is placed on a beam balance and that side goes DOWN, what does it mean?
questions.storyScenario: Observing a beam balance in science and math practical class.

options.text: That object is heavier than the object on the other side
That object is lighter than the object on the other side

questions.explanation: Gravity pulls heavier objects down more strongly, so the heavier side tips downwards.
questions.socraticHint: Think about a seesaw in the school playground: which side goes down?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Primary school playgrounds feature seesaws that naturally demonstrate mass balance.

questions.prompt: Which of these pairs has the heavier item first?

options.text: A single bean seed is heavier than a pumpkin
A piece of paper is heavier than an iron padlock
A ripe watermelon is heavier than a small tomato
A chicken feather is heavier than a stone

questions.explanation: A ripe watermelon has much more mass than a tiny tomato.
questions.socraticHint: Which item takes two hands to carry because it has so much weight?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Watermelons and tomatoes are sold alongside each other in Kenyan roadside kiosks.

questions.prompt: True or False: If a beam balance stays completely level, both pans have equal mass.
questions.explanation: True! When the beam is horizontal and level, the masses on both sides are equal.
questions.socraticHint: If neither side goes down or up, what can you say about their weights?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Fair balancing is the cornerstone of honest trade in open markets.

questions.prompt: A large cabbage balances exactly with 6 equal wooden blocks on a balance scale. The mass of the cabbage is [BLANK] wooden blocks.
questions.storyScenario: Measuring mass using non-standard block units.
questions.blankTemplate: The mass of the cabbage is [BLANK] wooden blocks.
questions.explanation: Because the scale balances, the cabbage has the same mass as the 6 wooden blocks.
questions.socraticHint: How many blocks did it take to balance the scale?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Wooden blocks and stone pebbles are used as early non-standard mass units in Grade 3.

questions.prompt: Which of the following objects is lighter than an empty school bag?
questions.explanation: A pencil sharpener is very light and has far less mass than a school bag.
questions.socraticHint: Which object can you easily lift with just two fingertips?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Schoolbags in Kenya carry textbooks and stationery daily.

questions.prompt: Match each item to the correct comparison with a 1-shilling coin:
questions.storyScenario: Comparing mass relative to a coin.
questions.explanation: A coconut is much heavier, a dry leaf is much lighter, and an identical coin has equal mass.
questions.socraticHint: Feel how light a leaf is in the wind compared to a metal coin or a heavy coconut.
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Kenyan coins provide concrete tactile reference points for children.

questions.prompt: True or False: A big inflated balloon is always heavier than a small metal stone because the balloon is bigger in size.
questions.explanation: False! Size does not mean heavier. A balloon is full of air and very light, while a small metal stone is heavy.
questions.socraticHint: Does a large puffy balloon hurt if it falls on your toe? Does a small heavy stone?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Disentangling volume from mass is a core cognitive development goal in CBC.

questions.prompt: Arrange these animals in order of their mass from lightest to heaviest:
questions.explanation: A weaver bird is lightest, followed by a chicken, then a cow, and an elephant is the heaviest.
questions.socraticHint: Think about how much effort it takes to lift each animal.
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Kenya's rich biodiversity provides memorable examples for mass ordering.

questions.prompt: Wanjiku places a pineapple on the left pan and 4 mangoes on the right pan of a beam balance. The balance rests completely level. What can she conclude?

options.text: The pineapple has the same mass as the 4 mangoes
The pineapple is heavier than the 4 mangoes
The 4 mangoes are heavier than the pineapple

questions.explanation: When the beam balance is level, the total mass on both sides is equal.
questions.socraticHint: The balance is level in the middle. Does one side have more weight than the other?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Market fruit comparisons in Nairobi markets.

questions.prompt: When two objects have the same weight on a beam balance, we say they have [BLANK] mass.
questions.explanation: Objects that balance evenly have equal mass.
questions.socraticHint: What word means "the exact same amount"?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Scientific language development in primary grades.

questions.prompt: If Object A is heavier than Object B, and Object B is heavier than Object C, which object is the heaviest of all?
questions.explanation: Object A is heavier than B, and B is heavier than C, so Object A is the heaviest.
questions.socraticHint: Object A beats Object B, and Object B beats Object C. Who is at the top?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Transitive deductive reasoning is cultivated in CBC Grade 3 mathematics.

questions.prompt: Baraka is holding a dictionary in his left hand and a single pencil in his right hand. How can he describe the pencil compared to the dictionary?

options.text: The pencil has the same mass as the dictionary
The dictionary is lighter than the pencil
The pencil is lighter than the dictionary
The pencil is heavier than the dictionary

questions.explanation: A pencil requires very little effort to hold compared to a thick dictionary, so it is lighter.
questions.socraticHint: Which hand feels heavy and tired after holding the object for a few minutes?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Tactile hefting is recommended in the KICD syllabus before formal weighing.

questions.prompt: What is the standard unit of mass used in Kenya and internationally?
questions.explanation: The standard unit of mass is the kilogram, abbreviated as 'kg'.
questions.socraticHint: What unit is written on packets of unga, rice, and sugar?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Packets of maize meal and wheat flour prominently display "1 kg" or "2 kg".

questions.prompt: What is the short symbol for kilogram?
questions.explanation: The abbreviation for kilogram is 'kg' in lowercase.
questions.socraticHint: Combines the first letter of kilo (k) and gram (g).
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Metric notation standards taught in primary education.

questions.prompt: True or False: 1 kilogram of dry maize flour has the exact same mass as 1 kilogram of metal nails.
questions.explanation: True! 1 kg is 1 kg regardless of the material. They both balance evenly on a scale.
questions.socraticHint: Both weigh exactly 1 kilogram! Does it matter whether it is fluffy flour or hard nails?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Classic concept check addressing material density misconceptions.

questions.prompt: Mama Amina bought 3 packets of maize flour. Each packet weighs 2 kg. What is the total mass of the flour? [BLANK] kg
questions.explanation: 3 packets × 2 kg = 6 kg of maize flour.
questions.socraticHint: Multiply 3 by 2 kg (or add 2 + 2 + 2).
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Ugali unga is frequently bought in 2 kg packets for family meals.

questions.prompt: A sack of potatoes weighs 25 kg. After selling 12 kg at the market, how many kilograms of potatoes remain?
questions.explanation: 25 kg - 12 kg = 13 kg of potatoes remaining.
questions.socraticHint: Subtract: 5 - 2 = 3 in ones, and 2 - 1 = 1 in tens.
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Irish potatoes (waru) from Kinangop and Nyandarua are retailed by the kilogram.

questions.prompt: Match each grocery purchase to its total mass in kilograms:
questions.socraticHint: Do the addition or subtraction for each item pair.
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Household grocery shopping in Kenyan trading centers.

questions.prompt: True or False: A standard 8-year-old child in Grade 3 weighs about 25 kg.
questions.storyScenario: Relating kilograms to child body weight.
questions.explanation: True! An average Grade 3 pupil in Kenya weighs approximately 22 to 28 kilograms.
questions.socraticHint: Could a healthy Grade 3 child weigh only 1 kg (like a bag of sugar) or 500 kg (like a cow)? 25 kg is sensible!
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Health monitoring and school physical measurements under CBC.

questions.prompt: Arrange these masses in order from lightest to heaviest:
questions.explanation: 2 kg < 5 kg < 10 kg < 50 kg.
questions.socraticHint: Look at the numbers before "kg" and place them in ascending order.
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Agricultural fertilizer and maize bags are sold in standard 50 kg packages.

questions.prompt: Juma carries two shopping bags home from the market. The left bag has 4 kg of meat, and the right bag has 6 kg of vegetables. What is the total mass Juma is carrying?
questions.explanation: 4 kg + 6 kg = 10 kg total mass.
questions.socraticHint: Add 4 and 6 together: 4 + 6 = ?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Children helping parents carry groceries from local shopping centers.

questions.explanation: 45 kg - 38 kg = 7 kg left.
questions.socraticHint: Borrow 1 ten: 15 - 8 = 7 in ones. 3 - 3 = 0 in tens.
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Local butcheries in Kenya sell meat measured precisely in kilograms.

questions.prompt: Which tool should a shopkeeper use to measure the mass of 3 kg of rice accurately?

options.text: A weighing scale with 1 kg weights

questions.explanation: Weighing scales measure mass, rulers measure length, jugs measure capacity, and clocks measure time.
questions.socraticHint: Which instrument is designed specifically for finding weight?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Digital and mechanical weighing scales in community retail stores.

questions.prompt: Grandmaster Challenge: A school feeding kitchen in Machakos has 3 bags of beans weighing 15 kg each, and 1 bag of maize weighing 50 kg. What is the total mass of food in the store?
questions.storyScenario: Multi-step arithmetic combining multiplication and addition of mass.
questions.explanation: Beans: 3 bags × 15 kg = 45 kg. Maize: 50 kg. Total: 45 + 50 = 95 kg of food!
questions.socraticHint: Step 1: Calculate the total mass of the 3 bags of beans (3 × 15 = 45). Step 2: Add the 50 kg bag of maize.

questions.prompt: Which container holds MORE water: a tea cup or a large plastic bucket?
questions.storyScenario: Comparing liquid capacities in the home.

options.text: A large plastic bucket holds more water
A tea cup holds more water
Both hold the exact same amount

questions.explanation: A bucket is much larger and can hold many cups of water, so it has greater capacity.
questions.socraticHint: Which container do you use to wash clothes, and which do you use to sip tea?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Plastic buckets (ndoo) are standard household water containers across Kenya.

questions.prompt: What does the word "capacity" mean in mathematics?

options.text: The cost of milk in shillings
The time shown on a clock
The amount of liquid a container can hold
The length of a wooden ruler

questions.explanation: Capacity refers to the volume or amount of liquid a container can hold.
questions.socraticHint: Think about filling a bottle or jerrycan with water. What are you measuring?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: CBC introduces capacity through practical pouring and filling exercises.

questions.prompt: True or False: If it takes 4 small glasses of water to completely fill a jug, the jug has a greater capacity than one glass.
questions.storyScenario: Comparing capacity using non-standard container counts.
questions.explanation: True! Because the jug holds 4 glasses combined, it holds much more than 1 single glass.
questions.socraticHint: Can 4 glasses fit inside 1 glass? No! So the jug is bigger in capacity.
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Classroom water pouring stations help pupils visualize capacity equivalence.

questions.prompt: Chebet pours water from 3 identical bottles to fill one cooking sufuria. The capacity of the sufuria is [BLANK] bottles.
questions.blankTemplate: The capacity of the sufuria is [BLANK] bottles.
questions.explanation: Since 3 bottles fill the sufuria completely, its capacity equals 3 bottles.
questions.socraticHint: How many bottles were emptied into the sufuria?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Sufurias are aluminum cooking pots used in every Kenyan kitchen.

questions.prompt: Which container holds LESS liquid than a standard soda bottle?
questions.explanation: A medicine spoon holds only a few drops (about 5 ml), which is much less than a soda bottle.
questions.socraticHint: Which container holds barely a mouthful of medicine syrup?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Measuring medicine accurately with teaspoons is taught in health and environmental activities.

questions.prompt: Match each container to its capacity relationship with a 1-litre bottle:
questions.explanation: A 20l jerrycan holds more; an eye-dropper holds less; two 500ml milk packets equal 1 litre.
questions.socraticHint: Think about how many litres each container holds.
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Comparing everyday household containers in Kenyan communities.

questions.prompt: True or False: A tall, thin glass ALWAYS holds more water than a short, wide bowl.
questions.explanation: False! A short wide bowl can often hold more water than a tall skinny glass because it is much wider.
questions.socraticHint: Could a wide soup bowl hold more liquid than a narrow drinking glass? Test by pouring!
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Hands-on pouring experiments help overcome Piagetian conservation traps.

questions.prompt: Arrange these containers in order of capacity from smallest to largest:
questions.explanation: Bottle cap < tea mug < 5l container < 1,000l water tank.
questions.socraticHint: Which holds only a few drops, and which can store water for an entire school?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Roto and Jumbo plastic rainwater tanks are standard fixtures in schools and homes in Kenya.

questions.prompt: Chebet pours 6 cups of water into Pot A, and it fills completely. She pours 6 cups of water into Pot B, and it also fills completely. What can she say about the two pots?
questions.storyScenario: Comparing two pots using the same unit.

options.text: Pot A and Pot B have the same capacity
Pot A holds more than Pot B
Pot B holds more than Pot A

questions.explanation: Since both pots require exactly 6 cups to fill, they have equal capacity.
questions.socraticHint: Both pots hold 6 cups. Are they equal, or is one bigger?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Traditional clay pots and modern metal sufurias can hold identical capacities.

questions.prompt: When a container cannot hold any more liquid without overflowing, it has reached its full [BLANK].
questions.explanation: Full capacity is the maximum amount of liquid a container can hold.
questions.socraticHint: Starts with the letter "c".
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Preventing water wastage by not overfilling tanks is taught in CBC.

questions.prompt: Why do we need a standard unit like the litre instead of measuring liquids with random cups?
questions.storyScenario: The need for standard units of volume in trade.

options.text: Because a litre is measured with a ruler
Because cups come in different shapes and sizes, but a litre is always the same
Because water turns into ice in cups

questions.explanation: A standard litre guarantees that buyers and sellers agree on the exact quantity everywhere.
questions.socraticHint: If a duka sold milk using a tiny tea cup as a "cup", would customers be happy?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Weights and Measures department inspects calibrated litres in retail stores.

questions.prompt: Pupils at a school in Bomet wash their hands before lunch. The handwashing bucket holds 10 litres. Each pupil uses about 1 litre of water. How many pupils can wash their hands before the bucket is empty?
questions.explanation: 10 litres ÷ 1 litre per pupil = 10 pupils.
questions.socraticHint: Divide 10 by 1: 10 ÷ 1 = ?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Tippy-tap handwashing stations outside primary school dining halls.

questions.prompt: What is the standard metric unit used to measure capacity (liquids)?
questions.explanation: The standard unit of capacity is the litre, abbreviated as 'l'.
questions.socraticHint: Which unit is used on milk bottles, cooking oil, and petrol pumps?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Litre measures are calibrated and certified by Kenya Bureau of Standards (KEBS).

questions.prompt: Which short symbol is used for the word "litre"?
questions.explanation: The symbol for litre is 'l' (or capital 'L').
questions.socraticHint: First letter of the word "litre".
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Writing unit symbols cleanly in Grade 3 mathematics exercises.

questions.prompt: True or False: 2 packets of milk containing 500 millilitres each equal 1 full litre of milk.
questions.storyScenario: Relating half-litres to one whole litre.
questions.explanation: True! 500 ml is half a litre. Two half-litres make 1 whole litre.
questions.socraticHint: Think of fractions: half a litre + half a litre = 1 whole litre!
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Standard Kenya Cooperative Creameries (KCC) and Brookside milk packets are 500 ml.

questions.prompt: Amina bought 3 litres of milk on Monday and 4 litres of milk on Tuesday. How many litres of milk did she buy in total? [BLANK] litres
questions.explanation: 3 litres + 4 litres = 7 litres of milk.
questions.socraticHint: Add 3 and 4 together: 3 + 4 = ?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Daily fresh milk purchases for family tea and porridge.

questions.prompt: A yellow jerrycan holds 20 litres of clean water. If Mama Chebet uses 8 litres to cook githeri, how many litres remain in the jerrycan?
questions.explanation: 20 l - 8 l = 12 litres of water remaining.
questions.socraticHint: Subtract 8 from 20: 20 - 8 = ?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Managing water reserves in rural homesteads.

questions.prompt: Match each liquid operation with its correct total in litres:
questions.socraticHint: Calculate each: 5+5, 15-7, and 4×3.
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Working with practical liquid volume calculations.

questions.prompt: True or False: A standard cattle dipping trough holds less water than a drinking glass.
questions.storyScenario: Comparing large agricultural tanks to small containers.
questions.explanation: False! A cattle dip tank holds thousands of litres of water, far more than a tiny glass.
questions.socraticHint: Cows walk through a cattle dip! Could an entire cow fit inside a drinking glass?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Cattle dips are vital agricultural infrastructure in pastoralist areas.

questions.prompt: Arrange these capacity measurements in order from least to greatest volume:
questions.socraticHint: Order the numbers from smallest to largest: 1, 5, 20, 100.
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Water storage containers used in residential compounds.

questions.prompt: A tea kiosk owner in Kericho prepares 18 litres of chai in the morning. By 10:00 AM, she has sold 11 litres to customers. How many litres of chai are left in the urn?
questions.explanation: 18 l - 11 l = 7 litres of chai remaining.
questions.socraticHint: Subtract 11 from 18: 18 - 11 = ?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Spiced chai (tea with milk) is served in roadside tea kiosks across Kenya.

questions.prompt: A farmer waters vegetable nursery beds with 4 watering cans. Each can holds 5 litres of water. How many litres of water did the farmer use in total? [BLANK] litres
questions.blankTemplate: The farmer used [BLANK] litres in total.
questions.explanation: 4 cans × 5 litres = 20 litres of water.
questions.socraticHint: Multiply 4 by 5 (or count in fives: 5, 10, 15, 20).
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Watering cans are standard gardening equipment in primary school agriculture plots.

questions.prompt: If 1 litre of fresh milk costs KES 60 at the milk ATM, how much will 2 litres of milk cost?
questions.explanation: 2 litres × KES 60 = KES 120.
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Connecting metric capacity measurements directly to commercial transactions.

questions.prompt: Grandmaster Challenge: A school water tank in Kitui has 80 litres of water. The kitchen uses 35 litres to boil beans, and 25 litres to clean utensils. How many litres of water are left in the tank?
questions.storyScenario: Multi-step real-world school water conservation challenge.
questions.explanation: Total water used: 35 + 25 = 60 litres. Remaining: 80 - 60 = 20 litres left!
questions.socraticHint: First add all the water that was used (35 + 25 = 60). Then subtract 60 from the starting 80 litres.
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Water budgeting is an essential survival and conservation life skill in arid regions of Kenya.

questions.prompt: When the short hand of a clock points to 8 and the long hand points to 12, what time is it?
questions.explanation: Short hand points to 8 (hour) and long hand points to 12 (exact hour), so it is 8:00 o'clock.
questions.socraticHint: Which hand tells the hour (the short one or the long one)?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Kenyan primary schools ring the morning bell at 8:00 AM.

questions.prompt: Where does the long minute hand point when the time is "half past" any hour?
questions.storyScenario: Understanding the position of the minute hand.
questions.explanation: Half past means 30 minutes, so the long hand has moved halfway around the clock to 6.
questions.socraticHint: Halfway around a 12-hour clock face lands on which number? (Half of 12 is ?)
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Reading analog wall clocks is a core CBC numeracy skill.

questions.prompt: True or False: There are 60 minutes in 1 whole hour.
questions.explanation: True! 1 hour contains exactly 60 minutes. Half an hour contains 30 minutes.
questions.socraticHint: Skip count by 5 around all 12 numbers of the clock face: 12 × 5 = 60 minutes!
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Standard time units taught in primary schools.

questions.prompt: If the short hand is between 10 and 11, and the long hand points directly at 6, the time is [BLANK] (or half past 10).
questions.explanation: The hour is 10 and 30 minutes have passed, so the time is 10:30.
questions.socraticHint: Write the hour (10) followed by a colon and the minutes (30).
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Morning tea break (stafahi) typically takes place at 10:30 AM.

questions.prompt: How many minutes are there in half an hour?
questions.explanation: Half of 60 minutes is 30 minutes (60 ÷ 2 = 30).
questions.socraticHint: Divide 60 by 2. What is half of 60?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Half-hour lesson blocks in school timetables.

questions.prompt: Match each digital time to its word description:
questions.storyScenario: Matching digital times with clock descriptions.
questions.explanation: 7:00 is seven o'clock; 7:30 is half past seven; 1:00 is one o'clock.
questions.socraticHint: Look at the minutes: :00 means o'clock, :30 means half past.
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Reading both digital and analog clocks.

questions.prompt: True or False: On a clock face, the short hand moves faster than the long hand.
questions.explanation: False! The long minute hand moves much faster; it makes a full circle every hour, while the short hand only moves to the next number!
questions.socraticHint: Which hand ticks past each minute mark while you watch?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Observation skills developed during science and mathematics.

questions.prompt: Arrange these daily school events in chronological order from morning to evening:
questions.explanation: The daily order is 8:00 AM (assembly), 10:30 AM (tea break), 1:00 PM (lunch), 4:00 PM (games).
questions.socraticHint: What happens when you first arrive at school in the morning?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Standard school day sequence in Kenyan primary education.

questions.prompt: A mathematics lesson starts at 9:00 AM. It lasts for exactly 30 minutes. What time does the lesson end?
questions.explanation: 9:00 + 30 minutes = 9:30 AM (half past 9).
questions.socraticHint: Add 30 minutes to 9:00. What do you get?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: CBC lessons are structured in 30-minute to 35-minute periods.

questions.prompt: There are [BLANK] hours in one complete full day (day and night combined).
questions.storyScenario: Hours in a day factual knowledge.
questions.blankTemplate: There are [BLANK] hours in one complete day.
questions.explanation: One full day has 24 hours (12 hours of day and 12 hours of night).
questions.socraticHint: How many hours are in a whole day? Think of 12 + 12.
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Earth rotation and solar day taught in environmental science.

questions.prompt: If the time is 2:30 PM, where are the two hands of the clock pointing?
questions.storyScenario: Interpreting analog clock hand positions at half-past.

options.text: Short hand points at 6, long hand points at 12
Short hand is between 2 and 3, long hand points at 6
Short hand points at 12, long hand points at 2

questions.explanation: At 2:30, the minute hand has reached 6 (30 mins), and the hour hand has moved halfway between 2 and 3.
questions.socraticHint: 30 minutes means the long hand is at 6. The short hand is halfway past 2.
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Clock reading mastery in Grade 3.

questions.prompt: Brian's father drives a matatu from Nairobi to Machakos. He leaves Nairobi at 6:00 AM and arrives at 7:30 AM. How long did the journey take?
questions.explanation: From 6:00 AM to 7:00 AM is 1 hour, and from 7:00 AM to 7:30 AM is another 30 minutes. Total time: 1 hour 30 minutes.
questions.socraticHint: Count from 6:00 to 7:00 (1 hour). Then add the 30 minutes to reach 7:30.
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Commuter journeys between Nairobi and eastern counties.

questions.prompt: How many days are there in one complete week?
questions.explanation: There are 7 days in a week: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday.
questions.socraticHint: Count them: Monday through Sunday.
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Reciting days of the week in English and Kiswahili.

questions.prompt: Which day comes immediately after Wednesday?
questions.explanation: Thursday (Alhamisi) comes right after Wednesday (Jumatano).
questions.socraticHint: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, ... what comes next?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: School weekly timetables.

questions.prompt: True or False: In a whole year, there are 12 months.
questions.explanation: True! A year has exactly 12 months, from January to December.
questions.socraticHint: January, February, March, April, May, June, July, August, September, October, November, December. That is 12!
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Yearly calendar awareness.

questions.prompt: The very first month of the calendar year is [BLANK].
questions.explanation: January is the 1st month of the year.
questions.socraticHint: Which month comes right after New Year's Day on January 1st?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Schools open for Term 1 in January across Kenya.

questions.prompt: Which month comes immediately before December?
questions.explanation: November (the 11th month) comes immediately before December (the 12th month).
questions.socraticHint: Think of the 11th month: September, October, ... , December.
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: End-of-year national primary assessments often take place in November.

questions.prompt: Match each Kenyan national holiday to the month it is celebrated:
questions.storyScenario: Connecting calendar months to national events.
questions.explanation: Madaraka Day is in June; Mashujaa Day is in October; Jamhuri Day is in December.
questions.socraticHint: Think about when Kenya celebrates heroes (Mashujaa in October) and republic day (Jamhuri in December).
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: National celebrations build patriotism and citizenship under CBC.

questions.prompt: True or False: Saturday and Sunday are called the weekend.
questions.explanation: True! Saturday and Sunday mark the end of the weekly work and school cycle and are called the weekend.
questions.socraticHint: Which two days are pupils usually at home resting or attending worship?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Weekend family and community routines in Kenya.

questions.prompt: Arrange the first four months of the year in correct chronological sequence:
questions.explanation: The order is January, February, March, April.
questions.socraticHint: Recite the first 4 months starting from the new year.
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Calendar literacy is practiced in daily classroom roll calls.

questions.prompt: If today is Friday, what day will it be after 2 days?
questions.storyScenario: Projecting days forward on the calendar.
questions.explanation: Friday + 1 day = Saturday. Saturday + 1 day = Sunday. So after 2 days it will be Sunday.
questions.socraticHint: Count forward 2 days: Friday -> Saturday (1), Sunday (2).
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Planning weekend activities with family.

questions.prompt: There are [BLANK] days in 2 weeks.
questions.explanation: 1 week = 7 days. 2 weeks = 2 × 7 = 14 days.
questions.socraticHint: Double 7: 7 + 7 = ?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Two-week school holiday mid-term breaks.

questions.prompt: Which month of the year has the fewest days (28 or 29 days)?
questions.explanation: February is the shortest month with 28 days (29 in a leap year).
questions.socraticHint: Which month comes between January and March?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Calendar oddities explained in CBC mathematics.

questions.prompt: Grandmaster Challenge: Zawadi's school Term 1 lasts for 13 weeks. If 8 weeks have already passed, how many weeks are left before the April school holidays?
questions.explanation: 13 weeks - 8 weeks = 5 weeks remaining.
questions.socraticHint: Subtract 8 from 13: 13 - 8 = ?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Kenya Ministry of Education term dates guide all primary schools.

questions.prompt: What is the official currency of Kenya?
questions.explanation: Kenya's official currency is the Kenyan Shilling (KES or Ksh).
questions.socraticHint: What money do you use to buy mandazi at the school canteen?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Kenyan Shilling is recognized across East Africa.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is the largest Kenyan coin in regular circulation?
questions.explanation: The 20-shilling coin is the highest-value coin in circulation in Kenya.
questions.socraticHint: Which coin is made with two rings of metal (bi-metallic brass and nickel)?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: The 20-shilling coin features a prominent elephant on the new generation currency.

questions.prompt: True or False: Two 50-shilling notes have the exact same total value as one 100-shilling note.
questions.explanation: True! 50 + 50 = 100 shillings.
questions.socraticHint: Add 50 and 50 together: does it equal 100?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Exchanging smaller notes for larger ones at local banks and dukas.

questions.prompt: If you have five 20-shilling coins, how much money do you have in total? KES [BLANK]
questions.explanation: 5 × 20 = 100 shillings.
questions.socraticHint: Count by 20s five times: 20, 40, 60, 80, ...?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Five 20-shilling coins equal exactly one 100-shilling note.

questions.prompt: What is the highest value banknote in Kenya?
questions.explanation: The 1,000-shilling note is the largest denomination note in Kenyan currency.
questions.socraticHint: Which note is reddish-brown and features the Kenyan Parliament and buffalo?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: The 1,000-shilling note (known informally as "thou" or "kapa") is used for larger transactions.

questions.prompt: Match each banknote denomination with its equivalent combination of smaller notes:
questions.socraticHint: Check the multiplication: 2×100=200, 5×100=500, 2×500=1000.
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Money conversion skills are used daily at bus stages and markets.

questions.prompt: True or False: Ten 10-shilling coins equal KES 100.
questions.explanation: True! 10 × 10 = 100 shillings.
questions.socraticHint: Count in tens 10 times: 10, 20, 30, ... 100!
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Coin counting at church offerings and school canteen queues.

questions.prompt: Arrange these Kenyan banknotes in order of value from lowest to highest:
questions.socraticHint: Order the numbers printed on the corners of the notes: 50, 100, 200, 500.
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Financial literacy starts with clear denomination identification.

questions.prompt: Baraka has one KES 50 note and three KES 10 coins in his pocket. How much money does Baraka have altogether?
questions.explanation: Note: 50 shillings. Coins: 3 × 10 = 30 shillings. Total: 50 + 30 = 80 shillings.
questions.socraticHint: First add the coins (10 + 10 + 10 = 30). Then add to the 50-shilling note (50 + 30).
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Everyday pocket money calculation.

questions.prompt: How many KES 100 notes are needed to make KES 500? You need [BLANK] notes.
questions.socraticHint: Count by 100s up to 500: 100, 200, 300, 400, 500. How many counts?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Cash transactions in local trading centers.

questions.prompt: Which combination of coins and notes equals exactly KES 250?

options.text: One KES 200 note and one KES 50 note
Two KES 100 notes and one KES 20 coin

questions.explanation: 200 + 50 = 250 shillings.
questions.socraticHint: Add 200 + 50: does it equal 250?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Smart cash management in shopping.

questions.prompt: Wanjiku wants to buy a storybook costing KES 150. She has one KES 100 note and two KES 20 coins. Does she have enough money to buy the book?

questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Budgeting and saving before purchase.

questions.explanation: 100 - 65 = 35 shillings change.
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Daily milk shopping in Kenyan neighbourhoods.

questions.prompt: Juma buys a loaf of bread for KES 60 and a packet of biscuits for KES 30. What is his total bill?
questions.explanation: 60 + 30 = 90 shillings.
questions.socraticHint: Add 60 and 30: 6 tens + 3 tens = 9 tens (90).
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Buying bread and snacks for school breaks.

questions.prompt: True or False: If you buy an item costing KES 180 and pay with a KES 200 note, your change is KES 20.
questions.explanation: True! 200 - 180 = 20 shillings.
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Accurate change calculation builds honesty in transactions.

questions.prompt: Mwangi had KES 500. He spent KES 350 on school shoes at Gikomba. How much money does he have left? KES [BLANK]
questions.explanation: 500 - 350 = 150 shillings remaining.
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Gikomba market shoe purchases.

questions.prompt: At a vegetable stall, Mama Chebet buys tomatoes for KES 50, onions for KES 40, and sukuma wiki for KES 20. What is the total cost?

questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Fresh vegetable stew ingredient shopping.

questions.prompt: Match each purchase with the correct change received from a KES 500 note:

questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Handling 500-shilling notes in business transactions.

questions.prompt: True or False: If an exercise book costs KES 25, then 4 exercise books will cost KES 100.
questions.explanation: True! 4 × 25 = 100 shillings.
questions.socraticHint: Add 25 four times: 25 + 25 = 50, and 50 + 50 = 100.
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Buying exercise books for the term.

questions.prompt: Arrange the steps for calculating your change when buying goods at a kiosk:

options.text: Add up the cost of all items to find the total bill
Hand your payment note to the shopkeeper
Subtract the total bill from the note you paid
Count the change handed back to ensure it matches your calculation

questions.explanation: Find total bill, hand money, calculate expected change, and verify the received change.
questions.socraticHint: What do you need to know before handing over your money?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Financial vigilance and consumer awareness in CBC.

questions.prompt: A passenger boards a matatu in Nakuru. The fare is KES 70. She gives the conductor a KES 200 note. What change should the conductor give back?
questions.explanation: 200 - 70 = 130 shillings change.
questions.socraticHint: Subtract 70 from 200: 200 - 70 = ?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Commuter matatu fare calculation.

questions.prompt: Brian saves KES 20 in his piggy bank every day. After 5 days, Brian has saved a total of KES [BLANK].
questions.explanation: 5 days × KES 20 = KES 100.
questions.socraticHint: Multiply 5 by 20 (or count by 20s five times).
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Cultivating a savings habit among young pupils.

questions.prompt: A customer buys 2 kg of sugar at KES 140 per kg. How much does she pay in total?
questions.explanation: 2 kg × KES 140 = KES 280.
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Sugar pricing per kilogram in local shops.

questions.prompt: Grandmaster Challenge: Amina went shopping with a KES 1,000 note. She bought a 2 kg packet of wheat flour for KES 190, cooking oil for KES 310, and washing soap for KES 150. How much change did she bring home?
questions.storyScenario: Multi-step shopping budget challenge with a 1,000 shilling note.
questions.explanation: Total spent: 190 + 310 + 150 = KES 650. Change: 1,000 - 650 = KES 350!
questions.socraticHint: Step 1: Add 190 + 310 = 500. Add 150 = 650 total spent. Step 2: Subtract 650 from 1,000.

questions.prompt: What tool should you use to draw a neat, straight line in your exercise book?

questions.socraticHint: Which instrument has a straight plastic or wooden edge with numbers on it?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: 30-cm plastic rulers in school geometry sets.

questions.prompt: A straight line that stands upright like a flagpole is called a:
questions.explanation: A line that stands straight up from bottom to top is a vertical line (mstari wa wima).
questions.socraticHint: Think of standing tall like a tree or pole.
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: The school flagpole standing upright in the parade ground.

questions.prompt: True or False: The edge of a flat classroom desk is a horizontal straight line.
questions.explanation: True! A line lying flat from side to side is a horizontal line (mstari wa mlalo).
questions.socraticHint: Does the desk edge lie flat like a sleeping person or stand up like a tree?
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Identifying geometric features on classroom furniture.

questions.prompt: A straight line that leans like a ladder against a wall is called a [BLANK] line.
questions.explanation: A line leaning at an angle is called a slanting (or diagonal) line.
questions.socraticHint: Starts with "sl-". It leans to the side.
questions.kenyanCulturalContext: Timber roof trusses on rural houses lean at slanting angles.

questions.prompt: Which of the following objects has straight edges all around it?
